## Page 1


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Categorification of Chemical Reactions:
a bottom-up tower from stoichiometry to quantum structure
Prepared for Chemical Reaction Networks in Hawai‘i 2026
Kyunghoon HAN 1,∗
1Department of Physics and Materials Science, University of Luxembourg, Luxembourg City,
Luxembourg
∗Correspondence: kyunghoon.h@gmail.com
Abstract
Chemistry is full of rules with exceptions. The octet rule, Hess’s Law, detailed
balance, and orbital symmetry selection rules all carry disclaimers that must be
memorised separately. These exceptions share a common cause: they arise when
a question belonging to a richer level of mathematical structure is posed using the
vocabulary of a simpler one — a level incompleteness.
This monograph makes the levels explicit.
It constructs a canonical tower
of nine categorical levels spanning stoichiometry, thermochemistry, equilibrium,
kinetics, electron-pushing mechanisms, stereochemistry, potential energy surfaces,
electronic structure, and all-particle quantum mechanics. The tower is mathematically
engineered bottom-up, at each stage by pairs of reactions that are physically distinct
yet indistinguishable at the previous level; the minimal categorical extension resolving
each such ambiguity is provably unique, certified by a non-trivial cokernel in an
automorphism exact sequence, and applied to reaction networks recovers Feinberg’s
deficiency theorems as homological corollaries.
The exact tower has a perpendicular dimension: every machine-learning model for
chemistry — yield predictors, neural kinetic networks, equivariant force fields, learned
wavefunctions — is a morphism in the parametric Para-enrichment of one specific
tower level, with equivariance and thermodynamic consistency following as universal
properties rather than architectural choices, and three architectural incompleteness
results — Eyring, Wegscheider, and topological output-type gaps — applying to the
current published literature.
The framework descends to running code in the final chapter, which constructs an
operational functor from a Para-enriched product of the first four tower levels into
the Kleisli category of the probabilistic sub-monad of Haskell IO, instantiated as
a working stochastic simulator of the Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction — the
first published Kleisli semantics of the Gillespie next-reaction method and the first
application of the Para construction outside machine learning.
The passage to all-particle quantum mechanics — realising the Born–Oppenheimer
approximation as the classical limit of a continuous field of 𝐶∗-algebras — remains the
deepest open construction, with four candidate conjectures, including Woolley–Primas,
whose obstructions the framework makes specific.

Acknowledgements
As a mathematician by training, I found chemistry difficult to study: the field is full of
exceptions to its rules, and the exceptions are typically presented as separate facts to
memorise rather than as consequences of any underlying structure. This manuscript is the
record of an effort to learn chemistry well enough that it would make sense to me during
my PhD in the Theoretical Chemical Physics group at the University of Luxembourg.
The categorical structure developed here was first sketched in the group’s Theoretical
Minimum sessions for incoming PhD students in 2021. From then to now, my colleagues, the
group leader Prof. Dr. Alexandre Tkatchenko, and my PhD supervisor Dr. Joshua T. Berry-
man have shown extraordinary patience in helping me understand the chemistry and physics
of complex molecules. The phrase level incompleteness, which threads through every
chapter of this monograph, was suggested by Prof. Tkatchenko.
Many colleagues absorbed the cost of my limited chemistry background along the way.
Dr. Ariadni Boziki took the time to walk me through how molecular vibrations work;
Dr. Miguel Gallegos showed me why chemical exceptions are interesting in their own right;
Sergio Suárez Dou gave me much-needed insight into the behaviour of biomolecules. I
thank Dr. Florian Brünig of the same group for his feedback on the introductory chapter of
this work.
Whatever errors and infelicities remain in the chemistry are entirely my own, and despite the
generous teaching of everyone listed above I remain, by professional chemists’ standards,
still learning the field.

§1. Introduction
§1.1. Rules, exceptions, and what they signal
Chemistry is a quantitative subject built on exact rules with long lists of exceptions. Hess’s
Law [1, 2, 3]; detailed balance, in both its physical-chemistry form [4, 5, 6, 7] and its
reaction-network form [8, 9, 10]; the Arrhenius equation [11, 12, 13]; the Woodward–
Hoffmann rules [14, 15, 16] — each is a sharp mathematical statement, each holds “in
most cases,” and the corrections are memorised separately from the rules themselves. The
position of this monograph is that chemistry’s rules sit at definite mathematical levels; that
the levels form a canonical ladder; and that the principal class of exceptions to those rules
is a level incompleteness, the use of tools from one rung to answer a question that belongs
to another.
A hydrogen atom in the reacting bond of an organic molecule replaced by deuterium —
twice the nuclear mass, the same electronic structure — slows the reaction, and the ratio
of the rate for the hydrogen-bearing compound to the rate for its deuterium analogue is
the primary kinetic isotope effect (𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷) [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Classical transition-state
theory [12, 22, 23, 13] computes this ratio from a Boltzmann factor whose activation energy
is shifted between isotopologues by the harmonic zero-point-energy difference of the carbon–
hydrogen and carbon–deuterium stretching modes, and for hydrogen transfer at laboratory
temperatures the resulting ratio cannot exceed approximately seven [24, 25, 20]. The double
mutant L546A/L754A of soybean lipoxygenase-1, by contrast, gives 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷= 661 ± 27,
essentially constant across six temperatures from 5 to 50 ◦C [26] — nearly two orders of
magnitude above the textbook ceiling.
The factor of one hundred between the two values is not, despite appearances, the signature
of a tower-level mismatch. Both calculations live at the same geometric level L5 (§8);
they differ only in how much of that level’s data is actually used — a barrier height and
harmonic vibrations at the saddle in the textbook formula, versus the full multidimensional
potential surface, semiclassical tunnelling paths along it, and vibronically nonadiabatic
proton-coupled electron transfer in the complete calculation. The L7 chapter (§10) records
this case as a careful caveat: large kinetic isotope effects do not, by themselves, force a
higher tower level, even when they spectacularly exceed textbook estimates. A different and
sharper kind of incompleteness — in which a question genuinely cannot be answered at
one level because the structural data required for it first appears at a higher one — is what
motivates this monograph. Three textbook examples of that kind, the cleanest available,
are recorded next.
Three level incompletenesses, stated plainly
Spontaneity versus rate. Diamond is thermodynamically unstable relative to graphite
at all laboratory temperatures (Δ𝐺< 0), so the conversion is spontaneous. Yet
no observable conversion occurs on any human timescale.
“Spontaneous” is a
thermodynamic statement about the sign of the free-energy change; “immeasurably
slow” is a kinetic statement about the activation barrier. The confusion is not chemistry
failing; it is two different questions being conflated.
Rate law versus mechanism. Under excess nucleophile, the bimolecular substitution
13


## Page 14


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
of CH3Br by OH– becomes pseudo-first-order in substrate, and its rate constant can be
tuned to match that of the genuinely first-order solvolysis of (CH3)3CBr. Kinetically
the two reactions are then indistinguishable — yet the solvolysis yields a racemic
mixture at the carbon centre while the bimolecular substitution inverts configuration.
The distinction belongs to mechanism: a concerted backside displacement against
a stepwise unimolecular ionisation, two electron-pushing pathways that no rate law
sees.
Geometry versus electronic structure. The retinal chromophore in rhodopsin
isomerises from 11-cis to all-trans in approximately 200 fs after photon absorption —
a timescale no model of thermal barrier-crossing on a single potential-energy surface
can reproduce [27, 28, 29]. The reaction passes through a conical intersection: a seam
of nuclear configurations where two electronic surfaces become degenerate and the
Born–Oppenheimer approximation breaks down. This is a phenomenon of electronic
topology, invisible to any description that works with a single smooth energy surface.
Chemistry’s rules are not wrong. Hess’s Law, detailed balance, the rate equation, the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules — each is exactly correct at the level of mathematical structure
for which it is defined. The principal class of exceptions, of which the three examples
above are the cleanest, arises when a question from one level is posed with the tools of a
different one.
The central claim of this monograph
The principal class of exceptions to a chemical rule is a level incompleteness: it arises
when a question that belongs to level L𝑘+1 is posed using only the tools of L𝑘. The

§1.2. The tower, built bottom-up
The tower is not constructed by surveying chemistry and assigning phenomena to levels. It
is forced, bottom-up, by an explicit argument at each step: there exist pairs of reactions that
are physically distinct but indistinguishable at level 𝑘, and the unique minimal categorical
extension that separates them is level 𝑘+1.
For instance, the concerted-versus-stepwise pair at phosphorus — identity methoxyl
exchange at methyl ethylphenylphosphinate [30], proceeding either through a single trigonal-
bipyramidal transition state (SN2-P) or through a discrete pentacoordinate intermediate
(TBI) by addition-elimination — is a forcing argument for the L3 →L4 step. At L3,
reactions are morphisms in a Markov category: their entire content is a rate law and a
14


## Page 15


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
net stoichiometric change. Under the quasi-steady-state reduction on TBI valid in the
experimentally relevant regime, both mechanisms yield the same bimolecular rate law
𝜆= 𝑘𝑥MeO−𝑥substrate and the same net stoichiometric change; they are the same morphism
at L3. Level L4 introduces a richer notion of morphism — a double-pushout (DPO)
derivation in the category of labelled molecular graphs — so that a morphism at L4
is an electron-pushing mechanism, not merely a rate law. The concerted pathway is a
single DPO span (one elementary bond rearrangement, no internal intermediate); the
stepwise pathway is two composable DPO spans bracketing TBI as an internal species.
The permutation swapping one for the other is a non-trivial element of coker(𝜑4), where
𝜑4 : Aut(L4) →Aut(L3) is the restriction map: it is an automorphism of the kinetic level
that lifts to no automorphism of the mechanistic one. That is the proof that L4 is necessary
given L3.
The forcing tool
The precise instrument is the automorphism sequence
1 −→ker 𝜑𝑘−→Aut(L𝑘)
𝜑𝑘
−−−→Aut(L𝑘−1) −→coker𝜑𝑘−→1.
A non-trivial coker𝜑𝑘witnesses the existence of automorphisms of L𝑘−1 that cannot
be lifted to L𝑘: the permutation swapping the two reactions in the forcing pair is
such an automorphism. Each level is the unique minimal extension with non-trivial
coker𝜑𝑘for the forcing pair listed in Table 4.
The motivating axis throughout is reaction networks, not isolated reactions. A network
at level 𝑘is a finite directed graph whose vertices are complexes and whose edges are
labelled by morphisms in L𝑘; open networks, exposed to their environment at specified
interface species, compose by pushout. This is the framework of Baez and Pollard [31]
at the kinetic level, extending the symmetric monoidal Petri-net language of Meseguer
and Montanari [32]; the present work applies it at every tower level. The forcing pairs are
always parallel reactions that the previous level cannot distinguish: parallel reactions with
different Δ𝐻force L0 →L1; same Δ𝐻but different Δ𝑆forces L1 →L2; same Δ𝐺but
different rate forces L2 →L3; same rate law but different mechanism forces L3 →L4,
and so on up the tower. Each chapter closes with worked examples drawn from systems
where the new datum at that level is most cleanly exhibited; the examples are deliberately
level-specific, since no single reaction sharpens every transition equally and forcing one to
do every job would flatten what each is meant to show. Table 4 records, for each transition
L𝑘−1 →L𝑘, the concrete pair of physically distinct reactions that L𝑘−1 conflates and L𝑘
separates; the corresponding worked example is given in the chapter introducing L𝑘.

Each summary below records the categorical structure added at L𝑘and closes with the
forcing pair that opens L𝑘+1.
Chapter 2 — L0, stoichiometry.
The base level is the free permutative category L0(𝑃)
on a Petri net 𝑃: objects are complexes in the free commutative monoid N[S] over
chemical species, morphisms are formal reactions, composition is sequential chaining, and
the monoidal product is mixture. The language is that of Meseguer and Montanari [32];

Four coloured environments serve mathematical and chemical audiences simultaneously
throughout: green for chemical content, blue for categorical statements, orange for forcing
pairs, and purple for the conceptual connections between them.
§1.4. A brief guide to categorical language
This subsection introduces the categorical vocabulary; readers comfortable with enriched
category theory may proceed directly to Chapter 2.
Category theory provides the mathematical grammar of this programme. The compact
dictionary below is aimed at readers fluent in chemistry or physics but new to categorical
ideas; every term is paired with its chemical meaning and a concrete example.
Category.
A category C consists of:
• a collection of objects — the states or species pools under study;
• for each ordered pair of objects 𝑋,𝑌, a set Hom(𝑋,𝑌) of morphisms from 𝑋to 𝑌,
i.e. all processes or transformations that lead from state 𝑋to state 𝑌;
• a composition law: if 𝑓∈Hom(𝑋,𝑌) and 𝑔∈Hom(𝑌, 𝑍), their composite
𝑔◦𝑓∈Hom(𝑋, 𝑍) is the process obtained by performing 𝑓first and then 𝑔;

• for each object 𝑋, an identity morphism id𝑋∈Hom(𝑋, 𝑋) — the trivial “do-nothing”
process;
satisfying associativity (ℎ◦𝑔) ◦𝑓= ℎ◦(𝑔◦𝑓) and unitality id𝑌◦𝑓= 𝑓= 𝑓◦id𝑋[36, 37].
Chemical meaning. Objects are complexes — formal non-negative integer combinations
of chemical species such as CH4 + 2 O2. The term complex is standard in chemical
reaction network theory [10]: it denotes precisely one side of a balanced reaction equation.
Morphisms are reactions or multi-step pathways between complexes. The identity idu is
the “no reaction” process on complex u; composition 𝑟2 ◦𝑟1 chains two steps sequentially.
A key example: 𝐵R. The real line forms a one-object category 𝐵R with a single object ∗
and one morphism 𝑎∈R for each real number, with composition 𝑏◦𝑎:= 𝑎+ 𝑏. Think of
𝐵R as a single node with one directed arrow per real number: concatenating two arrows
means adding their labels. A functor 𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R assigns to every reaction a real
number (e.g. enthalpy Δ𝐻) that is automatically additive along sequential and parallel steps
— this is the categorical formulation of Hess’s Law, developed fully at L1.
Functor.
A functor 𝐹: C →D is a structure-preserving map between categories: it
sends each object 𝑋to an object 𝐹(𝑋) and each morphism 𝑓: 𝑋→𝑌to a morphism
𝐹( 𝑓) : 𝐹(𝑋) →𝐹(𝑌), respecting composition (𝐹(𝑔◦𝑓) = 𝐹(𝑔) ◦𝐹( 𝑓)) and identities
(𝐹(id𝑋) = id𝐹(𝑋)).
Chemical meaning. A functor from the reaction category into 𝐵R is a consistent numerical
scoring of reactions: it assigns a real number to each elementary step in a way that the score
of any sequential or parallel combination is the sum of the individual scores. Enthalpy
(Δ𝐻), Gibbs free energy (Δ𝐺), and entropy change (Δ𝑆) are all consistent scorings of
this kind — each is a functor from the appropriate tower level into 𝐵R. The functoriality
conditions (𝐹(𝑔◦𝑓) = 𝐹(𝑔) ◦𝐹( 𝑓) and 𝐹(id) = 0) are precisely the additivity and
trivial-process conditions these thermodynamic quantities must satisfy.
Monoidal category.
A monoidal category (C, ⊗, 𝐼) is a category equipped with a tensor
product ⊗: C × C →C combining two objects or morphisms “in parallel”, a unit object 𝐼
satisfying 𝐼⊗𝑋 𝑋 𝑋⊗𝐼, and coherent isomorphisms (𝑋⊗𝑌) ⊗𝑍

identity maps, the category is strict monoidal [37].

The unit object is the empty mixture 0 ∈N[S]. Since addition in N[S] is already strictly
associative and 0 + u = u, the associator and unitors are identity maps: the tensor is strict
monoidal for chemical mixtures.
Symmetric monoidal category.
A monoidal category is symmetric if there is a coherent
family of isomorphisms 𝜎𝑋,𝑌: 𝑋⊗𝑌

the symmetry isomorphism is physically mandatory. All symmetric monoidal categories
in this chapter are permutative: symmetric strict monoidal. In this manuscript an acronym

Free construction.
A free object on given generators is the most general object of its
type built from those generators, subject to no relations beyond those forced by the axioms
of the type.
Example. The free group on one generator is Z — the integers with addition. Starting from
the generator +1 and its inverse −1, all combinations by addition are formed; no shortcut
is imposed (“+1 applied three times” is never identified with “+2 applied twice” unless
the group axioms force it, which they do not). The result is the smallest group containing
the generator, with no redundant identifications [37]. The key property is universality:
once +1 is sent to any element 𝑔of a target group 𝐺, the entire homomorphism Z →𝐺is
uniquely forced (𝑛↦→𝑛𝑔).
Chemical meaning. No equivalences between distinct reaction labels are imposed beyond
those forced by the permutative axioms. Two routes 𝑟1, 𝑟2 with the same reactant and
product complexes are kept as distinct morphisms at L0: no physical identification — same
Δ𝐻, same rate, same mechanism — is made until the tower level at which that information
first becomes available. Once you fix where each species and each reaction label map in
a target category, the entire strict symmetric monoidal functor out of L0(𝑃) is uniquely
forced (Theorem 2.14): there is no modelling choice left.
Commutative diagram.
A diagram of objects and morphisms commutes when every
directed path between the same two objects yields the same composite morphism. The
following example shows what this means in stoichiometric terms.

Petri net.
Petri nets were introduced by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 as a mathematical
framework for concurrent processes [38]. Places hold tokens (molecular populations
of species) and transitions represent reactions, consuming tokens from input places and
depositing tokens into output places according to stoichiometric arc multiplicities. This
is exactly the combinatorial skeleton of stoichiometric chemistry [32, 39]. The precise
definition, a worked chemical example, and the construction of L0(𝑃) from a Petri net are
given in §2.2.
The central gain of the categorical framework
A category is a precise language for processes that compose sequentially and run
in parallel. A functor is a consistent numerical scoring of those processes. Once a
thermodynamic or kinetic quantity is identified as a functor from the reaction category
into an appropriate target, its core properties — additivity along sequences, additivity
over parallel reactions — become theorems rather than separate postulates.
Each higher tower level adds a specific categorical extension to the previous level: a
new functor, an enrichment of the morphism category by a symmetry, a geometric
decoration, a topological invariant, or (at the final step) a deformation of the algebraic
structure itself. The taxonomy of the six extension types that arise across the present
tower is recorded in §10.8; each is forced at its level by a concrete pair of reactions the
previous level cannot distinguish. Freeness means no equivalences between reactions
are imposed beyond those forced by the algebra of mixtures; every reaction is kept
distinct unless explicitly identified for a physical reason.
Reading the tower as an ML foundation. Each level L𝑘admits a perpendicular Para
enrichment LPara
𝑘
of parametric equivariant maps (Chapter 11). The exact level L𝑘is
recovered as the zero-parameter limit of LPara
𝑘
; architectures for machine-learning mod-
els of chemistry — yield predictors, equivariant force fields, learned wavefunctions —
are lax algebra morphisms in LPara
𝑘
, with equivariance and thermodynamic-consistency
constraints following from universal properties rather than from architectural choices.
In summary: a stoichiometric scheme equipped with sequential composition (one
reaction following another), parallel composition (reactions in independent mixtures),
and order-independence of mixtures is the defining data of a symmetric monoidal
category; assigning numerical chemical content is providing a functor; starting from
the most general such structure is taking the free construction.
Monad.
A monad on a category C is an endofunctor 𝑇: C →C (a functor whose source
and target are the same category) equipped with two natural transformations (coherent
families of morphisms, one per object): a unit 𝜂: idC ⇒𝑇that injects each object 𝑋
into a 𝑇-decorated version 𝑇(𝑋), and a multiplication 𝜇: 𝑇◦𝑇⇒𝑇that collapses two
layers of decoration into one. These satisfy associativity (𝜇◦𝑇𝜇= 𝜇◦𝜇𝑇) and unit laws
(𝜇◦𝑇𝜂= 𝜇◦𝜂𝑇= id𝑇) [37, 36].
Operational meaning. A monad packages a kind of “effect” or “extra structure” that maps
can carry while remaining composable — randomness, state, partial information, time,
or symmetry. 𝑇(𝑋) is to be read as “a computation that ultimately yields a value of type
𝑋while carrying the effect of 𝑇”; 𝜂produces a trivially-decorated value, and 𝜇is what
makes two effectful computations compose into a single one.
The Kleisli category. The natural setting for 𝑇-effectful computations is the Kleisli category

𝑔• 𝑓:= 𝜇𝑍◦𝑇(𝑔) ◦𝑓: 𝑋→𝑇(𝑍),
lifting 𝑔to act on 𝑇(𝑌) via 𝑇’s functoriality, then flattening the resulting 𝑇(𝑇(𝑍)) via 𝜇.
Key example: Kl(𝐼𝑂). Haskell’s 𝐼𝑂monad packages every interaction with the outside
world — file reads, terminal output, random-number generation — into the type 𝐼𝑂(𝑋)
of computations that eventually produce an 𝑋, possibly with side effects on the way. A
morphism in Kl(𝐼𝑂) from 𝑋to 𝑌is then a function 𝑋→𝐼𝑂(𝑌): a procedure that, given
an input, may consume random bits or perform other side effects and yields an output.
Stochastic simulation of a reaction network is exactly such a procedure: the operational
functor Φop of Chapter 12 lands in the Kleisli category of the probabilistic sub-monad of
𝐼𝑂— the sub-monad generated by pseudo-random-number sampling.

Categorification of Chemical Reactions
§2. L0: The Stoichiometric Level
The simplest possible question about a chemical reaction is: what goes in and what
comes out? Before energy, before time, before geometry, before mechanism — purely the
bookkeeping of species consumed and produced.
Three structural features are present at this barest level of description:
(a) Steps compose. If reaction 𝑟1 produces a species that reaction 𝑟2 consumes, the two
steps together form a new composite reaction 𝑟2 ◦𝑟1.
(b) Steps run in parallel. Two reactions that do not interfere with each other can be
combined into a joint process 𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2, run simultaneously.
(c) The ordering of independent species is irrelevant. There is no intrinsic left-to-right
order in a mixture; 𝐴+ 𝐵and 𝐵+ 𝐴describe the same physical system.
Expressing these structural features in a precise mathematical language — rather than
leaving them as implicit chemical common sense — makes it possible to prove rigorously
which properties follow from which hypotheses and to compare different levels of chemical
description on equal footing. The language appropriate to features (a)–(c) is that of
symmetric monoidal categories: mathematical structures carrying exactly the sequential,
parallel, and order-irrelevant composition grammar those features demand. This language
was established by Meseguer and Montanari [32] for Petri nets, and extended into a
compositional framework for open reaction networks by Baez and Pollard [31]. The exact
tower backbone developed in this chapter and the subsequent ones admits a perpendicular
Para-enrichment dimension (Chapter 11, building on Gavranović et al. [33]) which places
machine-learning models for chemistry [40, 41] on an exact mathematical foundation as
parametric equivariant maps over the same tower levels.
A brief categorical glossary, aimed at readers fluent in chemistry or physics but new to
category theory, is provided in §1.4.
§2.1. Species, complexes, and the stoichiometric monoid
Stoichiometry is the branch of chemistry concerned with the quantitative relationships
between species in a chemical reaction: how many molecules of each substance are
consumed, and how many are produced. For a mathematician, it is the study of the additive
structure of molecular populations — which integer combinations of named species can
appear as the left- or right-hand side of a balanced equation, and how those combinations
pool together. No energy, no dynamics, no geometry: purely the arithmetic of molecular
counts.
The algebraic object capturing this arithmetic is the free commutative monoid on the set of
species.
Definition 2.1 (Species and the stoichiometric monoid). Fix a finite set S of chemical
species (e.g. S = {H2O, CH4, O2, CO2}). Species are abstract labels at this level; no
geometric, electronic, or energetic information is attached.
The stoichiometric monoid is the free commutative monoid on S:

Remark 2.2 (Relation to prior mathematical treatments of stoichiometry). The stoichiometric

been the standard mathematical representation of stoichiometry since the foundational
work of Feinberg [42, 10] and Horn–Jackson [8]. Meseguer–Montanari [32] recognise that
Petri net semantics naturally produces free commutative monoids, and Baez–Master [43]
exploit this structure for open Petri nets. The present treatment differs in making the
universal property of N[S] the primary organising principle of the stoichiometric level,
rather than a computational convenience: every additive species observable — mass, atom

universal property, and the entire tower of functors in Chapters 3–10 is built by iterating
this observation upward. The stoichiometric matrix 𝑁is recovered as the linear-algebraic

What is a complex?
A complex is what chemists call one “side” of a balanced equation. For CH4 +2 O2 →
CO2 + 2 H2O, the reactant complex is 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2 and the product complex is
1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O, both elements of N[S].
The monoid operation is simply pooling:
(1 · CH4 + 2 · O2) + (1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O) = 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2 + 1 · CO2 + 2 · H2O.
This is the mathematical version of mixing two portions together. The reaction arrow

says: this pool transforms into that pool. The monoid carries no information about
whether or how the transformation occurs; that belongs to later levels of the tower.
Proposition 2.3 makes precise something a chemist already knows: once you decide
what numerical value to assign to each individual species (its mass, its atom count, its
standard enthalpy of formation, . . . ), the value for any complex is completely forced
— there is no choice. The total mass of 1 · CH4 + 2 · O2 is 𝑀(CH4) + 2 𝑀(O2) and
nothing else; the universal property is precisely the theorem that says this.
Universal properties are one of the central organising tools of category theory: MacLane [37]
identifies them as the concept that unifies free constructions, adjunctions, and limits, and
Riehl [36] shows systematically how they eliminate arbitrary choices from mathematical
definitions. The stoichiometric monoid N[S] is the universal receptacle for additive species
data: any quantity that is additive over species — mass, elemental composition, standard
enthalpy of formation — extends uniquely to all complexes via Proposition 2.3, with no
modelling freedom left. Moreover, the universal property of N[S] is the first in a chain:
the universal property of L0(𝑃) (Theorem 2.14) extends it one step further, from species
and complexes to reactions and their composites, and every subsequent tower level adds
one more universal property governing the next kind of chemical data.

Concretely: once you decide what value each species receives, the value of every
complex is completely determined — there is no freedom left.
This universal

Remark 2.4 (Rate constants are not species data). Rate constants are associated with
reactions, not with individual species, and so lie outside the scope of Proposition 2.3. The
universal property of N[S] applies to species-level assignments only. Rate-constant data
enters at L3 as part of the kinetic functor 𝐹𝑃, whose domain is the category of reactions
L0(𝑃), not the monoid of complexes N[S]; its universal property is Theorem 2.14.
§2.2. Petri nets: the categorical input data
This subsection gives the precise definition of a Petri net and establishes the category Petri
of all Petri nets. The raw data of a stoichiometric scheme is a finite list of species and a finite
list of reaction labels, each label carrying a source complex (reactants) and a target complex
(products) in N|S|. This structure is a Petri net, introduced by Carl Adam Petri in 1962 as
a mathematical framework for concurrent processes [38], and recognised by Meseguer–
Montanari to be the natural input data for free symmetric monoidal categories [32]. The
27


## Page 28


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
stoichiometric category L0(𝑃) is the free categorical structure generated by a Petri net
𝑃: one imposes no relations beyond those forced by the axioms of a symmetric monoidal
category. The free construction occupies §2.3.
Definition 2.5 (Petri net [38, 32, 39]). A Petri net is a quadruple 𝑃= (S, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) where
S is a finite set of species, R is a finite set of reaction labels, and 𝑠, 𝑡: R →N|S| assign
to each label 𝑟∈R its source complex 𝑠(𝑟) and target complex 𝑡(𝑟), with 𝑠(𝑟) ≠𝑡(𝑟) in
general.
A Petri net in chemistry: hydrogen combustion
Consider the net stoichiometry of hydrogen combustion:
2 H2 + O2
𝑟−−→2 H2O.
As a Petri net: S = {H2, O2, H2O}, R = {𝑟}, with
𝑠(𝑟) = 2 · H2 + 1 · O2 ∈N|S|,
𝑡(𝑟) = 2 · H2O ∈N|S|.
In the standard Petri net picture, each species is a place (a pool holding molecular
tokens) and each reaction is a transition (consuming tokens from its input places and
depositing tokens into its output places according to the stoichiometric coefficients).
The arc multiplicities (2, 1, 2) encode stoichiometry; the transition 𝑟has no internal
structure beyond its input and output counts.
What the Petri net captures. The stoichiometric ratios (2:1:2), the direction of
transformation, and the connectivity between species and reaction. Conservation
vectors can be computed from the stoichiometric matrix 𝑁alone (see §2.6): here,
hydrogen-atom balance gives 𝑤H = (2, 0, 2)⊤, confirming two H atoms in each H2
and two H atoms in each H2O.
What the Petri net deliberately omits.
• Energy: the standard enthalpy of combustion Δ𝐻◦= −484 kJ mol−1 [44] is not
part of 𝑃; it enters at L1.
• Rate: the pre-exponential factor and activation energy are absent; they enter at
L3.
• Mechanism: whether the reaction proceeds via radical intermediates (H, OH,
HO2) or in a single elementary step is invisible at L0; mechanism enters at L4.
• Geometry: bond lengths, angles, and three-dimensional structure are absent;
they enter at L5.
The Petri net is the skeletal description: the minimal combinatorial input from which
the categorical construction L0(𝑃) is built. Every additional piece of chemical
information corresponds to additional structure at a higher tower level.
Remark 2.6 (Reaction labels are named generators). R is a set of named generators, not a
set of ordered pairs of complexes. Two distinct labels 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R with 𝑠(𝑟1) = 𝑠(𝑟2) and
𝑡(𝑟1) = 𝑡(𝑟2) represent two different reactions between the same complexes — for instance,
two mechanistically distinct routes with the same net stoichiometry. The free construction
of §2.3 keeps them as distinct generators; no physical identification is imposed until a later
level.
Petri nets assemble into a category: one can map one network into another by translating
species and reaction labels while respecting stoichiometry, and these translations compose

in the obvious way. This categorical structure on Petri nets is established in Meseguer–
Montanari [32] and is needed for two reasons: it allows chemical networks to be compared
and translated systematically, and it ensures that the construction 𝑃↦→L0(𝑃) is itself a
functor between categories rather than an ad hoc assignment.
Definition 2.7 (The category Petri). Petri is the category whose objects are Petri nets and
whose morphisms 𝑓: 𝑃→𝑃′ are pairs ( 𝑓S, 𝑓R) of functions
𝑓S : S →S′,
𝑓R : R →R′,
satisfying the source–target compatibility conditions
𝑠′ ◦𝑓R = ¯𝑓S ◦𝑠,
𝑡′ ◦𝑓R = ¯𝑓S ◦𝑡,
where ¯𝑓S : N|S| →N|S′| is the unique monoid homomorphism extending 𝑓S (Proposi-
tion 2.3). Composition is componentwise; the identity on 𝑃is (idS, idR).
Remark 2.8 (What a Petri morphism does). A morphism 𝑓: 𝑃→𝑃′ translates species to
species and reaction labels to reaction labels, in a way that respects stoichiometry: if 𝑟has
source complex u in 𝑃, then 𝑓R(𝑟) has source complex ¯𝑓S(u) in 𝑃′, and similarly for targets.
Non-injectivity is permitted: a non-injective 𝑓S coarsens species (merging two species into
one); a non-injective 𝑓R equates two distinct reaction labels at the stoichiometric level. The
compatibility conditions are exactly what is needed for ¯𝑓S — the unique extension supplied
by Proposition 2.3 — to be well-defined on complexes built from the translated species.
§2.3. The stoichiometric category L0(𝑃)
The categorical language of §1.4 now assembles into a single construction. A permutative
category is a strict symmetric monoidal category: associativity and unit hold as strict
equalities, while the symmetry 𝜎𝑋,𝑌: 𝑋⊗𝑌→𝑌⊗𝑋remains a (possibly non-trivial)
isomorphism between two distinct objects. The category L0(𝑃) we construct is a skeletal
permutative category: in addition to the strict associativity and unit, the underlying object
monoid (N|S|, +, 0) is itself strictly commutative, so u + v = v + u holds as an equality of
objects, not merely as an isomorphism. This skeletal structure is forced on us by chemistry:
a mixture has no intrinsic ordering, so 𝐴+ 𝐵and 𝐵+ 𝐴must literally name the same
complex. The non-trivial symmetry 𝜎u,v : u + v →u + v then becomes an endomorphism
encoding the permutation data that a non-skeletal permutative category would store in
distinct objects.
A Petri net 𝑃provides the chemical generators of L0(𝑃): the species S generate the
objects (via N|S|), and the reaction labels R become the basic morphisms, each typed by
its source and target complex. The free skeletal permutative category on 𝑃is built from
these generators by closing under sequential composition, parallel tensor, and the structural
morphisms (identities and symmetries), imposing only the permutative axioms and no
additional chemical identifications. This is L0(𝑃).
Definition 2.9 (Stoichiometric category L0(𝑃)). Let 𝑃= (S, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) be a Petri net.
The stoichiometric category L0(𝑃) is the free permutative category on 𝑃[32, 39]: the
unique (up to strict symmetric monoidal equivalence) permutative category satisfying the
following.
(i) Objects. The object set is N|S|, with monoidal product u ⊗v := u + v and monoidal
unit 0. Since + is commutative in N|S|, the tensor is strictly commutative: u⊗v = v⊗u
as the same object. Associativity and unitality are also strict.

(ii) Generating morphisms. The morphisms of L0(𝑃) have two distinct origins.
• Chemical generators (input data). The reaction generators 𝑟: 𝑠(𝑟) →𝑡(𝑟) for
each 𝑟∈R, supplied by the Petri net 𝑃. These are the only chemical input.
• Structural morphisms (forced by the skeletal permutative structure). The identity
morphisms idu : u →u for each u ∈N|S|, and the symmetry endomorphisms
𝜎u,v : u + v →u + v for each pair u, v ∈N|S|. These are not chemical input;
they are forced on L0(𝑃) by the requirement that it be a skeletal permutative
category at all.
The symmetry 𝜎u,v is an endomorphism — not an isomorphism between two distinct
objects — because u + v = v + u as the same element of N|S|, the skeletal property
of item (i) above.
(iii) All morphisms. Closed under sequential composition 𝑔◦𝑓(when cod( 𝑓) = dom(𝑔),
which holds in general as chemistry demands it) and parallel tensor 𝑓⊗𝑔.
(iv) Relations. Morphisms are equivalence classes under the smallest congruence
compatible with ◦and ⊗generated by the permutative axioms: identity laws;
associativity of ◦; interchange (𝑔1 ⊗𝑔2) ◦( 𝑓1 ⊗𝑓2) = (𝑔1 ◦𝑓1) ⊗(𝑔2 ◦𝑓2); tensor
unit; involutivity of 𝜎; naturality of 𝜎; and the hexagon axiom (all defined in
Remark 2.10 below). No equation 𝑟1 ≡𝑟2 is imposed for distinct 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R, even if
𝑠(𝑟1) = 𝑠(𝑟2) and 𝑡(𝑟1) = 𝑡(𝑟2).
(v) Functoriality. A Petri morphism 𝑓= ( 𝑓S, 𝑓R) : 𝑃→𝑃′ induces a strict symmetric
monoidal functor L0( 𝑓) : L0(𝑃) →L0(𝑃′), acting as ¯𝑓S on objects and by
𝑟↦→𝑓R(𝑟) on generators, making L0 : Petri →PermCat a functor.
Here PermCat denotes the category whose objects are small skeletal permutative categories
(strict symmetric monoidal categories whose object monoid (ObC, ⊗, 𝐼) is itself strictly
commutative, matching the structure of L0(𝑃)) and whose morphisms are strict symmetric
monoidal functors.
Remark 2.10 (The permutative axioms: involutivity, naturality, hexagon). The three axioms
governing the symmetry morphisms 𝜎in Definition 2.9(iv) are standard in the theory
of symmetric monoidal categories [45, 37]; we spell them out explicitly for readers
encountering them for the first time.
• Involutivity. 𝜎v,u ◦𝜎u,v = idu+v. Swapping the order of u and v twice returns to the
original arrangement.
Chemically: reordering a mixture and then reordering it back leaves it unchanged.
• Naturality. For any morphisms 𝑓: u →u′ and 𝑔: v →v′,
𝜎u′,v′ ◦( 𝑓⊗𝑔) = (𝑔⊗𝑓) ◦𝜎u,v.
Reordering before or after running two reactions in parallel gives the same result.
Chemically: it does not matter whether you relabel species before or after performing
the reactions — the stoichiometric outcome is identical.
• Hexagon axiom. For all complexes u, v, w,
𝜎u, v+w = (idv ⊗𝜎u,w) ◦(𝜎u,v ⊗idw).

The name comes from the hexagonal commutative diagram the equation generates.
It says that swapping u past the combined pool v + w is the same as swapping u past

Chemically: reordering one component past a mixture of two others can be done in a

In a non-skeletal permutative category, the symmetry 𝜎𝑋,𝑌: 𝑋⊗𝑌→𝑌⊗𝑋runs between
distinct objects, and involutivity composes the two arrows to land back at 𝑋⊗𝑌. In the

and involutivity says it is its own inverse: 𝜎u,v generates a Z/2-action on Hom(u+v, u+v)
rather than collapsing to the identity.
Remark 2.11 (The symmetry morphisms and coherence). In a non-skeletal symmetric
monoidal category, the symmetry 𝜎𝐴,𝐵: 𝐴⊗𝐵
∼
−−→𝐵⊗𝐴is an isomorphism between two
distinct objects 𝐴⊗𝐵and 𝐵⊗𝐴. In L0(𝑃), because N|S| is strictly commutative, u + v
and v + u are literally the same object, so 𝜎u,v is an endomorphism — an arrow from a
complex back to itself — rather than an isomorphism between two different complexes.
Despite living in Hom(u + v, u + v), 𝜎u,v is not the identity morphism idu+v: it is a
non-trivial endomorphism, the involutive generator of a Z/2-action on the hom-space. This
distinction matters for functors: a strict symmetric monoidal functor 𝐹: L0(𝑃) →C into a
target satisfying the hypothesis of Theorem 2.14 (object monoid strictly commutative) must
send 𝜎u,v to the symmetry 𝜎C
𝐹(u),𝐹(v), which is itself an endomorphism of 𝐹(u) ⊗𝐹(v).
That target endomorphism may be trivial (as in the Baez–Master CMC, Remark 2.17) or
non-trivial; L0(𝑃) maps coherently into both kinds of skeletal permutative target.
Remark 2.12 (No additional chemical relations). The only relations in L0(𝑃) are the
permutative axioms of Definition 2.9(iv). No equation 𝑟1 ≡𝑟2 is ever imposed between
distinct reaction labels: two routes sharing the same source and target complexes remain
distinct morphisms, kept apart by their names alone. Any physical identification — same
enthalpy change, same mechanism, same rate law — must be imposed explicitly at a higher
level of the tower, where the relevant structure is available to make such an identification
meaningful. In this sense L0(𝑃) is the most general stoichiometric category consistent
with the Petri net 𝑃: it retains every distinction that stoichiometry alone cannot collapse.
Example 2.13 (L0 of a three-reaction network). Let S = {𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶} and 𝑟1 : 𝐴→𝐵,
𝑟2 : 𝐵→𝐴, 𝑟3 : 𝐴+𝐵→𝐶.
Sequential composition. 𝑟2 ◦𝑟1 : 𝐴→𝐴is well-typed (𝑡(𝑟1) = 𝑠(𝑟2) = 𝐵) and is not
equal to id𝐴: no permutative axiom identifies a composite of two generating reactions with
an identity.

§2.4. The universal property of L0(𝑃)
A strict symmetric monoidal functor out of L0(𝑃) is the mathematical notion of a consistent
assignment of chemical content to a network: it sends species to objects of the target

sequential composition and parallel tensor. The universal property of L0(𝑃) says that
any such functor is completely determined by its values on the elementary generators —
species and individual reaction labels — with no further consistency conditions to verify.
This is the reaction-level analogue of Proposition 2.3: just as a monoid homomorphism out
of N|S| is fixed by its values on individual species, a symmetric monoidal functor out of
L0(𝑃) is fixed by its values on individual species and individual reactions.

as the base of the tower because the higher levels L2 (†-SMC), L3 (Markov category), and
L4 (DPO spans in LGraph) all carry non-trivial symmetry structure: a functor out of a
CMC, where all symmetries are identities, cannot map coherently into a target where they
are not.
What the universal property means for chemists
Any consistent additive assignment of chemical content to species and to individual
reaction labels extends uniquely to all composites and parallel combinations. The
extension is forced by the requirement of being a strict symmetric monoidal functor;
it is not a modelling choice.
Examples. Assigning enthalpies ℎ(𝑟) ∈R to generators and demanding functoriality
gives Hess’s Law (additivity over sequences and parallel reactions) as a consequence
of Corollary 2.16: not a separate postulate but a theorem. Assigning per-species
atom counts and demanding functoriality (Example 2.38) extends each generator’s
atom imbalance additively along all sequential and parallel composites, giving atom
conservation as a theorem whenever every generator is balanced. Rate constants at
L3 require different machinery: rates are not path-additive, so they enter via a kinetic
functor into a Markov category, not via the additive universal property of 𝐵R.
What is not forced. The state-function condition — that ℎ(𝑟) depends only on the
complexes 𝑠(𝑟) and 𝑡(𝑟), not on the particular reaction label 𝑟— is an additional
physical constraint, not a consequence of functoriality alone. Two distinct reaction
labels 𝑟1, 𝑟2 with the same source and target can carry different enthalpies ℎ(𝑟1) ≠
ℎ(𝑟2), and the functor axioms do not prohibit this. The distinction between functorial
additivity (supplied by L1) and the state-function condition (a separate physical
constraint on the particular functor 𝐹𝐻) is developed in §2.8.

§2.5. The automorphism exact sequence and the forcing principle
Theorem 2.14 establishes L0(𝑃) as the free skeletal permutative category on the Petri
net 𝑃: once species are assigned to objects of a target category and reaction labels to
morphisms of the correct type, the extension to all composites and tensors is uniquely
determined. This universal property now gives us a precise handle on the automorphisms
of L0(𝑃) itself, and — more importantly — on what they cannot see.
As previewed in §1.2, the tower L0 ↩→L1 ↩→· · · ↩→L7 is built bottom-up: at each step
there exist pairs of reactions that are physically distinct yet indistinguishable at the previous
level. The tool that makes “indistinguishable” mathematically precise is the automorphism
sequence, an adaptation to the categorical setting of a classical algebraic device. For a
homomorphism 𝜑: 𝐺→𝐻of groups, the kernel ker 𝜑measures what 𝜑collapses, and the
coset space 𝐻/im𝜑measures what lies outside its image [36, 46]. Applied to the restriction
map between the automorphism groups of adjacent tower levels, the kernel records new
symmetries that level 𝑘adds beyond level 𝑘−1, and the coset space records symmetries of
L𝑘−1 that fail to lift to L𝑘— precisely the distinctions a given level cannot express, and
that the next level must add. We do not assume the image of the restriction map to be a
normal subgroup, so the coset space is in general only a pointed set, not a group; this is
sufficient for the forcing diagnostic developed below.
Presentation-preserving automorphisms and the restriction map.
A presentation-
preserving automorphism of L𝑘is a strict symmetric monoidal autoequivalence 𝜙: L𝑘→
L𝑘that preserves the chemical input data — species set S and reaction labels R — as
subsets of objects and morphisms respectively. We write AutPetri(L𝑘) for the group of all
such automorphisms under composition. The presentation-preserving qualifier is essential:
an arbitrary categorical autoequivalence might rearrange composites and tensor products
in ways unrelated to any Petri-net relabelling, and the results below would not apply to it.
If some 𝜙∈AutPetri(L𝑘) swaps two reactions 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R, then the two are indistinguishable
by every L𝑘-level observable: any functor out of L𝑘must commute with 𝜙and therefore
cannot separate them. The converse fails in general — two reactions can agree under every
L𝑘-functor without there being a global presentation-preserving automorphism realising
the swap — so a swapping automorphism is a sufficient diagnostic for indistinguishability,
not a characterisation. This is exactly what the forcing argument needs: a swap that fails to
lift to L𝑘+1 exhibits a real distinction L𝑘misses.
Each tower inclusion 𝜄𝑘: L𝑘−1 ↩→L𝑘induces a restriction homomorphism
𝜑𝑘: AutPetri(L𝑘) −→AutPetri(L𝑘−1),
𝜙↦−→𝜙↾L𝑘−1,
sending each presentation-preserving automorphism of the richer level to its restriction to
the simpler one. Not every element of AutPetri(L𝑘−1) arises this way: those that do not are
symmetries present at level 𝑘−1 that level 𝑘breaks, precisely because the extra structure
at level 𝑘distinguishes what level 𝑘−1 could not.

Exactness at each term means the image of the incoming map equals the preimage of
the basepoint of the outgoing one. The three terms carry distinct chemical content.
• ker 𝜑𝑘: presentation-preserving automorphisms of L𝑘restricting to the identity
on L𝑘−1 — new symmetries first visible at level 𝑘. Example: time-reversal †
(sending each reaction to its reverse) is an automorphism of L2 invisible at L1,
where no reverse reaction exists.
• coker𝜑𝑘: cosets of presentation-preserving automorphisms of L𝑘−1 modulo
those that lift to L𝑘. A non-trivial coset is represented by an automorphism
of L𝑘−1 that fails to lift — a symmetry that L𝑘breaks. A non-trivial cokernel
is the precise statement that L𝑘−1 conflates objects (reactions, complexes, or
configurations) that L𝑘separates.
• 𝜑𝑘itself: records how much symmetry survives when the extra structure of
level 𝑘is forgotten.
Forcing principle (diagnostic direction). If coker𝜑𝑘is non-trivial, then L𝑘−1 admits
a genuine symmetry that L𝑘breaks: L𝑘−1 cannot distinguish reactions that L𝑘
separates, so the extension is necessary — i.e., no reformulation within L𝑘−1 can
capture the distinction.
Forcing principle (constructive direction). At each observed non-trivial coker𝜑𝑘,
an explicit minimal extension L𝑘−1 →L𝑘that breaks the cokernel class is exhibited
— adding exactly the new functor, enrichment, or deformation required and no more.
That this extension is the unique minimal extension breaking the cokernel class is
claimed level by level on construction, not as a general theorem about categorical
extensions; the full taxonomy of the six extension types that occur across the present
tower is given in §10.8.
What the exact sequence means for a chemist
An automorphism is a relabelling of the mathematical structure that leaves every
observable at that level unchanged. If a relabelling swaps two reactions 𝑟1 and 𝑟2,
then no measurement available at level 𝑘−1 can tell them apart.
The cokernel coker𝜑𝑘collects exactly those relabellings of L𝑘−1 that swap reactions
which are genuinely distinct in physical reality. A non-trivial cokernel means L𝑘−1 is
blind to a real distinction: it lacks the vocabulary to express it. Adding the minimal
structure needed to break that spurious symmetry yields L𝑘, and nothing more.
This is the categorical formalisation of a familiar experience: every time a chemical
rule has an exception, the exception reveals that a finer level of description was
implicitly being assumed. The automorphism exact sequence turns this intuition into
a working mathematical diagnostic.

The full tower, forced level by level.
The same argument at every subsequent tower step
yields the automorphism groups and forcing cokernels recorded in Table 3. The following
tour lists the levels in order; full developments occupy Chapters 3–10.
At L1, the automorphisms are isoenthalpic permutations, and the cokernel detects reactions
sharing Δ𝐻but differing in Δ𝑆, which shift their equilibria differently with temperature
and are therefore genuinely distinct at L2. At L2, adding the †-structure (time-reversal,
encoding detailed balance) breaks the remaining isothermodynamic symmetry; the cokernel
witnesses reactions with identical Δ𝐺but different rates, forcing L3. At L3, rate-preserving
permutations are the surviving symmetries, and the cokernel is generated by the swap
E2 ↔SN2: two reactions with identical empirical rate laws but mechanistically distinct
electron-pushing graphs, forcing L4. At L4, once full bond-graph structure is present,
the residual symmetry is Aut(𝐺) on typed molecular graphs; the cokernel detects the
same bond changes realised in different three-dimensional embeddings, forcing L4.5. At
L4.5, the full permutation-inversion group 𝐺∗governs enantiomeric and diastereomeric
distinctions, including symmetry-forbidden versus symmetry-allowed pathways under the
Woodward–Hoffmann rules; the cokernel forces L5 by exhibiting reactions whose transition
states occupy geometrically distinct points on a potential energy surface. At L5, isometries
of the configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) preserving the PES 𝑉are the automorphisms; the
cokernel distinguishes reactions with the same geometry but different topological Berry

With the automorphism diagnostic in hand, the remaining combinatorial content of L0 —
the stoichiometric matrix, Feinberg’s deficiency invariants, the Deficiency Zero Theorem,
and open-network composition — is the subject of the following subsection.
§2.6. The stoichiometric matrix, conservation laws, and deficiency
The previous subsections built L0(𝑃) as a categorical object. This subsection extracts
its classical linear-algebraic content — the stoichiometric matrix 𝑁, the conservation-law
space, and the deficiency 𝛿— and shows precisely which of these arise from the universal-
property machinery already established, and which are purely presentational invariants of
the Petri net 𝑃. In every case the derivation uses only Proposition 2.3, Theorem 2.14, and
Corollary 2.16. The dynamical significance of 𝛿— the Deficiency Theorems — requires
mass-action kinetics and belongs to L3; we state the theorems here and mark the level
boundary throughout.
The notion of a chemical reaction network used throughout the CRNT literature goes
back to Horn, Jackson, and Feinberg [47, 8, 42, 10]. The following definition adapts their
framework to the Petri-net presentation of L0, retaining named reaction labels so that
mechanistically distinct routes between the same complexes remain distinct morphisms in
L0(𝑃).
Definition 2.18 (Chemical Reaction Network at L0). A chemical reaction network (CRN)
at L0 is a quintuple (S, C, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) where C ⊂N|S| is a finite set of complexes, R is a finite
set of reaction labels, and 𝑠, 𝑡: R →C assign source and target complexes. The underlying
Petri net is 𝑃= (S, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) with 𝑠, 𝑡viewed as maps into N|S|, and the stoichiometric
category of the CRN is L0(𝑃). The reaction multigraph 𝐺(R) is the directed multigraph
with vertex set C and one directed edge per element of R.
Remark 2.19 (Relation to the classical Feinberg CRN). The classical CRNT triple [47, 8,
42, 10] (S, C, E) uses a set of directed edges E ⊆C × C, collapsing two reactions with
the same source and target to a single edge. The label-preserving quintuple is necessary for
the Petri-net presentation: distinct labels must remain distinct morphisms in L0(𝑃). The
classical triple is recovered by replacing R with {(𝑠(𝑟), 𝑡(𝑟)) : 𝑟∈R}.
Every generating morphism 𝑟∈R of L0(𝑃) has a source complex 𝑠(𝑟) ∈N|S| and a
target complex 𝑡(𝑟) ∈N|S|. Their difference 𝑡(𝑟) −𝑠(𝑟) lives in the group completion
Z[S]  Z|S| of N|S|. Collecting these differences as columns, after choosing linear
orderings of S and R, gives the stoichiometric matrix.

Conservation laws as a tower concept
Proposition 2.22 gives the categorical content of conservation laws entirely within L0:
A species potential 𝑤0 : S →R is a conservation law if and only if the functor
𝐹𝑤: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R it induces (via Proposition 2.3 and Corollary 2.16) assigns zero to
every morphism of L0(𝑃).
The reason conservation is preserved by all compositions and parallel combinations —
not just the generating reactions — is functoriality: 𝐹𝑤(𝑔◦𝑓) = 𝐹𝑤(𝑔) + 𝐹𝑤( 𝑓) = 0
and 𝐹𝑤( 𝑓⊗𝑔) = 0 follow automatically once 𝐹𝑤= 0 on generators. No separate
proof is needed; the functor axioms carry it.
This also explains what ker(𝑁⊤) is from the tower’s point of view: it is the set of
species potentials for which the induced L1-level functor (Corollary 2.16) happens to
be identically zero. Conservation is not an additional axiom imposed on L0(𝑃); it is
a condition on functors out of L0(𝑃), and functoriality does the work.

A feel for 𝑛, ℓ, 𝜌, 𝛿
𝑛counts the distinct molecular pools appearing as complexes. ℓcounts the reaction
islands: groups of complexes linked by some directed path, with no connection to other
groups. 𝜌counts the independent directions in concentration space along which any
trajectory can move. 𝛿counts the independent ways the complex graph can “circulate”
while producing zero net species change: complex-level degrees of freedom invisible
to species-level accounting. A 𝛿= 0 network has no such hidden structure.
To give 𝛿a precise meaning in terms of L0(𝑃), we factor the stoichiometric matrix through
the complex level. The inclusion 𝜄: C ↩→N|S| (each complex 𝑐∈C is already an element
of N|S|) is a function from the set C to the commutative monoid N|S|. By Proposition 2.3
applied with generator set C and target monoid N|S|, this extends to a unique monoid
homomorphism

from the free commutative monoid on complexes to the free commutative monoid on
species. Its matrix representation (after choosing orderings) is 𝑌∈R|S|×𝑛, the complex
composition matrix, whose column 𝑐is the coordinate vector of complex 𝑐∈C in R|S|.

Deficiency as a failure of the canonical monoid map
Proposition 2.26 has a direct tower interpretation.
The matrix 𝑌is the real-linear extension of the monoid homomorphism ¯𝜄: N[C] →
N|S| induced by Proposition 2.3 from the inclusion 𝜄: C ↩→N|S|. This map sends any
formal combination of complexes to the corresponding combination of species counts.
The matrix 𝐼𝑎records the net complex-level flows induced by the reaction labels:
each column 𝑟is 𝑒𝑡(𝑟) −𝑒𝑠(𝑟) in R𝑛, the net movement from source complex to target
complex.
The factorization 𝑁= 𝑌𝐼𝑎(part (i)) says: the net species displacement of a reaction
factors as first, compute the net complex-flow (𝐼𝑎), then project complexes to species
counts (𝑌= ¯𝜄).
Deficiency 𝛿measures exactly the failure of ¯𝜄to be injective on the image of the
complex-flow matrix: it counts the dimension of the space of complex-level circulations
that produce zero net species change. When 𝛿= 0, ¯𝜄is injective on im(𝐼𝑎): every
complex-graph flow leaves a detectable trace in species space. The Deficiency Zero
Theorem uses this injectivity crucially. When 𝛿> 0, there are “hidden” complex-level
circulations that L0(𝑃), viewed through the species map ¯𝜄, cannot detect.
Weak reversibility is a property of the presentation (S, C, R, 𝑠, 𝑡), not a categorical invariant
of L0(𝑃) up to equivalence (Remark 2.21). It records whether every directed path in the
generating graph 𝐺(R) can be returned to its starting complex by further generators — not
by arbitrary composites, but specifically by further elements of R. This is a strictly L0
datum: no kinetics, no thermodynamics, no reverse-reaction functor.
It is distinct from the †-structure at L2. At L2, the † operator provides an explicit reverse
generator 𝑟† : 𝑡(𝑟) →𝑠(𝑟) for each 𝑟∈R, subject to the categorical axiom 𝑟†† = 𝑟. Weak
reversibility at L0 requires only that the reverse direction is achievable by some directed
path of generators in 𝐺(R) — a much weaker condition, expressible purely in terms of the
multigraph. Introduced by Horn and Jackson [47, 8], it is the graph-theoretic hypothesis
that, together with 𝛿= 0, guarantees the conclusions of the Deficiency Zero Theorem.
Boros [49] later showed that weak reversibility alone (without 𝛿= 0) guarantees existence
of a positive steady state in each compatibility class.
Definition 2.27 (Weak reversibility [47, 8]). A CRN (S, C, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) is weakly reversible if
for every directed path 𝑐0 →𝑐1 →· · · →𝑐𝑘in 𝐺(R), there exists a directed path from
𝑐𝑘back to 𝑐0 in 𝐺(R). Equivalently, every connected component of 𝐺(R) is strongly
connected.
Remark 2.28 (Level stratification and compatibility classes). The invariants 𝑛, ℓ, 𝜌, 𝛿and
weak reversibility are purely L0 data: computable from (S, C, R, 𝑠, 𝑡) with no functor into
any target category.

stoichiometric compatibility classes: the class of x0 is

Remark 2.31 (Tower framework and Feinberg’s CRNT). The combinatorial backbone
is identical to classical CRNT [42, 51, 10]: species, complexes, reaction multigraph,
stoichiometric matrix, and the Deficiency Theorems originate there. The architectural
difference is that classical CRNT does not separate the stoichiometric layer from the kinetic
layer. The tower makes this explicit: L0 carries the hypotheses and the compatibility-class
partition; L3 carries the kinetics and the conclusions.

Remark 2.36 (Conservation laws are modular; deficiency is not). Proposition 2.35(iii) is
a positive result: a species potential 𝑤0 on the assembled network is a conservation law
if and only if it is a conservation law for each sub-network independently. This follows
cleanly from Proposition 2.22 applied to 𝑃12, and is an instance of the tower language
doing genuine work.

interface species create linear dependencies. Each of these quantities can change in a

sub-networks can assemble into a 𝛿> 0 network, and vice versa. In particular, the DZT
conclusion — unique stable steady state per compatibility class — does not compose under
pushout.
Open networks as composable chemical systems
An open CRN is a chemical system with designated inlet species (Σ𝐼) and outlet
species (Σ𝑂). Pushout composition connects two such systems in series.
Proposition 2.35 tells us what L0 knows about the assembly: the stoichiometric matrix
is the column-concatenation of the two sub-matrices, and a potential is conserved in
the assembly if and only if it is conserved by both sub-networks. Conservation laws
are therefore modular at L0.
What is not modular is deficiency: the assembly can create or destroy linkage-class
connections and stoichiometric dependencies in ways 𝛿1 and 𝛿2 alone cannot predict.

§2.7. L0 as a working tool
The previous sections established L0(𝑃) as a mathematical object. This section demon-
strates it as a working tool. The three examples below correspond to the three main structural
components introduced above: §2.3 (morphism calculus), §2.4 (universal property), and
Definition 2.34 (open composition). Each derives a non-trivial fact from L0 data alone —
no energy, no rates, no geometry.

catalytic event — substrate binding followed by product release — as a single process in
the stoichiometric calculus. This composite is a distinct morphism 𝐸+𝑆→𝐸+𝑃from any
hypothetical direct reaction generator 𝑟′ : 𝐸+𝑆→𝐸+𝑃that one might add to the Petri

generator, so 𝑟3 ◦𝑟1 and 𝑟′ remain distinct morphisms in L0(𝑃).
Running binding and release in parallel. The tensor product
𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2 : (𝐸+𝑆) + 𝐸𝑆−→𝐸𝑆+ (𝐸+𝑆)
is a morphism representing simultaneous substrate binding in one part of the system and
enzyme–substrate dissociation in another. It is not equal to id𝐸+𝑆+𝐸𝑆: the two processes
happen at different molecular sites and are kept as a non-trivial parallel process.
A type error. The composite 𝑟3 ◦𝑟2 is ill-typed: 𝑡(𝑟2) = 𝐸+𝑆while 𝑠(𝑟3) = 𝐸𝑆, and
𝐸+𝑆≠𝐸𝑆in N|S| since 𝐸+ 𝑆(the unbound enzyme–substrate pair) and 𝐸𝑆(the enzyme–
substrate complex) are distinct species. L0(𝑃) refuses to form this composite, encoding at
the categorical level the mechanistic fact that 𝐸𝑆must form before it can release product:
product release cannot follow dissociation.
Example 2.38 (Atom balance via the imbalance functor). Chemical balancedness — the
requirement that every reaction preserves atom counts — is not an axiom of L0(𝑃). It
is expressed by a functor out of L0(𝑃): every Petri net, balanced or not, admits an
atom-imbalance functor that records the elemental discrepancy of each reaction, and
balancedness is the condition that this functor takes value zero on every generator. The
construction uses two successive applications of the universal property.

Balancedness as a vanishing condition on 𝐹𝑎. For a general Petri net 𝑃′ and atom map
𝑎: S′ →N|𝐸|, the imbalance functor 𝐹𝑎: L0(𝑃′) →𝐵Z|𝐸| always exists: the assignment

that 𝐹𝑎is the zero functor on every morphism of L0(𝑃′). An unbalanced Petri net is a
perfectly valid stoichiometric category equipped with a non-zero imbalance functor; the
values 𝐹𝑎(𝑟) ≠0 record exactly which reactions fail to conserve atoms and by how much.
Balancedness is therefore not a condition on the existence of 𝐹𝑎, but a vanishing condition
on its values — a condition on a functor out of L0(𝑃′), not an axiom of L0 itself.

The limits of L0
The three examples above exhaust what L0 can do: track stoichiometric type, extend
additive assignments from generators to all processes via the universal property, and
assemble networks from modular parts via pushout. What L0 cannot do is distinguish
two reactions with the same source and target by any numerical criterion, because
L0(𝑃) carries no numerical data as part of its structure. The next section identifies
this gap precisely and shows that extending L0 by exactly one additional piece of data
— a functor 𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R — is the minimal and canonical next step.

§2.8. What L0 cannot express: the forcing of L1
Section 2.5 established, via the automorphism sequence (3) at 𝑘= 0, that any two reaction
labels 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R with identical source and target complexes — whenever L0(𝑃) contains
such a pair — represent a class [𝑟1 ↔𝑟2] ∈coker𝜑1 that L0 cannot break, forcing the
existence of L1. This subsection gives the chemical realisation of that abstract argument
using the nitrogen–oxygen–nitric oxide system, and then develops the subtler content of L1
itself: the distinction between the additivity condition (satisfied by any strict symmetric
monoidal functor into 𝐵R) and the state-function condition (satisfied only by functors
induced by an object potential). The first is the categorical content of L1; the second is an
additional physical constraint that only some L1-functors satisfy.
The gap at L0: a worked chemical instance
A single reaction. Consider the oxidation of nitrogen,
𝑟: N2(g) + O2(g) −→2 NO(g),
Δ𝐻◦= +180.5 kJ mol−1 [44].
L0(𝑃) contains the generating morphism 𝑟: u →v with u = N2 + O2 and v = 2 NO.
It does not contain the scalar +180.5: L0(𝑃) carries no real-valued functor as part of
its data, so there is no structure at this level in which the enthalpy can reside.
Parallel routes — the forcing instance. In practice, a reaction network frequently
contains two distinct reaction labels 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R sharing source and target complexes:
𝑠(𝑟1) = 𝑠(𝑟2) = u,
𝑡(𝑟1) = 𝑡(𝑟2) = v,
for example, two experimentally identified pathways with the same gross stoichiometry,
or the same reaction studied under different catalytic conditions. Both appear as
distinct generating morphisms in L0(𝑃) (Remark 2.6); the free construction imposes
no identification on them.
Suppose these two reaction labels carry distinct enthalpies: Δ𝐻1 ≠Δ𝐻2. The label
swap 𝑟1 ↔𝑟2 extends to an element of AutPetri(L0(𝑃)) — specifically, a label
permutation within the fibre (𝑠, 𝑡)−1(u, v), the second family identified in §2.5. It
preserves every structure of L0(𝑃): source and target complexes are unchanged, and
no numerical data exists at L0 to be disturbed. Yet this swap is not the restriction of
any element of AutPetri(L1): every presentation-preserving automorphism at L1 must
commute with the enthalpy functor 𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R whose existence defines L1,
and 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) ≠𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) prevents the swap from preserving the L1-structure. By (4), the
swap represents a non-trivial class in coker𝜑1. The minimal extension resolving this
conflation is to equip L0(𝑃) with the functor 𝐹𝐻itself: L1, developed in Chapter 3.
Remark 2.40 (The additivity condition: equipping L0(𝑃) with 𝐹𝐻). Passing to L1 means
equipping L0(𝑃) with a strict symmetric monoidal functor
𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) −→𝐵R.
By Corollary 2.16, such a functor is uniquely determined by specifying one real number
𝐹𝐻(𝑟) ∈R for each generating reaction 𝑟∈R; the values on composites and tensors are
then forced:
𝐹𝐻(𝑔◦𝑓) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑔) + 𝐹𝐻( 𝑓),
𝐹𝐻( 𝑓⊗𝑔) = 𝐹𝐻( 𝑓) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑔),
𝐹𝐻(idu) = 0.

## Page 50


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
These are the additivity conditions on 𝐹𝐻. The first is the additivity form of Hess’s Law
— enthalpy changes add along sequential reaction steps; the second is additivity over
independent parallel processes. Both follow from functoriality, not from any separate
physical postulate.
In terms of the automorphism sequence, equipping L0(𝑃) with 𝐹𝐻breaks the spurious
label-swap symmetry in coker𝜑1: once distinct real values 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) ≠𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) are assigned,
the swap 𝑟1 ↔𝑟2 no longer preserves structure, and the two reaction labels are numerically
distinguishable.
The values {𝐹𝐻(𝑟)}𝑟∈R are free parameters: any assignment of real numbers to reaction
generators extends to a valid strict symmetric monoidal functor. This is the additivity
condition for L1: it adds exactly one real parameter per reaction label, and no other
structure.
Remark 2.41 (The state-function condition). The physical fact that enthalpy is a state
function — that the enthalpy change of a reaction depends only on its initial and final
complex, not on the reaction label — is strictly stronger than the additivity condition of
Remark 2.40. It requires 𝐹𝐻to be induced by an object potential: a monoid homomorphism
ℎ: (N|S|, +, 0) →(R, +, 0) satisfying
𝐹𝐻(𝑟) = ℎ(𝑡(𝑟)) −ℎ(𝑠(𝑟))
for every generating 𝑟∈R.
By the universal property of N|S| (Proposition 2.3), any function ℎ0 : S →R — one real
value per species, typically the standard enthalpy of formation Δ𝐻◦
𝑓(𝑆) — extends to a
unique such ℎ, and then to a valid 𝐹𝐻via Corollary 2.16. When such an ℎexists, the
enthalpy change of any morphism 𝑓: u →v (whether a single generator, a composite, or a
tensor product) equals ℎ(v) −ℎ(u), depending only on the source and target and not on the
particular morphism. Path independence then holds automatically: for any two morphisms
𝑓, 𝑔: u →v, 𝐹𝐻( 𝑓) = ℎ(v) −ℎ(u) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑔).
The two conditions are distinct. The additivity condition (Remark 2.40) provides a
real number per reaction label, allows 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) ≠𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) for two labels with identical
source and target, and is the categorical content of L1. The state-function condition
imposes 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) whenever 𝑠(𝑟1) = 𝑠(𝑟2) and 𝑡(𝑟1) = 𝑡(𝑟2), by requiring ℎto be
well-defined on complexes, but does not identify 𝑟1 with 𝑟2 as morphisms in the category:
the two reaction labels remain distinct elements of R, they simply receive the same enthalpy
value. The state-function condition is therefore a constraint on the particular functor 𝐹𝐻,
not a relation imposed on L0(𝑃) itself.
An 𝐹𝐻satisfying only the additivity condition but not the state-function condition is a
perfectly valid strict symmetric monoidal functor, representing a situation in which the
same gross stoichiometry is associated with distinct energetic signatures across different
realisations (e.g., different catalysts, different solvents, or mechanistically distinct pathways).
Both conditions are of physical interest, and the distinction between them is central to how
L1 and L2 differ.

strict symmetric monoidal functor satisfying the additivity condition, is the L1-level data
associated with 𝑃. The complete development of L1 — its relationship to equilibrium
thermodynamics via the entropy functor 𝐹𝑆, the †-structure of L2 encoding detailed balance,
and the Wegscheider cycle conditions for rate constants — is given in Chapter 3.

What structure resolves the ambiguity? Before writing any mathematics, three physical
observations constrain the answer.
(a) Sequential additivity (Hess’s Law). If reaction 𝑟1 is followed by 𝑟2, the total
enthalpy change is Δ𝐻(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = Δ𝐻(𝑟1) + Δ𝐻(𝑟2). The label must be compatible
with categorical composition.

Δ𝐻(𝑟2). The label must be compatible with the monoidal product.
(c) No spurious energy. Δ𝐻(idu) = 0 for every complex u — unitality.
These three constraints specify a strict symmetric monoidal functor
𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) −→𝐵R
— the one-object additive category 𝐵R introduced in §1.4. The fit between the three physical

• No weaker structure suffices. A plain (non-monoidal) functor satisfies (a) but misses
(b): functoriality constrains composition, not the tensor product. A lax monoidal
functor weakens (b) to

Dropping the unit condition loses (c). Each weakening fails at least one of the three
physical axioms.
• No stronger structure is needed. The three axioms fix 𝐹𝐻uniquely on all morphisms
given its values on generators (Proposition 3.2 in §3.2). Any further structure —
requiring 𝐹𝐻to be a monoidal equivalence, an adjunction, or a faithful functor —
would impose conditions (surjectivity, invertibility, injectivity on morphisms) with
no physical interpretation for an enthalpy assignment.
The extension presented here is the minimal categorical object resolving the coker𝜑1 class
identified at L0: a decorator functor adjoined to L0(𝑃) without modifying its underlying
category. That this is the unique minimal extension resolving the cokernel is claimed
constructively at the present level, not as a general theorem about categorical extensions;
the full taxonomy of the six extension types that occur across the tower is recorded in §10.8.
The next subsection makes the construction precise.

Unpacking Definition 3.1
The domain of 𝐹𝐻is L0(𝑃), the free skeletal permutative category already constructed

category in its own right).
The target 𝐵R is a one-object category, so its object monoid {∗} is trivially strictly
commutative; this is exactly the hypothesis on the target required by Theorem 2.14,
and it is satisfied here without further work. The action of 𝐹𝐻is therefore entirely
determined by its action on morphisms:
• Every object u ∈L0(𝑃) maps to the single object ∗.
• Every morphism 𝑟: u →v in L0(𝑃) maps to a real number 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) ∈R.
The “strict symmetric monoidal” conditions then read:
• Functoriality: 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1).
• Monoidality: 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2).
• Unitality: 𝐹𝐻(idu) = 0 for all u.
The adjective strict means that the coherence isomorphisms of a monoidal functor—the
natural transformations 𝜙𝐴,𝐵: 𝐹𝐻(𝐴) ⊗𝐹𝐻(𝐵) →𝐹𝐻(𝐴⊗𝐵) and 𝜙0 : 𝐼→𝐹𝐻(𝐼)—
are required to be identity morphisms, not merely natural isomorphisms [37, Ch. XI,
§1]. In 𝐵R each 𝜙𝐴,𝐵is an endomorphism of the unique object ∗, i.e. a real number;
strictness requires it to equal 0 (the identity in 𝐵R), which is precisely the monoidality
equation above. These three equations are the complete content of the thermochemical
decoration.
The existence and uniqueness of 𝐹𝐻given its values on generating reactions follows directly
from the universal property of L0(𝑃).
Proposition 3.2 (Existence and uniqueness of 𝐹𝐻). Let 𝑃be a Petri net with reaction set R.
Given any assignment Δ𝐻0 : R →R, there is a unique strict symmetric monoidal functor

§3.3. Layer 1: the generic additive functor
The functor 𝐹𝐻of Definition 3.1 as stated — one free real parameter per generating
reaction — constitutes Layer 1 of the thermochemical structure. The following theorem
encodes Hess’s Law and its monoidal counterpart as the two defining axioms of 𝐹𝐻. The
physical content of Hess’s Law has been understood since 1840 [53]; its formulation as the
functoriality condition of a strict monoidal functor into 𝐵R is, to the authors’ knowledge,
original to this work.
Theorem 3.3 (Hess’s Law and parallel additivity — Layer 1). Let 𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R be
the thermochemical functor (Layer 1 data).
(i) (Sequential additivity / Hess’s Law) For composable reactions 𝑟1 : u →v, 𝑟2 : v →
w:
𝐹𝐻(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2).
(ii) (Parallel additivity) For any reactions 𝑟1, 𝑟2:
𝐹𝐻(𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2).
(iii) (No spurious energy) 𝐹𝐻(idu) = 0 for every complex u.
Proof. Parts (i)–(iii) are the functoriality, monoidality, and unitality axioms of 𝐹𝐻respec-
tively. They hold by definition of a strict symmetric monoidal functor; the content of the
theorem is that such an 𝐹𝐻exists and is unique given values on generators, as established
in Proposition 3.2.
□
Remark 3.4 (Two postulates, one equation). Traditional thermochemistry textbooks state
Hess’s Law (part (i)) and parallel additivity (part (ii)) as two separate empirical postulates
[3]. Categorically, both are instances of the single requirement that 𝐹𝐻is a monoidal
functor: sequential additivity is functoriality, parallel additivity is monoidality. The
classical textbook presentation reflects the same mathematical structure, stated in the
language of experiments rather than of categories.
Physically, the full path-independence form of Hess’s Law — the enthalpy of a process
depends only on initial and final complexes, regardless of route — is classically derived
from the first law together with the identification of enthalpy as a state function [54].
Theorem 3.3 captures the additive content of Hess’s Law (along sequential composites and
across parallel processes) directly from functoriality, without invoking the state-function
identification. The path-independence form proper requires the Layer 2 coboundary
condition 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎdeveloped in §3.4.

§3.4. Layer 2: the state-function condition
Warning 3.5 shows that Layer 1 alone permits thermochemical cycles to accumulate
non-zero enthalpy, in conflict with the first law of thermodynamics. The culprit is that
Layer 1 assigns a real number to each reaction independently; it imposes no relationship
between the enthalpy of a reaction and any intrinsic property of the complexes it connects.
The first law demands more: enthalpy must be a state function, meaning its value for any
process depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken. Mathematically,
this means the enthalpy assignment must be expressible as a difference of potentials defined
on the complexes themselves. Layer 2 is the additional datum that enforces this.
Definition 3.6 (Layer 2: state-function / coboundary condition). A thermochemical functor
𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R satisfies the state-function condition (Layer 2) if there exists a monoid
homomorphism
ℎ: ␀N[S], +, 0 −→␀R, +, 0
such that, for every generating reaction 𝑟: u →v,
𝐹𝐻(𝑟) = ℎ(v) −ℎ(u).
We write this condition as 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎand call ℎan object potential (or additive potential)
for 𝐹𝐻.
The notation 𝛿0 and the term object potential require some comments. The map ℎassigns
a real number (a “height” or “potential”) to each complex in N[S], and the identity
𝐹𝐻(𝑟) = ℎ(v) −ℎ(u) says that the enthalpy of a generating reaction is the difference of
the endpoint potentials. This is the discrete analogue of a conservative field on a graph:
individual reactions are directed edges, while sequences of reactions are directed paths.
For an exact edge-labeling, the total enthalpy along a directed path depends only on its
endpoints, and hence vanishes on directed cycles [56, 57].
The symbol 𝛿0 is borrowed from graph cohomology.

The condition 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎencodes the first law of thermodynamics in a single equation.

§3.5. Worked examples
The three examples below are standard exercises from undergraduate thermochemistry
curricula [3, 44]. Every introductory chemistry student learns to add enthalpies along
reaction pathways, to close thermochemical cycles, and to use tabulated formation enthalpies
to predict unmeasurable quantities. The categorical language of L1 reveals the common
mathematical skeleton behind all three: Hess’s Law is functoriality, cycle closure is the
coboundary condition, and a thermochemical data table is an object potential. Nothing
new is computed; what is new is the identification of the precise categorical structure that
makes the computations valid.

3.5.3. Organic combustion network: cycle consistency
Example 3.16 (Combustion network: testing Layer 2 consistency). The previous two

direction: to check whether a set of experimentally measured enthalpies is internally
consistent, i.e. whether a single object potential ℎ𝑓exists that accounts for all of them. This
is exactly the test a calorimetrist applies when verifying a new thermochemical dataset.
