§3.6. Thermochemical networks and the Wegscheider pre-condition
In 1901, Rudolf Wegscheider showed that in a reversible mass-action reaction network
obeying detailed balance, the rate constants — equivalently the elementary-step equilibrium
constants — cannot be chosen independently; stoichiometric cycle relations impose
multiplicative constraints, now called the Wegscheider conditions [61]. These conditions
are the cornerstone of thermodynamic consistency in chemical kinetics and underpin
everything from enzyme network analysis to the theory of detailed balance [62, 9].
The constraints enter the tower in two stages. At L2, the full Wegscheider conditions
arise as the coboundary condition for the Gibbs functor 𝐹𝑇
𝐺= 𝐹𝐻−𝑇𝐹𝑆, restricting the
allowed equilibrium constants via ker 𝐹𝑇
𝐺(see Section 4). At the present level L1, the same
mathematical structure appears in a purely enthalpic form: any thermochemical network
with directed cycles must satisfy additive cycle conditions on the enthalpy assignment.
This is the thermochemical pre-condition — the enthalpic-additive analogue of the full
Wegscheider conditions, visible already at L1 before entropy and free energy enter at L2.
Isolating it here makes the tower structure explicit: the Wegscheider conditions are not a
kinetic accident but a consequence of the coboundary structure that is already forced at the
thermochemical level.
The following definition places this classical notion on the categorical footing provided
by L0(𝑃). The underlying idea — that a thermochemical network is a reaction graph
decorated by an enthalpy assignment — goes back to Hess [53] and was made explicit in
the cycle-condition language by Wegscheider [61]; the formulation below is new in casting
it as a pair (𝑃, ℎ) where ℎis a monoid homomorphism into R and the enthalpy functor is
the induced coboundary 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎ.
Definition 3.17 (State-function thermochemical network). A state-function thermochemical
network (a Layer 2 thermochemical network) is a pair (𝑃, ℎ) where 𝑃is a Petri net
and ℎ: N[S] →R is a monoid homomorphism (an object potential in the sense of
Definition 3.6). The induced functor 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎ: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R automatically satisfies
both Layer 1 (functoriality) and Layer 2 (the coboundary condition), and is uniquely
determined by ℎ. This is the Layer 2 specialisation of the generic L1-decoration of
Definition 3.1: a generic L1-functor 𝐹𝐻is required only to be strict symmetric monoidal,
while a state-function thermochemical network requires 𝐹𝐻to factor through an object
potential.
Thermochemical networks in this sense pervade chemistry. The Born–Haber cycles of ionic
compounds (Example 3.15), the Hess cycles for combustion enthalpies (Examples 3.13,
3.16), and the thermodynamic cycles for ATP hydrolysis coupled to biosynthetic reactions
[63] are all instances: in each case, the physically meaningful quantity is the object
potential ℎ, and the measurable reaction enthalpies are its coboundary. The parameter count
𝜌= rank𝑁of Observation 3.9 is the number of independent calorimetric experiments

To the author’s knowledge, the connection between this proposition and Kirchhoff’s Voltage
Law has not previously been stated as a theorem in the chemical reaction network literature,
though the analogy between thermochemical cycles and electrical circuits has been used
informally since the early network thermodynamics of Oster, Perelson, and Katchalsky
[64]. The categorical proof makes the connection exact.
Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law in disguise
In an electrical circuit, Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL) states that the algebraic sum of
voltage drops around any closed loop of circuit branches is zero [65]: in a conservative
(electrostatic) network, voltage drops are differences of an electric scalar potential, so
traversing a directed cycle returns to the starting potential. Formally: for any directed
cycle of circuit branches, the sum of the voltage drops equals zero.
Proposition 3.18 and KVL are the same mathematical statement in different physical
guises. In both cases, a functor (the voltage assignment in circuits; the enthalpy
functor 𝐹𝐻in thermochemistry) maps into the one-object additive category 𝐵R and
must assign zero to every closed loop. The reason is identical: both the voltage in a
circuit and the enthalpy of a reaction are coboundaries of a scalar potential (electric
potential 𝜙in circuits; the object potential ℎin thermochemistry). The Born–Haber
cycle, Hess’s Law for formation enthalpies, and the ATP–ADP free energy cycle in
cellular metabolism [63] are all chemical instances of the same categorical fact.
The non-coincidence is the point: both laws derive from the coboundary structure
𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎ(or Δ𝜙= 𝛿0𝜙in circuits), and the cycle condition Í

§3.7. What L1 cannot express: forcing of L2
Layer 1 assigns a single real number 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) to each generating reaction and propagates it
additively. The physical question it cannot answer is: how does a reaction network respond
to changes in temperature? The temperature dependence of equilibrium is governed by
the Gibbs free energy Δ𝐺= Δ𝐻−𝑇Δ𝑆; two reactions with identical Δ𝐻but different Δ𝑆
accumulate different free energies at every temperature, yet are indistinguishable by 𝐹𝐻
alone. The following makes this gap precise.
Forcing empirical result for L2: enthalpy-indistinguishable, entropy-separated
Let 𝑃be a coarse-grained Petri net with species
S = {H, I, HI},
where H denotes Hsp90, I denotes the aryl-dihydroxyphenyl-thiadiazole inhibitor
class, and HI the bound complex. Consider two generating reactions
𝑟𝐸, 𝑟𝐹: H ⊗I −→HI,
representing, after coarse-graining, the binding of ICPD26 and ICPD34. Chemically
these are distinct ligands; they become parallel morphisms only because the label I
forgets substituent identity.
Kazlauskas et al. report that the modification ICPD26 →ICPD34 weakens binding by
about 3.1 kJ mol−1, while the binding enthalpies remain essentially unchanged within
the experimental uncertainty of the isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) analysis;
the observed change in binding free energy is therefore attributed to entropy [66].
This exposes a genuine limitation of the L1 description. At the coarse-grained
stoichiometric level, the two binding events have the same source, the same target,
and the same enthalpy label to experimental resolution:
𝐹𝐻(𝑟𝐸) ≈𝐹𝐻(𝑟𝐹).
Yet they are not thermodynamically equivalent, since their binding free energies differ
measurably. Thus 𝐹𝐻alone does not contain enough information to separate them.
Indistinguishability at L1. If L1 records only stoichiometry together with the
enthalpy assignment, then 𝑟𝐸and 𝑟𝐹are indistinguishable at that level: every invariant
visible to L1 treats them as the same reaction.
Why L1 is not enough. The Hsp90 example therefore forces an extension of the
theory. There exists thermodynamic information relevant to binding that is invisible to
L1 but necessary to explain the experimentally observed difference in affinity. In other
words, once one reaches this point, an enthalpy-only level of the tower is no longer
adequate: the tower must be refined by adjoining a further thermodynamic datum.
Methodological caution. This formulation must be stated at the level of intrinsic
thermodynamic parameters rather than raw observed heats. For protein–ligand binding,
calorimetric enthalpies can be shifted by linked protonation and buffer effects, so
comparison of reaction labels should be made only after such corrections [67, 68].
This forces L2, which must add:
(i) A second strict symmetric monoidal functor 𝐹𝑆: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R recording standard

§4. L2: The Equilibrium Level
§4.1. Forcing the extension: what L1 cannot express
Section 3.7 identified the gap at L1: two reactions with equal enthalpy changes but
different entropy changes respond to temperature in completely opposite ways, yet are
indistinguishable by 𝐹𝐻alone. Before making this precise categorically, we establish the
chemical reality that such pairs are not exotic but generic in complex reaction networks
like a biochemical system.
Abstract forcing pair for L2
The mathematical content of the gap at L1 is a pair of generating reactions
𝑟1, 𝑟2 : u →v
in some Petri net 𝑃, with the same enthalpy but different entropies:
𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2),
𝐹𝑆(𝑟1) ≠𝐹𝑆(𝑟2).
The label swap 𝜎: 𝑟1 ↔𝑟2 preserves the L1-decoration (𝐹𝐻◦𝜎= 𝐹𝐻on chemical
generators) but does not preserve any decoration recording entropy, since 𝐹𝑆◦𝜎≠𝐹𝑆
on {𝑟1, 𝑟2}. By the automorphism sequence of §2.5, 𝜎represents a non-trivial coset
in coker𝜑2: the forgetful operation 𝑈2 (Definition 4.1) is not injective on decorated
triples — the underlying L1-decoration (L0(𝑃), 𝐹𝐻) alone does not determine 𝐹𝑆.
L1 conflates the two reactions; L2 separates them, since their Gibbs free energies
𝐹𝑇
𝐺(𝑟𝑖) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟𝑖) −𝑇𝐹𝑆(𝑟𝑖) differ at every 𝑇> 0.
The chembox below establishes that such pairs are generic in real chemistry — a
feature of biochemical reaction networks under coarse-graining, not a mathematical
contrivance.
Binding thermodynamics: Δ𝐻and Δ𝑆need not covary
Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) studies of protein–ligand binding show that the
enthalpic and entropic contributions to binding can vary separately across a ligand
series. This is a structural feature of molecular recognition: Δ𝐻and Δ𝑆report on
different physical aspects of binding and there is no general law forcing them to change
together [69].
The binding enthalpy Δ𝐻is often associated with the quality of direct intermolecular
interactions, such as hydrogen bonding, electrostatics, van der Waals contacts, and
the enthalpic cost of desolvating polar groups. The binding entropy Δ𝑆reflects
changes in solvent organisation and molecular freedom, including favorable release of
ordered water and unfavorable losses of ligand and protein conformational freedom
upon complex formation. Because these contributions arise from different physical
mechanisms, modifying one does not in general determine the other [70, 71, 72].
A useful illustration is provided by Biela et al.’s ITC and crystallographic study of
thrombin inhibitors with systematically varied P3 substituents [73]. These ligands
probe the same hydrophobic S3/4 pocket and therefore belong to the same stoichio-

increasing hydrophobic bulk produced an overall affinity enhancement of about 40-fold
that was attributed mainly to a more favorable entropy term, consistent with stepwise
disruption of the pocket water network [73]. At the same time, the enthalpy changed
much less strongly than the entropy, so the dominant thermodynamic trend in the
series was entropy-driven rather than enthalpy-driven.
For broader context, thermodynamic profiling of marketed HIV-1 protease inhibitors
shows a wide spread of binding enthalpies. In Freire’s analysis, Indinavir is en-
thalpically unfavourable (Δ𝐻≈+7.6 kJ mol−1), whereas Darunavir is strongly
enthalpy-driven (Δ𝐻≈−53.1 kJ mol−1). Across this inhibitor class, the progres-
sion from earlier to later, more potent compounds is accompanied by increasingly
favourable binding enthalpies [70].
What minimal additional structure allows the tower to distinguish the two reactions of the
forcing pair? The same three physical observations that forced 𝐹𝐻in Section 3.1 apply to
entropy:
(a) Sequential additivity of standard reaction entropy. Δ𝑆(𝑟2◦𝑟1) = Δ𝑆(𝑟1)+Δ𝑆(𝑟2):
the total entropy change of a sequence of reactions is the sum of each step’s
contribution.
(b) Parallel additivity. Δ𝑆(𝑟1⊗𝑟2) = Δ𝑆(𝑟1)+Δ𝑆(𝑟2): independent reactions contribute
independently to the total entropy change.
(c) No spurious entropy. Δ𝑆(idu) = 0 for every complex u: the identity process
produces no entropy change.
These are the same three constraints that characterised 𝐹𝐻in Section 3.1, with enthalpy
replaced by entropy. They uniquely identify a strict symmetric monoidal functor 𝐹𝑆:
L0(𝑃) →𝐵R. The universal property of L0(𝑃) (Theorem 2.14) guarantees existence and
uniqueness of 𝐹𝑆given one real number per generating reaction — the same theorem applied
a second time, with Δ𝑆◦

4.2.1. Reversible Petri nets and the dagger
Physical chemical reactions are, in principle, reversible: thermodynamics does not forbid
the transformation in either direction. For ordinary chemical systems governed by classical
or non-relativistic quantum dynamics, the principle of microscopic reversibility is a
consequence of the time-reversal symmetry of the underlying equations, so each elementary
reaction step has a corresponding reverse step [77, 78, 79]. The thermodynamic data
(𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆) therefore determines not whether the reverse process exists, but how the equilibrium
is biased toward reactants or products [62, 54]. This has a direct modelling consequence: a
faithful Petri net for a system at or near equilibrium should contain both 𝑟and 𝑟† for every
reaction 𝑟it models.
The following definition formalises this and introduces the reversible closure — the
smallest reversible Petri net containing a given one. The term closure is used in its standard
algebraic sense: just as the algebraic closure of a field adjoins all missing roots and nothing
more, the reversible closure of a Petri net freely adjoins, for each generator 𝑟, the reverse
generator 𝑟† that is missing, and nothing more. The result is characterised by a universal
property: it is the initial reversible Petri net equipped with an embedding of 𝑃. Petri nets
as freely generated categorical / monoidal structures go back to Meseguer–Montanari [32],
while open Petri nets and reaction networks are treated categorically by Baez–Pollard and
Baez–Master [31, 43]. Reversibility via adjoining reverse transitions is also standard in the
reversible-Petri-net literature [80, 81]. In the present paper, we call the resulting initial
reversible completion of 𝑃its reversible closure.
Definition 4.5 (Reversible Petri net and reversible closure). A Petri net 𝑃is reversible if
for every generator 𝑟: u →v in R, its reverse 𝑟† : v →u is also a generator in R, with
(𝑟†)† = 𝑟. The reversible closure ¯𝑃of any Petri net 𝑃is the reversible Petri net obtained
by freely adjoining, for each 𝑟∈R, a new generator 𝑟† : v →u subject to (𝑟†)† = 𝑟. It is
the initial reversible Petri net equipped with a Petri net embedding 𝜄: 𝑃↩→¯𝑃.
Dagger structures and opposite categories
For any category C, the opposite category Cop has the same objects as C but every
morphism 𝑓: 𝑋→𝑌in C becomes a morphism 𝑓op : 𝑌→𝑋in Cop, with
composition reversed: 𝑔op ◦𝑓op = ( 𝑓◦𝑔)op [82, 83]. This is a purely formal
construction; it does not equip C with any extra structure, only relates C to a “mirror”
category with the same objects.
A dagger structure on C is something stronger: an identity-on-objects contravariant
involution
(−)† : Cop −→C,
( 𝑓: 𝑋→𝑌) ↦−→( 𝑓† : 𝑌→𝑋),
satisfying
( 𝑓†)† = 𝑓,
id†
𝑋= id𝑋,
(𝑔◦𝑓)† = 𝑓† ◦𝑔†.

chemical generators and then extended contravariantly to composite morphisms,

functor axioms. Under Layer 2 for both functors (Definition 3.6 for 𝐹𝐻, Definition 4.18
below for 𝐹𝑆), anti-symmetry is not an additional constraint but a theorem: if 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎ𝑓
and 𝐹𝑆= 𝛿0ℎ𝑆on the reversible closure ¯𝑃, then for every generator 𝑟: u →v,
𝐹𝐻(𝑟†) = ℎ𝑓(u) −ℎ𝑓(v) = −𝐹𝐻(𝑟),
𝐹𝑆(𝑟†) = ℎ𝑆(u) −ℎ𝑆(v) = −𝐹𝑆(𝑟),
by applying Proposition 3.7 separately to each functor. Anti-symmetry is thus a Layer 1
axiom — required to state detailed balance without invoking Layer 2 structure — that
becomes a Layer 2 theorem.
Anti-symmetry: state functions force sign flips
Both conditions are direct consequences of the state-function character of enthalpy
and entropy — among the most firmly established facts in chemical thermodynamics
[54, 84].
Enthalpy anti-symmetry. Since enthalpy 𝐻is a state function, its change along
any path from complex u to complex v depends only on the endpoints: 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) =
𝐻(v) −𝐻(u) for 𝑟: u →v (Layer 2/coboundary form, Proposition 3.11). Reversing
the reaction gives
𝐹𝐻(𝑟†) = 𝐻(u) −𝐻(v) = −𝐹𝐻(𝑟).
This is Hess’s Law applied to a single step: if the forward reaction releases Δ𝐻kJ/mol,
the reverse absorbs exactly |Δ𝐻| kJ/mol, and vice versa [53, 54].
Entropy anti-symmetry. Entropy 𝑆is likewise a state function (a consequence
of the second and third laws [54]). By the same coboundary argument: 𝐹𝑆(𝑟†) =
𝑆(u) −𝑆(v) = −𝐹𝑆(𝑟). At the molecular level this reflects microscopic reversibility
[62]: at equilibrium, the forward and reverse fluxes through every elementary step are
equal, so any state-function difference associated with the step must reverse sign upon
reversal of the step. A process that increases the system’s entropy by |𝐹𝑆(𝑟)| in the
forward direction decreases it by the same amount in the reverse.
What this is, and what it is not. The sign-flip refers to the reaction entropy change
Δ𝑆◦
𝑟— a state-function difference that is positive, negative, or zero depending on
the reaction. It must not be confused with the entropy production rate 𝜎≥0, a non-
negative quantity in nonequilibrium thermodynamics that quantifies irreversibility and
belongs to the kinetic/open-system level L3, not to the standard-state L2 decoration.
Reaction entropy changes flip sign upon reversal; entropy production does not.
Both axioms are imposed as constraints on the functor pair (𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆), not on the
category L0(𝑃) itself. The underlying category remains the free skeletal permutative

Remark 4.8 (Anti-symmetry halves the parameter count, matching thermochemical tables).
For a reversible Petri net with |R| = 2𝑚generators (forward/reverse pairs), anti-symmetry
reduces the free parameter space of (𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆) from 4𝑚to 2𝑚real numbers: 𝑚values of
Δ𝐻◦and 𝑚values of Δ𝑆◦, one per forward reaction — precisely the entries of a standard
thermochemical table [85, 54].
This matters for two distinct reasons.
First, it is canonical: the reduced parameter count matches exactly the format in which
experimental thermochemical data is tabulated and used. Standard references [85] list
one Δ𝐻◦
𝑓and one 𝑆◦per species, not separate entries for forward and reverse reactions.
The anti-symmetry axiom is not an extra mathematical assumption but the categorical
encoding of an empirical convention that is itself forced by energy conservation and the
state-function property.
Second, it is consistency-enforcing: without anti-symmetry, assigning independent values
to 𝑟and 𝑟† would permit 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟†) ≠0, violating energy conservation and making
the thermodynamic model internally inconsistent. Anti-symmetry is therefore the minimal
algebraic condition that keeps the decorating functors in agreement with the physical
content they are supposed to represent.
§4.3. The Gibbs functor and the equilibrium locus
With both 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆available on L0(𝑃), the Gibbs free energy functor is an immediate
derived object: no new axiom, no new structure, only a linear combination of the two
functors already in hand.

concept as zero set, vanishing locus, or level set at zero, and appears throughout algebra
and geometry [87].

ideal: the algebraic set of concentration vectors 𝑥∈R𝑛

4.3.1. Reversal symmetry of the standard Gibbs-zero locus
Detailed balance is a central principle of chemical kinetics and non-equilibrium thermody-
namics. Chemically, it states that at thermodynamic equilibrium, every elementary reaction
step is individually balanced by its reverse: the forward and reverse fluxes through each
step are equal, not merely the net flux around each cycle [62, 9]. For a single reversible step
𝑟: 𝐴⇌𝐵with forward rate constant 𝑘+ and reverse rate constant 𝑘−, detailed balance at
an equilibrium concentration vector requires
𝑘+[𝐴]eq = 𝑘−[𝐵]eq,
which gives 𝐾eq = 𝑘+/𝑘−. This is a kinetic flux equality, requiring rate constants and
equilibrium concentrations — data that lives at L3, not L2.

§4.4. Layer 1 and Layer 2 for 𝐹𝑆, the third law, and standard chemical potential
The Layer 1/Layer 2 split introduced for 𝐹𝐻in Sections 3.3 and 3.4 applies to 𝐹𝑆with the
same categorical structure but one physically decisive difference at Layer 2.
At Layer 1, the structure is identical for both functors: 𝐹𝑆is any strict SMC functor
𝐹𝑆: L0(𝑃) →𝐵R, with no constraint beyond the functor axioms (and anti-symmetry
𝐹𝑆(𝑟†) = −𝐹𝑆(𝑟) for reversible nets, Definition 4.6). The Layer 1 parameter space for 𝐹𝑆
has |R| free real numbers, reduced to |R|/2 by anti-symmetry for reversible Petri nets.
This is entirely parallel to 𝐹𝐻: one real number per generating reaction, freely chosen, with
no further constraint.
At Layer 2, both 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆are required to satisfy a state-function condition: each must
arise as the coboundary 𝛿0ℎof a species-level potential ℎ. The categorical machinery

4.4.1. Layer 2 for 𝐹𝑆: the entropy state-function condition

This is the sole asymmetry between 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆at Layer 2, and it has no categorical source:

physical convention used to fix a distinguished representative.

§4.5. Thermodynamic theorems at L2
The Gibbs family 𝑇↦→𝐹𝑇
𝐺= 𝐹𝐻−𝑇· 𝐹𝑆suffices to derive, within the categorical framework
of L2, four classical results of chemical thermodynamics as theorems for reaction networks:
the second law criterion for chemical spontaneity (Proposition 4.24), the van ’t Hoff equation
for the temperature dependence of equilibrium constants, the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation
recovering the reaction enthalpy from free-energy measurements, and Le Chatelier’s
principle for temperature perturbations. Each is a statement about morphisms in L0(𝑃)
labelled by the Gibbs family; none requires data beyond what is already in L2.

4.5.3. The van ’t Hoff equation
The van ’t Hoff equation: history and use
The van ’t Hoff equation describes how the equilibrium constant of a reaction changes
with temperature. It was derived by Jacobus Henricus van ’t Hoff in 1884 from
the Clausius–Clapeyron equation and Hess’s Law [94, 54], and is one of the most
practically important equations in chemical thermodynamics.
Its primary use is measurement: plotting ln 𝐾eq against 1/𝑇(the van ’t Hoff plot)
gives a straight line with slope −𝐹𝐻(𝑟)/𝑅and intercept 𝐹𝑆(𝑟)/𝑅when 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆
are temperature-independent. This allows 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) and 𝐹𝑆(𝑟) to be extracted from
equilibrium constant measurements at multiple temperatures, without calorimetry.
The van ’t Hoff plot is the experimental foundation for the Layer 1 parameter space: it
is the direct measurement procedure that assigns one real number (𝐹𝑇
𝐺, at any chosen
reference temperature) to each reaction.
In our framework, the equation is not a separate physical input but a two-line
consequence of differentiating the affine function 𝑇↦→ln 𝐾eq(𝑟,𝑇) = −𝐹𝑇

with respect to𝑇. The approximation that 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) and 𝐹𝑆(𝑟) are temperature-independent
corresponds to a 𝑇-independent reading of the Layer 2 potentials — i.e., using fixed
ℎ𝑓(𝑆,𝑇ref) and ℎ𝑆(𝑆,𝑇ref) at a reference temperature and ignoring heat-capacity
corrections. Fully temperature-dependent Layer 2 data — available for both ℎ𝑓(𝑆,𝑇)
and ℎ𝑆(𝑆,𝑇) in the references like JANAF tables [44] — gives the integrated form of
the van ’t Hoff equation accounting for 𝐶𝑝(𝑇).

4.5.4. The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation: physical meaning and practical use
The Gibbs–Helmholtz equation [93, 95, 54] is the relation between the temperature
dependence of the Gibbs free energy and the enthalpy of a process. Physically, it
answers the following question: if one measures Δ𝐺◦
𝑟= 𝐹𝑇
𝐺(𝑟) at two temperatures 𝑇1
and 𝑇2 without calorimetry, can one recover 𝐹𝐻(𝑟)?
The answer is yes: 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) is the slope of the function 𝐹𝑇

4.5.5. Le Chatelier’s principle
Observation 4.29 (Le Chatelier’s principle, under the constant-𝐹𝐻approximation). Under
the temperature-independent-enthalpy approximation inherited from Proposition 4.26, for
any generator 𝑟:
• 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) > 0 (endothermic): 𝑑ln 𝐾/𝑑𝑇> 0, so 𝐾increases with 𝑇. Heating shifts
equilibrium toward products.
• 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) < 0 (exothermic): 𝑑ln 𝐾/𝑑𝑇< 0, so 𝐾decreases with 𝑇. Heating shifts
equilibrium toward reactants.
• 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) = 0 (thermoneutral): 𝐾is independent of 𝑇.

This is Le Chatelier’s principle [96] for temperature perturbations: a system at equilibrium
responds to heating by shifting in the endothermic direction. At L2 it is a theorem in the
same approximation that supports the van ’t Hoff equation; if heat-capacity effects change
the sign of Δ𝐻◦over the temperature interval considered, the directional statement must be
re-evaluated using the integrated van ’t Hoff form.
§4.6. Wegscheider conditions at L2
Wegscheider conditions in the CRNT literature
The Wegscheider conditions were introduced by Rudolf Wegscheider in 1901 [61] as
necessary constraints on the equilibrium constants of a reversible reaction network
with cycles. For a directed cycle 𝑟1, . . . , 𝑟𝑘in the reaction graph, the conditions state:
𝑘
Ö
𝑖=1
𝐾eq(𝑟𝑖, 𝑇) = 1,
equivalently,
𝑘
∑︁
𝑖=1
ln 𝐾eq(𝑟𝑖, 𝑇) = 0.
Their physical content is that thermodynamics forbids perpetual motion: no network
of reactions can have a cycle in which every step is spontaneous, since that would
allow work to be extracted from a system at uniform temperature and pressure.
In the CRNT literature, the Wegscheider conditions appear as linear constraints on
the vector of ln 𝐾eq values. Horn and Jackson [8] showed that they are equivalent
to the existence of a thermodynamic potential (a species- level free energy function)
whose coboundary gives the reaction free energies — precisely the Layer 2 condition
𝐹𝑇
𝐺= 𝛿0ℎ𝜇◦of Proposition 4.22. Feinberg [9] used the conditions as a necessary
criterion for detailed balance in mass-action systems. Müller and Regensburger [97]
gave a systematic treatment of the conditions in the context of generalised mass-action
kinetics.
What is new in Proposition 4.31 below is not the conditions themselves but their
derivation: they follow directly and necessarily from Layer 2 applied independently
to 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆, without invoking kinetics or rate constants. In the standard CRNT
treatment, the conditions on Δ𝐻◦and Δ𝑆◦are stated separately from the multiplicative
condition on 𝐾eq values. The proof below shows they are the same condition at
different levels of the tower.
Before stating the proposition, we fix notation for the reaction graph.
Definition 4.30 (Reaction graph 𝐺(R) and directed cycle). The reaction graph 𝐺(R) of
a Petri net 𝑃is the directed graph whose vertices are the complexes u ∈N|S| and whose
directed edges are the generating reactions 𝑟: u →v in R. A directed cycle in 𝐺(R) of
length 𝑘is a sequence of generators 𝑟1, . . . , 𝑟𝑘∈R such that the target of each 𝑟𝑖equals
the source of 𝑟𝑖+1 (indices modulo 𝑘):
𝑟1 : u1 →u2,
𝑟2 : u2 →u3,
. . . ,
𝑟𝑘: u𝑘→u1.
Such a cycle determines a composite morphism 𝑟𝑘◦· · · ◦𝑟1 : u1 →u1 in L0(𝑃) whose
source and target coincide. This composite need not equal idu1 — in the free skeletal
permutative category L0(𝑃), distinct sequences of chemical generators can yield distinct
morphisms with the same source and target. The cycle conditions that follow are the
statement that this composite maps to 0 under 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, and 𝐹𝐺, despite not being the identity
morphism.

independently, and consistency at all temperatures forces both to satisfy the cycle
condition separately.

the uncatalysed pathway and the enzyme-catalysed pathway. Both pathways coexist in

The swap is an L2-automorphism not lifting to L3. The swap 𝜎: 𝑟𝐴↔𝑟𝐵

What L3 adds: rates, time, and stochastic dynamics
At L2, two physically distinct systems can be indistinguishable: they share the same

These are the three axioms of a strict symmetric monoidal functor, now targeting 𝔤S rather
than 𝐵R. The extension is forced by the same physical logic; what changes is the additive
monoid in which the new datum lives — from R to the cone 𝔤S of Markov-semigroup

§5.2. Definition of L3(𝑃) and the target Stoch
5.2.1. The Markov generator algebra and the ambient Stoch
The stochastic description of a chemical reaction network is classical: given the countable
state space of species-count vectors x ∈N|S| — or a finite closed irreducible subset of
it, when conservation laws bound the total copy numbers — the network evolves as a
continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) whose generator encodes the rates at which each
reaction fires [107, 10]. This description underlies a large body of work in the CRNT
literature — on stationary distributions [108, 109], on product-form Poisson distributions
and their extensions [110], and on stochastic approximation of arbitrary distributions [111]
— without requiring a categorical language.
Two categorical objects are needed to make the compositional structure of CTMCs explicit:
• the symmetric monoidal category Stoch, in which finite-time Markov kernels
𝐾( · | 𝑥) compose by Chapman–Kolmogorov integration — the ambient setting in
which the time-evolved chain lives;
• the cone 𝔤S of Markov generators on N|S|, viewed as the morphism set of the
one-object strict SMC 𝐵𝔤S, with sequential composition by addition, monoidal
product by Kronecker sum, and unit the zero generator — the actual functorial target
of the kinetic functor FP.
Generators and kernels are linked by exponentiation exp𝑡: 𝐿↦→𝑒𝑡𝐿, which sends a
generator 𝐿∈𝔤S to its one-parameter Markov semigroup {𝑒𝑡𝐿}𝑡≥0 in EndStoch(N|S|). This
section defines both, and shows that FP targets 𝐵𝔤S at the categorical level — with Stoch
entering only as the home of finite-time evolution.
Definition 5.1 (Stoch). The category Stoch has:
• Objects: measurable spaces (𝑋, Σ𝑋).
• Morphisms: Markov kernels 𝐾: 𝑋→𝑌, i.e. functions 𝐾: 𝑋× Σ𝑌→[0, 1] such
that (i) for each 𝑥∈𝑋, 𝐾(𝑥, ·) is a probability measure on (𝑌, Σ𝑌), and (ii) for each
𝐴∈Σ𝑌, the map 𝐾(·, 𝐴) : 𝑋→[0, 1] is measurable.
• Composition: for 𝐾: 𝑋→𝑌and 𝐿: 𝑌→𝑍, (𝐿◦𝐾)(· | 𝑥) :=
∫
𝑌𝐿(· | 𝑦) 𝐾(𝑑𝑦| 𝑥)
(Chapman–Kolmogorov integration).
• Monoidal product: (𝑋, Σ𝑋) ⊗(𝑌, Σ𝑌) := (𝑋× 𝑌, Σ𝑋⊗Σ𝑌), with (𝐾1 ⊗𝐾2)(· |
𝑥1, 𝑥2) := 𝐾1(· | 𝑥1) ⊗𝐾2(· | 𝑥2).
• Monoidal unit: the one-point space 𝐼= ({∗}, {∅, {∗}}).
Stoch is a symmetric monoidal category under this structure; it is moreover a Markov
category in the sense of Fritz [103], with a canonical copy/discard structure that encodes
conditional independence [103, 104].
Definition 5.2 (The generator algebra 𝐵𝔤S). The Markov-generator algebra 𝔤S is the
positive cone of generators of Markov semigroups on N|S|: a (possibly unbounded) operator
𝐿on observables 𝑓: N|S| →R with off-diagonal-non-negative matrix entries and rows
summing to zero, closable to a CTMC under standard non-explosion conditions [112]. The
one-object category 𝐵𝔤S has a single formal object ∗— interpreted as the global state
space N|S|, the carrier on which every complex u ∈L0(𝑃) acts under FP — and morphism
set End(∗) = 𝔤S. 𝐵𝔤S is a strict symmetric monoidal category:

• sequential composition: addition, 𝐿1 + 𝐿2;
• monoidal product: Kronecker sum, 𝐿1 ⊗𝐼+ 𝐼⊗𝐿2 (the infinitesimal of the kernel
tensor product in Stoch);
• unit: the zero generator on N|S|.
All associativity, unit, and symmetry equations hold as equalities, not merely up to
isomorphism.
𝐵𝔤S versus 𝐵R
At L1 and L2 the target was 𝐵R: one object, morphisms R, sequential composition
and monoidal product both given by addition. 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆were essentially monoid
homomorphisms (Mor(L0(𝑃)), ◦, ⊗) →(R, +, +), labelling each reaction by a single
real number.
At L3 the target 𝐵𝔤S is structurally parallel — one object, morphism set additive, with
sequential composition and monoidal product both additive in their respective senses
— but the additive monoid is enriched from R to the cone 𝔤S of Markov-semigroup
generators on N|S|. This enrichment has three direct probabilistic consequences:
• Morphisms encode full stochastic transitions. A generator 𝐿∈𝔤S encodes,
via exponentiation 𝑒𝑡𝐿, the entire family of finite-time transition probabilities
𝑃(x(𝑡) ∈· | x(0) = x) of the underlying CTMC [107]. At L1 and L2, a
reaction 𝑟was labelled by a single real number; at L3 the label FP(𝑟) ∈𝔤S is
an unbounded operator on observables that determines, after exponentiation,
every conditional probability associated with 𝑟.
• Sequential composition is operator addition, extending real addition. For
composable reactions, FP(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = FP(𝑟2) + FP(𝑟1) in 𝔤S (Proposition 5.10).
This sum is the generator of the CTMC in which both reaction channels are
simultaneously available; it is not an effective single-step rate law for the
coarse-grained reaction u →w obtained by eliminating the intermediate (which
would require a quasi-steady-state reduction outside the strict L3 functorial
assignment). The collapse to scalar addition recovers L1/L2 additivity in the
degenerate one-state case.
• Monoidal product is Kronecker sum, extending real addition. For reactions
on independent subsystems with disjoint species sets, FP(𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2) = FP(𝑟1) ⊗𝐼+
𝐼⊗FP(𝑟2) as generator contributions on the joint state space (Proposition 5.11).
This is the infinitesimal of the kernel tensor product in Stoch and encodes
probabilistic independence [103]: each subsystem evolves on its own Poisson
clock. Again, this collapses to real addition in the degenerate one-state case.
The three axioms of a strict SMC functor FP : L0(𝑃) →𝐵𝔤S have non-trivial
probabilistic content while preserving the structural role of “additive functor” that 𝐹𝐻
and 𝐹𝑆played at lower levels. The Markov-kernel interpretation of these data — the
finite-time transition probabilities — lives in Stoch and is recovered from FP(𝑟) by
exponentiation 𝑒𝑡FP(𝑟), which intertwines addition with kernel composition only on
the abelian locus of 𝔤S (the Trotter–Kato obstruction; this non-functoriality of exp𝑡is
the categorical content of the L3 →L4 forcing pair, Section 5.9).
Remark 5.3 (Why exp𝑡is not an SMC functor). The functor FP : L0(𝑃) →𝐵𝔤S takes
values in generators, not in finite-time Markov kernels. The link to Stoch proper is the
exponential exp𝑡: 𝐿↦→𝑒𝑡𝐿, which sends 𝐿∈𝔤S to its one-parameter Markov semigroup of

5.2.2. The state space is L0 data
In classical CRNT, species counts in N|S| is read off directly from the reaction network: the
species set S is part of the network definition, and a state is simply a non-negative integer
count for each species. No kinetic data — no rate constants, no activation energies — are
needed to write down N|S|. The stoichiometric change vector n𝑟of a reaction 𝑟is likewise
determined by the network’s stoichiometry alone (the left- and right-hand side complexes),
as discussed in Chapter 2. In the tower language, this means N|S| and n𝑟are L0 data: they
are visible at the stoichiometric level before any rate constants are introduced.
Observation 5.4 (State space from L0). The kinetic state space N|S| is determined entirely
by L0 data:
• The species set S is a L0 datum.
• A state is a species-count vector x = (𝑥𝑠)𝑠∈S ∈N|S|.
• The stoichiometric change vector of generator 𝑟: u →v is n𝑟:= 𝝂(v) −𝝂(u) ∈Z|S|,
directly read from the L0 morphism 𝑟.
The single new datum at L3 is a positive rate constant 𝑘𝑟∈R>0 per generator. Everything
else required to define FP(𝑟) is already present in L0(𝑃).

𝑃: given any strict SMC C with strictly commutative object monoid, an assignment of
(i) species in S to objects of C and (ii) chemical generators 𝑟∈R to morphisms in C
with matching sources and targets extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor L0(𝑃) →C.
The target C = 𝐵𝔤S (Definition 5.2) is one-object, so its object monoid is the singleton
— trivially strictly commutative — and the species assignment (i) is forced to map every
species to the unique object ∗; only the morphism assignment (ii) carries information.
The proposed assignment 𝑟↦→𝑀𝜆𝑟(𝑅𝑟−𝐼) ∈𝔤S is well-typed: 𝜆𝑟≥0 pointwise, the
matrix entries of 𝑀𝜆𝑟(𝑅𝑟−𝐼) are off-diagonal-non-negative with zero row sums (the
defining structure of a Markov generator), and the assembled Í
𝑟FP(𝑟) admits a closure
generating a Markov semigroup under standard non-explosion conditions [107, 112].
Applying the universal property of L0(𝑃) to this assignment yields the unique strict SMC
functor FP : L0(𝑃) →𝐵𝔤S extending 𝑘; the value on each generator is determined by n𝑟
(from L0, fixing 𝑅𝑟) and 𝑘𝑟(the new datum at L3).
□
Proposition 5.7 has the same logical structure as the existence-and-uniqueness statements
for 𝐹𝐻(Proposition 3.2) and 𝐹𝑆(Proposition 4.2): in all three cases, the universal property
of the free skeletal permutative category L0(𝑃) guarantees that a single real-valued
assignment per chemical generator extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor on all of
L0(𝑃). The only difference is what the real number labels and where it lands, which is
precisely what the insightbox below records.

5.3.2. Functoriality unpacked
Two reactions 𝑟1 and 𝑟2 can be arranged in sequence in L0(𝑃): the target complex of
𝑟1 is the source complex of 𝑟2, giving a composite morphism 𝑟2 ◦𝑟1 in L0(𝑃). The
functor axiom FP(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = FP(𝑟2) ◦FP(𝑟1) in the target 𝐵𝔤S unpacks — since sequential
composition in 𝐵𝔤S is operator addition (Definition 5.2) — as the additivity of generator
contributions:
FP(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = FP(𝑟2) + FP(𝑟1)
in 𝔤S.
This is a statement about generator-level assembly: the right-hand side is the generator
of the CTMC in which both reaction channels 𝑟1 and 𝑟2 are simultaneously available
on the joint state space. It is not an effective single-step rate law for the coarse-grained
reaction u →w; eliminating the intermediate complex v requires a quasi-steady-state or
rapid-equilibrium reduction outside the strict L3 functorial assignment, recovered only as
a derived approximation under additional hypotheses on the rate constants. At the level

addition (Definition 5.2; the standard additivity of CME generator contributions [107]), so

in 𝔤S.

tions FP(𝑟𝑖) = 𝑀𝜆𝑟𝑖(𝑅𝑟𝑖−𝐼) add. The two live in different algebras — the shift semigroup
of bounded operators on observables and the additive cone 𝔤S of Markov generators —
and FP uses each in its proper place: the multiplicative structure of 𝑅𝑟inside the individual
𝑀𝜆𝑟(𝑅𝑟−𝐼), and the additive structure of 𝔤S when assembling contributions along a L0
composite. This additive assembly is the generator of the joint CTMC, not an effective
rate law for the coarse-grained one-step reaction u →w; recovering an effective rate law

strict L3 functorial assignment.
□
What this proposition means physically, and what it does not
What it says. Sequential reactions compose correctly at the levels of stoichiometry
and generator-of-joint-CTMC: if 𝑟1 consumes species 𝐴and produces 𝐵, and 𝑟2
consumes 𝐵and produces 𝐶, then the net stoichiometric change of doing both is the
shift from the 𝐴-count to the 𝐶-count, and the generator of the CTMC with both
channels available is FP(𝑟2) + FP(𝑟1). This is the additive content of Hess’s Law
applied to stoichiometry — the overall stoichiometric balance is independent of how
it is decomposed into elementary steps.
What it does not say. The proposition does not claim that the effective rate at which
the coarse-grained reaction 𝐴→𝐶proceeds is some simple function of 𝜅𝑟1 and 𝜅𝑟2.
The actual time evolution of the joint CTMC depends on both propensities through
the Gillespie waiting times [113], and eliminating the intermediate species 𝐵to
obtain an effective one-step rate law requires quasi-steady-state or rapid-equilibrium
103

reduction — a chemical-engineering approximation valid only when 𝐵is short-lived,
and not part of the strict L3 assignment. The proposition captures stoichiometric
composition and joint-CTMC assembly; effective coarse-grained rates are a separate,
approximation-dependent question.
5.3.3. Monoidality unpacked
Two reactions 𝑟1 and 𝑟2 can also be placed in independent parallel subsystems with disjoint
species sets S1 and S2. The monoidal product 𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2 is their simultaneous presence in
the joint system, and the functor axiom FP(𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2) = FP(𝑟1) ⊗FP(𝑟2) demands that the
joint generator contribution decomposes correctly. This is the categorical expression of the
familiar CTMC independence result: two reactions on disjoint species evolve independently,
and their joint generator is the sum of the individual generators, a fact used constantly when
constructing modular kinetic models [116].
Proposition 5.11 (Monoidality of FP: parallel reactions). For generators 𝑟1 and 𝑟2 in
independent subsystems with disjoint species sets S1, S2,
FP(𝑟1 ⊗𝑟2) = FP(𝑟1) ⊗FP(𝑟2)
as generator contributions on the joint state space N|S1| ×N|S2|. At the level of the assembled
CME generators (Definition 5.13 in Section 5.4), this corresponds to the Kronecker sum:
Ω12 = Ω1 ⊗𝐼+ 𝐼⊗Ω2.
Proof. Independent reactions act on independent coordinates of the joint state (x1, x2).
Reaction 𝑟1 fires at propensity 𝜆𝑉
𝑟1(x1) independently of x2, and 𝑟2 fires at propensity 𝜆𝑉
𝑟2(x2)
independently of x1 (volume scaling per Definition 5.8). The generator contribution of 𝑟1 on

□
Remark 5.12 (Kronecker sum versus tensor product of generators). The Kronecker sum
Ω12 = Ω1 ⊗𝐼+ 𝐼⊗Ω2 is the generator of independent parallel evolution: each subsystem
runs on its own Poisson clock, and the two clocks are independent. The tensor product
Ω1 ⊗Ω2 would describe simultaneous firing of both reactions at every event — a different
(and physically unnatural) process. This distinction is the categorical precision behind the
everyday CRNT modelling choice to write ¤c = 𝑁1v1 + 𝑁2v2 for a combined network rather
than any product structure [10].
§5.4. The Chemical Master Equation
The chemical master equation (CME) was introduced by McQuarrie [114] as the master
equation for stochastic chemical kinetics and was given its definitive probabilistic foundation
by Gillespie [113, 115], who derived it from first principles of molecular collision theory.
Within the tower, the CME is not an independent postulate: it is the object obtained by
assembling all the generator contributions {FP(𝑟)}𝑟∈R assigned by the kinetic functor.
Specifically, FP assigns an operator FP(𝑟) = 𝑀𝜆𝑟(𝑅𝑟−𝐼) to each generating reaction 𝑟via
the universal property of L0(𝑃) (Proposition 5.7). The CME generator Ω is the sum of all

image of FP.
This assembly step — summing over all reactions — is what distinguishes L3 from L1 and
L2: the functors 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) ∈R and 𝐹𝑆(𝑟) ∈R are direct numerical outputs of the functor on a
single morphism, whereas the CME generator requires summing FP(𝑟) over all generators
in R. The analogue at L1 would be to form Í

sum vanishes identically by the additive content of Hess’s Law on cycles (§3.3), so it
produces no new object; here the sum genuinely produces a new mathematical entity, the
infinitesimal generator of a Markov semigroup.

Reading the CME term by term
Each summand in the CME has two contributions, familiar from any textbook treatment
of CTMCs [116]:
• Gain term: 𝜆𝑟(x −n𝑟) 𝑝(x −n𝑟, 𝑡) — probability flowing into state x from the

• Loss term: 𝜆𝑟(x) 𝑝(x, 𝑡) — probability flowing out of state x via reaction 𝑟.
The net change in 𝑝(x, 𝑡) is the algebraic sum of all gains and losses across all reactions.

The RRE is the image of FP under the scaling limit: a derived object, not a primitive.
The CME is primary at L3; the deterministic mass-action equation that CRNT
practitioners reach for first is, from the tower’s perspective, the large-volume shadow
of the stochastic truth, and the time-𝑡Markov kernels in Stoch are its exponentiation.
This ordering — CME primary, RRE derived — is the precise sense in which L3 is a
stochastic level.
§5.5. Layer 1 and 2 for FP: thermodynamic consistency and detailed balance
Every level of the tower so far has had two sub-layers. Layer 1 is the minimal structure
forced by the universal property of L0(𝑃): given any assignment of the new datum to
generators, a unique functor extension exists. Layer 2 is an additional coherence condition
that locks the new functor to the structure already present at lower levels of the tower. At
L1, Layer 2 was the coboundary condition 𝐹𝐻= 𝛿0ℎ𝑓(Proposition 3.7), which forced 𝐹𝐻
values around closed loops to sum to zero — a condition internal to L1. At L2, Layer 2
was the Wegscheider cycle condition (Proposition 4.31), requiring 𝐹𝑇
𝐺to vanish on every
closed loop in 𝐺(R) — a condition forced by the †-SMC structure of L2.
At L3, the new functor FP inherits from below: both 𝐹𝑇
𝐺(an L2 derived quantity) and
the †-structure on L0(𝑃) (which gives every generator 𝑟a reverse 𝑟†) are already present
in the tower. The question is: what does it mean for FP to be compatible with this
inherited structure? The answer, derived below, is that FP must be †-compatible: the
Markov chain generated by Ω = Í
𝑟FP(𝑟) must satisfy detailed balance with respect to the
thermodynamic equilibrium locus E𝑇from L2. This compatibility condition is precisely
the kinetic Wegscheider condition [61, 9], and it is not an independent postulate — it is
forced by the tower’s †-structure.
5.5.1. Layer 1: any positive rate constants form a valid CME
Layer 1 for FP: any assignment 𝑘: R →R>0 defines a valid strict SMC functor
FP : L0(𝑃) →Stoch by Proposition 5.7. For a reversible Petri net with |R| = 2𝑚
generators (forward and reverse pairs), there are 2𝑚free positive-real parameters. The
assembled CME generator Ω = Í
𝑟∈R FP(𝑟) (Definition 5.13) is a valid Markov generator
for any such assignment: the columns of Ω sum to zero and off-diagonal entries are
non-negative.
This means FP at Layer 1 is decoupled from the thermodynamics of L2: the rate constants
𝑘𝑟and 𝑘𝑟† can be chosen independently, with no reference to 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, or 𝐹𝑇
𝐺. The following
insightbox shows what goes wrong categorically when this decoupling persists.

5.5.3. Cycle form of the kinetic Wegscheider condition
The pairwise condition of Definition 5.21 extends to all closed loops in the reaction graph
— this is the classical content of Wegscheider’s original 1901 result [61], and it is the
condition used in modern CRNT to characterise detailed-balanced networks [8, 9, 10]. In
the tower language, a closed loop is a composable sequence of generators 𝑟1, . . . , 𝑟𝑛∈R in
L0(𝑃) such that 𝑟𝑛◦· · · ◦𝑟1 = idu for some complex u; equivalently, it is a cycle in the
directed graph 𝐺(R). The cycle form of Layer 2 is then a direct consequence of applying
the functoriality of 𝐹𝑇
𝐺to such a cycle, combined with Definition 5.21.

§5.6. The Deficiency Zero Theorem: level stratification
The Deficiency Zero Theorem (DZT) is the central result of classical CRNT [47, 42].
Within the tower, it has a specific structural role: its hypotheses belong entirely to L0,
while its conclusion is an L3 statement holding uniformly across every choice of FP over
a fixed L0 structure. This section analyses the L0 →L3 transition that makes such a
quantification possible, and relates it to the forgetful map 𝑈3 : L3(𝑃) →L0(𝑃).
The DZT hypotheses — weak reversibility and deficiency 𝛿= 0 — were stated in
Definition 2.25 as properties of the Petri net 𝑃alone. Within the tower, this places them
squarely at L0: the complex count 𝑛, the linkage-class count ℓ, the stoichiometric rank 𝑠,
the deficiency 𝛿= 𝑛−ℓ−𝑠, and the weak-reversibility condition on the directed reaction
graph 𝐺(R) are all invariants of L0(𝑃), computable without reference to rate constants,
enthalpies, or entropies.
The conclusion of the DZT — existence, uniqueness, and asymptotic stability of a positive
steady state — has no analogue at L0: there is no notion of dynamics, let alone a steady
state, without the rate functor FP. The new content at L3 is therefore entirely on the
conclusion side. Specifically, the DZT makes a statement not about one particular FP, but
about the entire fiber of the forgetful map 𝑈3 : L3(𝑃) →L0(𝑃) over a fixed L0 structure:
𝑈−1

5.6.2. The stochastic DZT: Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz
Theorem 5.26 and the tower-native fragment of Proposition 5.28 are both statements
about the large-volume limit Φ∞(Ω): they concern the vector field obtained by sending
the stochastic system to its deterministic mean-field RRE. Proposition 5.28(iii) gave a
partial stochastic counterpart under reversibility and Layer 2. A natural question within
the tower is whether the same L0 hypotheses — 𝛿= 0 and weak reversibility, without a
Layer-2 requirement — enforce a canonical form for the stationary distribution of the full
stochastic system on the assembled CME generator Ω directly, before any large-volume
limit. The answer is yes: the Anderson–Craciun–Kurtz theorem [107] establishes that Ω
has a stationary distribution of product-of-Poissons form, with Poisson parameters given
by the complex-balanced equilibrium c∗(𝑘) of Theorem 5.26(iii). This is the stochastic
analogue of the DZT: the same L0 hypotheses, now applied to the full L3 object Ω rather
than its large-volume shadow, and — unlike Proposition 5.28(iii) — without requiring
reversibility.

§5.7. Compositional kinetics: gluing open L3 networks
The tower’s L3 assembly is already well-behaved under two operations on reaction sets:
sequential composition of reactions (Proposition 5.10) and disjoint union of species sets
(Proposition 5.11). A mild extension of these properties handles a third operation that is
ubiquitous in real chemistry: gluing two networks at shared boundary species. Enzymatic
modules feeding a metabolic pathway, a receptor coupled to a downstream signalling
cascade, an autocatalytic network buffered by a reservoir — all are composites of smaller
networks joined at interface species. The compositional framework of Baez and Pollard
[31] makes this gluing rigorous and shows that the tower’s deterministic limit Φ∞(Ω) and
its steady states compose correctly under it.
Informally, an open L3 network is a closed L3(𝑃) together with two distinguished subsets
of S playing the role of inputs and outputs (boundary species where material may flow
in or out of the network), with the remaining species internal. Two open networks are
glued by identifying the output species of the first with the input species of the second;
shared species become internal to the composite, and the rate constants of both networks
are retained. The formal framework uses Fong’s decorated cospans [119, 31]: cospans
of species sets in FinSet decorated by L3 data, with composition given by pushout of the
underlying cospans combined with functorial composition of decorations.
Theorem 5.30 (Compositional kinetics [31, Thms. 18 and 23]). Gluing of open L3 networks
is compatible with both the deterministic dynamics and the steady-state boundary behaviour.
Specifically, for composable open networks L3(𝑃1) and L3(𝑃2) sharing an interface of
boundary species:
(i) (Gray-boxing) The large-volume vector field Φ∞(Ω12) of the composite decomposes
as the sum of the individual vector fields Φ∞(Ω1) and Φ∞(Ω2), extended across the
shared interface by restriction and summation of reaction velocities.

For a metabolic pathway built from 𝑛enzymatic modules, each reduced to its Michaelis–
Menten input–output relation by gray-boxing, Theorem 5.30 says the pathway’s
steady-state boundary behaviour is the relational composite of the individual module
relations under the Baez–Pollard cospan structure. For monotone cascades — each
module’s steady-state map strictly increasing in its input concentration — the relational
composite is itself functional, and the pathway inherits a single-valued input–output
rate law that recovers classical pipelined Michaelis–Menten analysis. For feedback or
multistable subnetworks, the relation is genuinely multi-valued: a single boundary
input may correspond to several internal steady states, and the relational composition
framework is the natural setting in which to track this — the cospan structure does
not collapse the multi-valuedness, whereas a functional-composition framing silently
would. This compositional treatment is the mathematical foundation of modular
metabolic control analysis.

Deficiency check. Treating the reaction as irreversible: 𝑛= 2 complexes (u and v), ℓ= 1
linkage class, 𝑠= 1 (rank of stoichiometric matrix 𝑁), so 𝛿= 2 −1 −1 = 0. The network

and irreversible reactions sit outside its scope.
What L3 cannot express. The propensity 𝜆𝑟(x) = 𝑘𝑟𝑥CH3Cl · 𝑥OH−describes the rate of
product formation, but encodes nothing about how the bonds rearrange. Any second-order
nucleophilic substitution R −X + Nu−→R −Nu + X−on a primary substrate gives the
same propensity functional form 𝜆∝𝑥R−X 𝑥Nu−, regardless of which substrate, leaving
group, and nucleophile are involved. The backside-attack geometry, the pentacoordinate
transition state, and the Walden inversion at the carbon centre are all invisible to FP.
The forcing observation for L4 is sharper still: two reactions with the same L3 data —
same complexes, same propensity functional form, same rate constant — can still differ at
the level of bond-level mechanism. The classical L3 →L4 forcing pairs are the concerted
SN2 versus the stepwise ion-pair SN1, and the concerted E2 versus the irreversible-stepwise
E1cb; both are taken up in the L4 chapter (Chapter 6), where the bond-graph rewriting
machinery of double pushout (DPO) provides exactly the discriminating structure that L3
lacks.
A common misreading should be guarded against: SN2 versus E2 is not an L3 →
L4 forcing pair. The bimolecular elimination of, say, 2-chlorobutane with hydroxide
␀C4H9Cl + OH−→C4H8 + H2O + Cl− is also second-order in concentrations, but it
produces an alkene plus water rather than a substitution product. The two reactions therefore
have different stoichiometric change vectors n𝑟and different target complexes, so they are
already separated at L0 by stoichiometry alone — not at L4 by bond-level mechanism.
Genuine L3 →L4 forcing requires reactions that agree on every L0, L1, L2, L3 datum
and differ only at the bond-graph rewriting layer; this is strictly subtler than the SN2 versus
E2 comparison.
§5.9. What L3 cannot express: forcing of L4
The tower so far — L0, L1, L2, L3 — shares a common underlying category L0(𝑃), the
free skeletal permutative category on 𝑃(Theorem 2.14), with each successive level adding
a decorating functor on top of it. Sections 5.1–5.7 have shown what L3 buys us: the CME,
the RRE, the Layer-2 coboundary condition, and compositional kinetics for open networks.
This subsection identifies what L3 cannot express, setting up the forcing pair that Chapter 6
resolves.
Forcing pair for L4: identity substitution at phosphorus
Consider the identity methoxyl exchange at the phosphorus center of methyl
ethylphenylphosphinate [30], with isotopic labelling on the incoming methoxide:
𝑟: 18OMe−+ Et(Ph)P(= O)OMe −→Et(Ph)P(= O)18OMe + OMe−.
127


## Page 128


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Source and target complexes are identical up to the 18O permutation; the only chemical
change is which methoxyl group is bound to phosphorus and which is free.
This transformation is realised in the laboratory by two distinct mechanisms:
System A (concerted SN2-P): methoxide attacks the phosphorus apically and displaces
the leaving methoxide through a single trigonal-bipyramidal transition state.
System B (addition-elimination): methoxide adds first to form a discrete pentacoordi-
nate trigonal-bipyramidal intermediate (TBI) with five P-bonds; the leaving methoxide
then eliminates from TBI in a second step.
At the bulk-kinetic level of L3, the two mechanisms are indistinguishable. System A
is a single bimolecular generator with propensity 𝜆(x) = 𝑘𝑥MeO−𝑥substrate. System B
has TBI as an internal species and two elementary steps; under the quasi-steady-state
reduction on TBI (valid when TBI is high-energy and short-lived, the standard regime
for phosphoryl chemistry under laboratory conditions), elimination of TBI from the
rate equations yields a coarse-grained generator with the same bimolecular form
𝜆(x) = 𝑘𝑥MeO−𝑥substrate,
where the effective 𝑘aggregates the addition rate constant and the elimination
selectivity at TBI. In this regime — the experimentally relevant one — Systems A and
B share every L3 datum. Outside the quasi-steady-state regime, System B exhibits a
Michaelis–Menten rate law that L3 can distinguish from System A’s strict bimolecular
form; the L3 ambiguity between concerted and stepwise phosphoryl mechanisms is
therefore contingent on the coarse-graining, not categorical, but the contingent regime
is precisely the one in which the laboratory operates.
Mikolajczyk et al. [30] note explicitly that “the kinetic measurements are often unable
to distinguish” SN2-P from addition-elimination at phosphorus; DFT computation
of the full energy profile, together with stereochemical analysis through Berry
pseudorotation, was required to settle the mechanism for the substrate above (System
B applies; the analogous chloride exchange in (EtO)Et(P=S)Cl goes by System A
[30]). The same kinetic blindness pervades enzymatic phosphoryl transfer, where the
concerted-versus-stepwise question has been a central mechanistic debate for decades
[131].
The two mechanisms correspond to distinct chemical generators
𝑟concerted, 𝑟stepwise ∈R

of L3(𝑃). It does not lift to any structure that records whether the reaction proceeds
via a single elementary bond rearrangement (one DPO span; the concerted pathway,
no internal intermediate) or via two composable bond rearrangements bracketing a
discrete TBI intermediate (two composable DPO spans, with TBI as a species in L4):

What minimal new structure resolves the ambiguity? The principled content distinguishing
𝑟concerted from 𝑟stepwise is the mechanism: which bonds break and form, whether the
reaction proceeds through a single transition state or through a discrete intermediate, and
— if an intermediate exists — what species it is. Encoding this requires replacing the
underlying category L0(𝑃) with a richer one in which morphisms carry bond-level data
and intermediates are themselves species. This is not a decoration of L0(𝑃) but a structural
extension, and constructing it is the task of Chapter 6.
This forces L4, which must add two ingredients [132, 133, 134]:
(i) A category LGraph of labelled molecular hypergraphs whose vertices carry atom
type, formal charge, and lone-pair count, and whose edges carry bond order. Species
in S become objects of LGraph.
(ii) Double pushout (DPO) rewriting: a reaction mechanism is a span 𝐿←𝐾→𝑅in
LGraph, specifying which bonds break (𝐿\𝐾) and which form (𝑅\𝐾). Application
to a molecular graph is a DPO in LGraph [135]. The underlying category L4(𝑃)
has DPO spans in LGraph as morphism generators, with composition by sequential
rewriting and monoidal product by disjoint union (Chapter 6).
The two pathways correspond to distinct DPO morphisms on the same input graph (methyl
ethylphenylphosphinate + isotopically labelled methoxide):
• Concerted (SN2-P): a single DPO span 𝐿←𝐾→𝑅in LGraph in which the
P–OMe bond is broken and the P–18OMe bond is formed simultaneously. The
interface 𝐾retains the phosphorus and its three non-participating ligands.
• Stepwise (addition-elimination): a composable pair of DPO spans 𝐿1 ←𝐾1 →𝑅1
followed by 𝐿2 ←𝐾2 →𝑅2, with the intermediate state graph encoding the
pentacoordinate TBI as an additional species in L4. The first span forms the P–
18OMe bond without breaking any bonds (addition); the second breaks the P–OMe
bond (elimination).
The two DPO morphisms are genuinely different in L4(𝑃) but project to the same morphism
in L3(𝑃) under the forgetful functor 𝑈4. The non-trivial element of coker(𝜑4) is the swap
between these two morphisms while fixing their common L3 image. The extension to L4
is forced by the existence of mechanistically distinct reactions whose L3 data coincide —
a phenomenon documented across substitution chemistry [30, 131], phosphoryl-transfer
biochemistry, and beyond.

§6. L4: The Mechanistic Level
§6.1. Forcing the extension: a structural break in the tower
The previous chapter identified the gap at L3: two reactions with the same source complex,
target complex, enthalpy, entropy, and mass-action propensity — the latter agreeing in
functional form by stoichiometry and in rate constant under steady-state on a buried
intermediate — can proceed through a single transition state, or stepwise through a
discrete intermediate species, yet L3 records no trace of the distinction. The cleanest
documented case is identity nucleophilic substitution at phosphorus, where concerted
SN2-P and stepwise addition–elimination through a pentacoordinate intermediate are
routinely indistinguishable by bulk kinetics [30, 131]. This section pinpoints the minimal
structural change at L4 required to separate them.
The conflation is in the underlying category
At L0 through L3, the underlying category is always L0(𝑃) = FreeSMC(𝑃):
morphisms are stoichiometric transitions u →v generated by reactions of 𝑃, and the
functors 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, FP decorate this category by assigning values to each morphism.
The Petri net 𝑃may contain distinct generators 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R with identical source and
target complexes — two reactions consuming and producing the same species in the
same quantities, differing only in mechanism. L0(𝑃) is therefore not thin: it can carry
several distinct morphisms between the same pair of complexes.
For genuinely competing mechanisms with the same source and target, identity at
L3 obtains whenever all four decoration values agree. 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆depend only on
source and target by Hess’s law and agree automatically. The mass-action functional
form of FP is fixed by the stoichiometry, hence agrees automatically. The remaining
datum is the rate constant: this agrees when the rate-limiting step in either mechanism
couples the same molecules in the same orders — in particular, under steady-state on
a buried intermediate with matching effective rate constants [30, 131]. The forcing
pair below is an idealisation in which all four L3 decorations agree exactly; this is the
regime in which bulk kinetic measurements cannot distinguish the mechanisms, and
is the regime in which the categorical indistinguishability witnessed by an element of
Aut(L3(𝑃)) holds.
The principled content separating 𝑟1 from 𝑟2 is the mechanism: which bonds break
and form, whether the reaction proceeds through a single transition state or through a
discrete intermediate, and what that intermediate is. Encoding this requires replacing
L0(𝑃) with a category in which morphisms carry bond-level data and intermediates
are themselves species — a structural extension, not a decoration.
The forcing pair for L4
For the methoxyl exchange at methyl ethylphenylphosphinate [30],
𝑟: 18OMe−+ Et(Ph)P(= O)OMe −→Et(Ph)P(= O)18OMe + OMe−,
two distinct generators 𝑟concerted, 𝑟stepwise ∈R realise the same source-target transfor-
mation:

• 𝑟concerted: a single trigonal-bipyramidal transition state, simultaneous P–OMe
cleavage and P–18OMe formation. No intermediate.
• 𝑟stepwise: a discrete pentacoordinate intermediate TBI, bracketed by addition
and elimination transition states.
Source and target are identical at the L0 species level (isotopes are below the species
resolution), so 𝐹𝐻and 𝐹𝑆agree by Hess’s law and Layer 2 is automatic (𝐾eq = 1).
Under steady-state on TBI, both mechanisms have rate law 𝜆= 𝑘𝑥MeO−𝑥substrate, and
within experimental resolution the effective rate constants agree, so FP takes the same
value on the two generators [30]. The full L3 tuple (L0, 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, 𝐹𝑇
𝐺, FP) therefore
takes the same value on 𝑟concerted and 𝑟stepwise, and the swap 𝑟concerted ↔𝑟stepwise
extends to a category automorphism of L3(𝑃) preserving all four decorations — an
element of Aut(L3(𝑃)).
At L4 the swap does not lift. The asymmetry is structural: 𝑟concerted is the 𝑈4-image
of a single double pushout (DPO) rule 𝑝concerted in L4(𝑃), whereas the stepwise
mechanism is realised at L4 only as the two-step composite 𝑝elim ◦𝑝add through the
intermediate molecular graph TBI; there is no single DPO rule 𝑝stepwise at L4. A
lift e𝜎∈Aut(L4(𝑃)) of the swap 𝜎would have to send the generator 𝑝concerted to
a generator of L4(𝑃) whose 𝑈4-image is 𝑟stepwise; no such generator exists. Hence
𝜎∉im(𝜑4), where 𝜑4 : Aut(L4(𝑃)) →Aut(L3(𝑃)) is the forgetful homomorphism.
Equivalently, 𝜎represents a non-trivial coset in the quotient Aut(L3(𝑃))/im(𝜑4),
which we call coker(𝜑4):

recurs across nucleophilic substitution at heteroatoms, biological phosphoryl transfer,
and a wide class of identity reactions [30, 131]; the explicit verification appears in

Structural rather than decorating extension. Earlier transitions added a functor while
keeping L0(𝑃) fixed — decorator extensions. At L4 the underlying category itself changes.
The tower is not forked: the L1–L3 decorations are retained at L4 by pullback along a
forgetful functor 𝑈4 : L4(𝑃) →L0(𝑃) (Section 6.6), with

What minimal structure resolves the ambiguity.
(i) Molecular graphs as objects. Each species becomes a labelled hypergraph: vertices
carry atom type, isotope, charge, lone-pair count, and radical count; edges carry bond
order [134, 133]. Reaction intermediates such as TBI become first-class species.
(ii) DPO derivations as morphisms. A reaction mechanism is a span 𝐿←𝐾→𝑅in
LGraph, specifying which bonds break and form [132, 136]; a multi-step mechanism
is a sequential composite through intermediate molecular graphs.

The substitution/elimination split is resolved already at L0 (different products). The
bimolecular/unimolecular split within each class (SN2 vs. SN1, E2 vs. E1) corresponds to
different rate-law forms, so it is resolved already at L3 — not a coker(𝜑4) pair, but a useful
illustration of how L4 realises the distinction structurally (carbocation as intermediate
species, two DPO spans versus one).
§6.2. Labelled molecular graphs: the ambient adhesive category
Section 6.1 identified two generators 𝑟concerted, 𝑟stepwise ∈R with identical L3 data, dis-
tinguished only by their identity tags in the Petri net. The tower up to L3 accepts them
as distinct only by fiat: no categorical structure on L0(𝑃) = FreeSMC(𝑃) supplies a
principled reason why they are different morphisms. The resolution requires a new under-
lying category whose morphisms carry bond-level information — atoms, bonds, formal
charges, electron counts — so that two generators projecting to the same stoichiometric
transition can nonetheless be distinct morphisms by virtue of their internal structure. This
section constructs that category in three steps: the label algebra that replaces species names
with molecular graphs (§6.2.1), the category LGraph of such graphs with its monoidal
and adhesive structure (§6.2.2–§6.2.3), and the grounded variant LGraph𝑃that connects
molecular graphs back to the species set S of the Petri net 𝑃(§6.2.4).
6.2.1. Label algebra and chemical validity
At L0(𝑃) through L3(𝑃), an object is an element of N|S|: a formal sum of species names
𝑆𝑖, recording how many molecules of each type are present but recording nothing about their
internal structure. To distinguish mechanisms with the same source and target complexes

## Page 134

— whether already separated at L3 or not — we need objects that encode atoms, bonds,
formal charges, and electron pairs. The following label algebra does precisely this.
The label set below is not original: it is a categorical reformulation of the data encoded in the
bond-electron (BE) matrix of Dugundji and Ugi [137], the standard matrix representation
of molecular structure in cheminformatics and computer-aided synthesis planning since
its introduction in 1973, in continuous use [138, 139], and the basis of some modern
machine-learning approaches to reaction prediction that enforce electron conservation [140].
What is new here is the organisation of that data into a quintuple (el, iso, 𝑞, 𝜌, ℓ) that
serves as a vertex label in a typed graph, making the connection to the DPO rewriting
framework canonical. Chemical graph transformation with typed molecular graphs is
developed in detail in Andersen et al. [138, 134]; our formulation is tailored to make the
validity condition explicit and to sit naturally inside the adhesive category framework of
Section 6.2.3.
Definition 6.2 (Atom label and bond label). Let Λ𝑉denote the set of all atom labels, where
each atom label is a quintuple 𝜆𝑣= (el, iso, 𝑞, 𝜌, ℓ) consisting of:
• el ∈{H, C, N, O, F, P, S, Cl, Br, I, . . .}: element type;
• iso ∈Iso(el) ∪{∗}: nuclear-mass label (e.g. 16O, 18O) or the wildcard ∗for natural
abundance / unspecified;
• 𝑞∈Z: formal charge;
• 𝜌∈{0, 1, 2}: radical electron count (0 closed-shell, 1 monoradical, 2 diradical);
• ℓ∈N: lone-pair (nonbonding electron-pair) count.
A bond label is an integer 𝑏∈{1, 2, 3} encoding bond order (single, double, triple). Absent
bonds carry the implicit value 𝑏= 0.
Remark 6.3 (Isotope labels at L4 as classical tracers). The component iso records nuclear
identity classically: it tracks 16O vs. 18O, 12C vs. 13C, etc., as label data attached to
vertices. This is what is needed to formulate identity-substitution forcing pairs (Section 6.1,
where the incoming methoxide is tagged 18O). What is postponed to L7 is not isotope
bookkeeping but isotope-dependent quantum phenomena: nuclear quantum statistics,
tunnelling, vibrational zero-point kinetic isotope effects. The wildcard ∗is the default for
atoms whose chemistry is isotope-independent.

6.2.2. The category LGraph
The label algebra of the preceding section gives data for individual atoms and bonds. To
speak categorically about reactions, we need molecular graphs to be objects and structure-
preserving maps between them to be morphisms. The following definition assembles these
ingredients into a symmetric monoidal category LGraph, which will serve as the ambient
category for the DPO rules that generate L4(𝑃).
Originality and comparison to existing work. The use of typed molecular graphs in
chemical graph transformation goes back to Ehrig et al. [133] and Andersen et al. [134].
Those works use a general typing morphism to a type graph, without committing to a
specific label algebra; our specialisation to the quintuple (el, iso, 𝑞, 𝜌, ℓ) of Definition 6.2
is what makes LGraph a suitable ambient category for mechanistic organic chemistry. The
architectural choice that distinguishes our development is to keep LGraph as the ambient
typed-graph category (adhesive in the sense of Lack–Sobociński [136], Proposition 6.10),
with chemical validity (Definition 6.4) imposed as a predicate on objects rather than as
a defining feature of category membership. This separation matters because pushouts of
chemically valid graphs in LGraph may produce chemically invalid graphs: adhesivity
holds for the ambient typed-graph category, while validity is enforced as an admissibility
condition on rule patterns and their products (Remark 6.11 below).
Definition 6.6 (Labelled typed graph). A labelled typed graph is a tuple 𝐺= (𝑉, 𝐸, 𝜆𝑉, 𝜆𝐸)
where:
• 𝑉is a finite set of vertices (atoms).
• 𝐸⊆

is a set of edges (bonds), i.e. a set of unordered pairs
of distinct vertices.
• 𝜆𝑉: 𝑉→Λ𝑉is the atom-label function, assigning to each vertex an atom label
(el, iso, 𝑞, 𝜌, ℓ) ∈Λ𝑉in the sense of Definition 6.2.
• 𝜆𝐸: 𝐸→{1, 2, 3} is the bond-order function.
No chemical-validity constraint is imposed on 𝐺at the level of object membership; chemical
validity (Definition 6.4) is a predicate on objects of LGraph used as an admissibility
condition on rule patterns (Remark 6.11).

The monoidal product is the disjoint union 𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2 (disjoint vertex and edge sets, labels
inherited), with unit the empty graph ∅. We work in a strictified skeleton in which disjoint
copies are fixed by a chosen tagging convention, so that ⊔is strictly associative and unital.
Proposition 6.8 (LGraph is a well-defined strict symmetric monoidal category). LGraph
with the structure of Definition 6.7 is a strict symmetric monoidal category.
Proof. Category. Composition of label-preserving monomorphisms is again a label-
preserving monomorphism (injectivity and label preservation are both stable under
composition). The identity injection id𝐺is label-preserving by definition, and serves as the
two-sided identity. Associativity of composition is inherited from function composition.
Strict monoidal. By the strictification convention adopted in Definition 6.7, disjoint copies
are fixed by a chosen tagging, so ⊔is strictly associative ((𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2) ⊔𝐺3 = 𝐺1 ⊔(𝐺2 ⊔𝐺3)
as objects) and strictly unital (𝐺⊔∅= 𝐺). The symmetry isomorphism 𝐺1⊔𝐺2  𝐺2⊔𝐺1
is the swap of tagged copies, natural in 𝐺1 and 𝐺2.
□
Remark 6.9 (Restriction to monomorphisms). Working with label-preserving monomor-
phisms rather than arbitrary label-preserving graph homomorphisms is standard in chemical
graph transformation [134]: it ensures that atoms are not identified and bond structures are
faithfully embedded. Concretely, a non-injective map could collapse two distinct atoms of
the same element type into one, destroying structural information. All results cited from
the DPO literature hold for injective matches [133].
6.2.3. Adhesivity of LGraph
The category LGraph carries more than just a monoidal structure: it is adhesive in the
sense of Lack and Sobociński [136], a property that makes DPO rewriting internally
consistent.
Adhesive categories. A category C is adhesive [136] if: (i) it has pushouts along monomor-
phisms; (ii) monomorphisms are stable under pushout (the pushout of a monomorphism
is again a monomorphism); and (iii) pushout squares along monomorphisms satisfy the
van Kampen condition: they are also pullbacks in a suitable double-categorical sense.
137


## Page 138


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Condition (iii), the van Kampen condition, is what makes DPO rewriting well-behaved:
combined with conditions (i) and (ii), it guarantees that pushout complements are unique up
to isomorphism (so the gluing context 𝐷in a DPO step is well-defined; see Remark 6.12 on
why 𝐷is not a chemical intermediate) and that independent rewriting steps can be applied
in either order with the same result (Local Church–Rosser). Without adhesivity, neither of
these properties is guaranteed and DPO rewriting in LGraph would be ill-defined.
Proposition 6.10 (LGraph is adhesive). The category LGraph with label-preserving
monomorphisms is adhesive in the sense of Lack and Sobociński.
Proof. The category Graph of (directed or undirected) graphs can be presented as a presheaf
topos: it is the functor category [G, Set] where G is the graph schema 𝑠, 𝑡: 𝐸⇒𝑉(two
objects and two parallel morphisms, encoding source and target of edges). Every presheaf
topos is adhesive [136, Corollary 3.6], so Graph is adhesive.
Now identify LGraph with the slice category Graph/𝑇𝐺Λ, where 𝑇𝐺Λ is the type graph:
the graph whose vertices are the atom labels Λ𝑉and whose edges carry all possible
bond labels {1, 2, 3} between every pair of label vertices. A labelled typed graph 𝐺in
the sense of Definition 6.6 is precisely a graph homomorphism 𝐺→𝑇𝐺Λ (the typing
morphism assigns each atom its label and each bond its order); LGraph  Graph/𝑇𝐺Λ
as categories. This identification is standard in typed graph transformation; see Ehrig et
al. [133, Chapter 2].
By Lack–Sobociński [136, Proposition 3.5(ii)], if C is adhesive then so is C/𝑋for every
object 𝑋. Since Graph is adhesive and LGraph  Graph/𝑇𝐺Λ, it follows that LGraph
is adhesive.
□
The three consequences of adhesivity for mechanism-level rewriting deserve explicit
statement. Adhesivity is what makes DPO derivations well-defined: without unique
pushout complements, the gluing context in a DPO step would not be well-defined;
without Local Church–Rosser, the order of independent steps would matter and sequential
composition would be ambiguous. These are not abstract concerns — they correspond to
concrete questions about mechanism: “Is the carbocation produced by ionisation in SN1
uniquely determined by the rule and the substrate?” (yes, by uniqueness of gluing contexts
and by the fact that the carbocation is a distinct molecular graph between two derivations);
“Does it matter whether we first abstract the proton or first ionise the leaving group in an E1
mechanism?” (Local Church–Rosser says no, when the steps are independent).
What adhesivity gives for chemistry
Proposition 6.10 guarantees three essential properties for DPO rewriting of labelled
typed graphs:
(i) Unique gluing contexts: if a DPO rule applies to a labelled graph, the gluing
context 𝐷(the host with the reaction-centre bonds removed, prior to gluing of 𝑅)
is unique up to isomorphism (Lemma 4.5 of [136]). 𝐷is a categorical artefact
of a single rule application, not, in general, a chemically isolable intermediate
(Remark 6.12).
(ii) Local Church–Rosser: two independent reaction steps (steps whose reaction
centres share no atoms) applied to the same molecule can be sequenced in
either order, reaching the same product (Theorem 7.7 of [136]). This is the
138


## Page 139


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
mechanism-level analogue of the fact that parallel reactions in distinct parts of
a molecule do not interfere.
(iii) Concurrency: a sequence of independent DPO steps can be represented by a
single composite rule (Theorem 7.11 of [136]). This is a semantic statement
about independent steps, not the basis of the free SMC structure of L4(𝑃),
which is by construction (Section 6.4).
Together, these guarantee that mechanism-level rewriting in LGraph is well-defined
and compositional — exactly what is needed for L4(𝑃) to be a category.
Remark 6.11 (Chemical validity is admissibility, not membership). Pushouts of chemically
valid graphs in LGraph may produce chemically invalid graphs: a pushout that introduces
a bond at an atom already saturated produces a graph whose row-sum law fails at that atom.
The full subcollection LGraphch ⊂LGraph of chemically valid graphs (Definition 6.4) is
therefore not closed under pushouts in LGraph and is not adhesive in its own right. The
architectural choice taken in this chapter is to perform all DPO constructions in the ambient
adhesive category LGraph and to require chemical validity as a separate admissibility
condition: a chemical DPO rule (Section 6.3) is a span 𝐿←𝐾→𝑅in LGraph with 𝐿
and 𝑅chemically valid, and a chemically admissible match 𝑚: 𝐿↩→𝐺into a valid host 𝐺
requires the resulting product graph 𝐻to be chemically valid. The validity check is local —
the row-sum law (or its hypervalent extension) at every atom of the product — and is the
content of Layer 2 at L4 (Section 6.7).
Remark 6.12 (The gluing context 𝐷is not a chemical intermediate). The pushout com-
plement 𝐷supplied by adhesivity is the host graph 𝐺with the reaction-centre bonds of
𝐿\ 𝑙(𝐾) deleted, prior to gluing of 𝑅. 𝐷is a categorical construction internal to a single
DPO step and is in general not a chemically isolable intermediate. A chemical intermediate,
when present, is a complete molecular graph appearing as the target of one DPO derivation
and the source of the next: the carbocation in SN1 (Section 6.9), the trigonal-bipyramidal
phosphorus intermediate in stepwise identity substitution (Section 6.8). The categorical role
of 𝐷is to mediate the two pushouts of a single rule application; its chemical interpretation,
when it has one, is a transient gluing context, not a species of the network.
6.2.4. The grounded category LGraph𝑃
The category LGraph treats labelled typed graphs as abstract combinatorial objects with
no reference to the Petri net 𝑃. But L4(𝑃) must sit in the tower above L0(𝑃): its host
objects must be compatible with the stoichiometric generator set of 𝑃, so that the forgetful
functor 𝑈4 : L4(𝑃) →L0(𝑃) (Section 6.6) is well-defined. The grounded category
LGraph𝑃enforces this compatibility: it equips every host graph with an assignment of its
connected components to species names in S, binding the abstract graph structure to the
chemical species of the network.
Definition 6.13 (Grounded labelled graph category LGraph𝑃). Given a Petri net 𝑃with
species set S, the grounded category LGraph𝑃has:
• Objects: pairs (𝐺, spec) where 𝐺∈LGraph and spec : 𝜋0(𝐺) →S assigns each
connected component of 𝐺to a species in S.
• Morphisms: label-preserving monomorphisms 𝑓: 𝐺↩→𝐻compatible with spec
(each component of 𝐺maps into the component of 𝐻bearing the same species
label).
