The monoidal product is grounded disjoint union; the unit is the empty graph with vacuous
spec. The category LGraph𝑃is adhesive; the proof reduces to adhesivity of LGraph via
a comma-category argument analogous to the slice argument for LGraph itself (Ehrig et
al. [133]).
The BE-matrix shadow of a DPO rule
A DPO rule (𝐿←𝐾→𝑅) in LGraph𝑃admits a BE-matrix shadow: a pair (𝐵, 𝐵′)
of BE-matrices [137] related by the reaction matrix 𝑅BE = 𝐵′ −𝐵[138, 141]. The
reactant graph 𝐿supplies 𝐵(off-diagonal entries = bond orders, diagonal entries =
2ℓ(𝑣) + 𝜌(𝑣)); the product graph 𝑅supplies 𝐵′; the context 𝐾identifies the rows and
columns on which 𝑅BE vanishes.
The shadow is faithful for net electron rearrangement but strictly weaker than the
DPO rule. What it does not record: isotope labels (16O and 18O share the same
matrix); atom-tracking under composition (BE matrices add, but the addition does
not say which atom in one matrix corresponds to which atom in the next — supplied
categorically by 𝐾and the match 𝑚); the species-grounding spec; and the categorical
match data of a derivation. The DPO framework on LGraph𝑃is therefore strictly
richer than the matrix shadow.
With LGraph𝑃in hand, the three ingredients needed for L4(𝑃) are in place: host graphs are
S-typed labelled graphs in LGraph𝑃, the generating morphisms are admissible chemical
DPO rules (chemically valid spans, Section 6.3), and the ambient adhesive structure of
LGraph guarantees that DPO derivations are well-defined. The free strict SMC structure
of L4(𝑃) is supplied by the universal property of the free SMC on the directed signature
of admissible DPO derivations (Section 6.4).
§6.3. DPO rules and derivations in LGraph𝑃
Section 6.2 built the ambient category LGraph𝑃: a strict symmetric monoidal adhe-
sive category whose objects are S-typed labelled graphs and whose morphisms are
label-preserving monomorphisms. Chemical validity (Definition 6.4) is enforced as an
admissibility condition on rule patterns and matches, not as a defining feature of object
membership (Remark 6.11). The morphisms of L4(𝑃) will be sequences of DPO deriva-
tions in LGraph𝑃— the precise way of saying “bonds break and form according to a
specified rule.” A DPO (double pushout) derivation specifies a reaction by two pushout
squares in LGraph𝑃, encoding the following chemical information:
• 𝐿(left graph) — the reactant pattern: the subgraph that must be present in the host
molecule for the rule to fire; contains the reaction-centre atoms with their pre-reaction
labels and the bonds to be broken.
• 𝐾(context graph) — the unchanged frame: atoms and bonds that persist through the
reaction, embedded in both 𝐿and 𝑅by label-preserving monomorphisms.
• 𝑅(right graph) — the product pattern: the subgraph produced by the reaction;
contains the reaction-centre atoms with their post-reaction labels and the bonds
formed.
• 𝐺(host graph) — the substrate molecule: the full molecular graph to which the rule
is applied.
140


## Page 141


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
• 𝐷(derived context) — the gluing context: 𝐺with the atoms and bonds of 𝑚(𝐿\𝑙(𝐾))
removed; the unique pushout complement guaranteed by the adhesivity of LGraph𝑃.
𝐷is a categorical artefact of a single rule application and is not, in general, a
chemically isolable intermediate (Remark 6.12).
• 𝐻(host graph after reaction) — the product molecule: obtained by gluing 𝑅onto 𝐷
via the second pushout.
Together the two pushouts implement the chemical intuition that a reaction (i) removes the
bonds and relabels the atoms of the reaction centre, and (ii) installs the new bonds and
relabelled atoms, leaving everything outside the reaction centre unchanged. This is the
categorical replacement for the stoichiometric transition used as a morphism at L0(𝑃):
instead of merely recording which species disappear and appear, a DPO derivation records
exactly which bonds break and form, in what sequence, and on which atoms. The free
SMC on such derivations is L4(𝑃), constructed in Section 6.4.

generator for every named chemical transformation in the reaction network under study,

6.3.2. DPO derivations and the dangling condition
A DPO rule is an abstract pattern. A DPO derivation is the application of a rule to a
specific host molecule 𝐺: it specifies where the rule fires (the match) and produces the
concrete product molecule 𝐻. This is the level at which a mechanism becomes an actual
chemical transformation on a named substrate.
Definition 6.16 (DPO derivation). Let 𝑝= (𝐿←𝐾→𝑅) be a DPO rule and 𝐺∈

reactant pattern occurs in 𝐺.

precisely when no atoms outside the reaction centre are left with “half-broken” bonds —
the dangling condition. This is not a restriction on chemistry but a consistency requirement:
any correctly specified mechanism must close off all bond changes at the reaction centre
before the rule fires.

and only if the dangling condition holds: no atom in 𝐺\ 𝑚(𝐿) is bonded to an atom in

and only if the dangling condition holds (the gluing condition of [136, Def. 7.2], which
in LGraph𝑃unpacks to the dangling condition [133]); when it exists, it is unique up to

The dangling condition in chemistry
The dangling condition says: a reaction-centre atom or bond cannot be deleted if an
atom outside the reaction centre is still attached to it. Concretely, consider an SN2 rule
for the substitution CH3Br + OH−→CH3OH + Br−: the rule deletes the C–Br bond,
repurposes a lone pair on OH−as the new bonding pair, and creates the C–O bond.
The rule’s 𝐿must include every atom that, in the host 𝐺, is bonded to a reaction-centre
atom; for instance, the three hydrogens on C must be present in 𝐿(and hence in 𝐾, as
unchanged context), since otherwise the carbon’s relabelling between 𝐿and 𝑅would
leave them with bonds into a deleted vertex. In practice, reaction mechanisms are
formulated so that the reaction centre 𝐿is self-contained: all atoms incident to the
reaction-centre atoms are included in 𝐿, making the dangling condition automatically
satisfied for any well-posed rule.
6.3.3. Elementary generators
A DPO rule in LGraph𝑃can describe any bond rearrangement, however complex. For
the free SMC structure of L4(𝑃) (Definition 6.22), we need a generating set: a minimal
collection of rules from which every organic reaction mechanism can be built by sequential
composition (Definition 6.16) and monoidal product (parallel juxtaposition on disjoint
molecular graphs).
The decomposition of any reaction mechanism into elementary electron-pair or radical
movements is the foundation of the mechanistic approach to organic chemistry and has
been formalised independently by Herges [142] (topological classification), Dugundji and
Ugi [137] (BE-matrix reaction types), and Andersen et al. [138] (algorithmic rule compo-
sition). The six generators below are the categorical counterpart of this decomposition,
expressed as explicit DPO spans in LGraph𝑃. In the tower, they are the generators of
L4(𝑃) in the sense of Proposition 6.25: any assignment of these six spans to morphisms
of a strict SMC C extends uniquely to a functor L4(𝑃) →C.

Remark 6.19 (Status of the generating set). Definition 6.18 proposes six generators as a
working basis for all organic reaction mechanisms. The claim that these six generators
suffice to generate every organic reaction mechanism by sequential composition and
monoidal product is supported by the following evidence:
• Herges [142] partitions all concerted organic reactions into three topological types
(linear, pericyclic, coarctate); the linear type aligns with the topological shape of
patterns built from 𝑔1–𝑔3, while pericyclic and coarctate types require additional
primitive generators (§6.3.4).
• Dugundji and Ugi [137] identify ∼30 reaction-matrix types; ∼10 types cover ∼93%
of all single-step transformations, consistent with a small generating set.
• Andersen et al. [138] develop the algorithmic machinery for rule composition in
typed-graph DPO and apply it to ionic organic chemistry, where rules of the 𝑔1–𝑔3
shape suffice. The radical and SET generators 𝑔4–𝑔6 are added here to cover homolytic
and single-electron-transfer chemistry, which are needed for the radical sub-network
of the Briggs–Rauscher reaction (Section 6.9) and for organic photochemistry more
broadly.
A formal proof that Definition 6.18 is both minimal and complete is not available in
the published literature. The tower provides a framework for investigating this question:

6.3.4. Pericyclic rules: cyclic reaction-centre topology
The six generators of Definition 6.18 cover stepwise bond rearrangements: each generator
acts on two atoms (or three, in the case of 𝑔3), and larger mechanisms are built by sequential
composition and monoidal product. But a significant class of organic reactions is concerted
across a closed ring of atoms — pericyclic reactions — and cannot be decomposed into a
sequential chain of two-atom steps without introducing intermediate molecular graphs that
the mechanism provably lacks. These reactions require DPO rules of a different shape.
Definition 6.20 (Pericyclic DPO rule). A pericyclic DPO rule is a chemical DPO rule
𝑝= (𝐿←𝐾→𝑅) in LGraph𝑃for which the reaction centre 𝐿\ 𝑙(𝐾) (together with its
incident atoms in 𝐾) forms a cycle in the underlying graph of 𝐿, with the corresponding
cycle in 𝑅obtained by a simultaneous reassignment of bond orders around the ring.
No vertex labels change; all bond-order changes occur within the cycle and are applied
concurrently as a single rule.
Remark 6.21 (Pericyclic rules are primitives). A pericyclic rule is not a composite of 𝑔1–𝑔6.
Attempting to decompose, say, a Diels–Alder step into sequential applications of 𝑔1 and 𝑔3
would force the derivation to pass through intermediate molecular graphs (the host after
one 𝑔1, before the next 𝑔3, etc.) that carry formal charges or unpaired electrons not present
in either the reactant or the product, and that the concerted mechanism does not produce. A
single pericyclic DPO step has the entire ring of bond-order changes occurring in one rule
application, with no intervening discrete molecular graphs at all. The correct treatment
within our framework is to admit pericyclic rules as additional primitive generators, one
for each pattern of cyclic bond-order reassignment. These primitives are characterised by
Herges’ topological classification [142]: linear (no cycle in the reaction centre), pericyclic
(a single cycle), or coarctate (two cycles sharing an atom). The generator basis for L4(𝑃)
is therefore {𝑔1, . . . , 𝑔6} ∪{pericyclic primitives}, with the pericyclic primitives indexed
by cycle length and Herges type. A complete classification of pericyclic primitives — and
the question of whether they can be further reduced to a finite subset — is an open problem
left to future work.
Pericyclic reactions in the DPO framework
The three canonical pericyclic reaction types all have cyclic reaction-centre topology:
• Diels–Alder cycloaddition [143]: a diene and a dienophile combine through a
six-membered cyclic concerted step; three 𝜋-bonds break and one 𝜋-bond plus
two new 𝜎-bonds form, all within a single ring of six atoms.
• Electrocyclic ring closure [15]: a terminal 𝜋-bond becomes a 𝜎-bond closing a
ring; the reaction centre is the newly formed ring itself.
• [1, 𝑗] sigmatropic shift [144]: a 𝜎-bond migrates across a 𝜋system; the reaction
146

Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
centre is the cycle traced by the migrating group and the atoms it visits.
At L4, all three are handled by pericyclic primitives of Definition 6.20 with the
appropriate cycle length and Herges topology. What L4 cannot do is predict whether a
given pericyclic rule is thermally or photochemically allowed — that is the content of
the Woodward–Hoffmann rules, which depend on orbital symmetry along the reaction
coordinate and are treated at L4.5 in the stereochemistry chapter.
§6.4. Definition of L4(𝑃)
Definition 6.22 (Mechanistic level L4(𝑃)). Let 𝑃be a Petri net with species set S. The
mechanistic level L4(𝑃) is the strict symmetric monoidal category defined as follows.
• Objects: finite disjoint unions of S-typed molecular graphs in LGraph𝑃.
• Generating morphisms: valence-conserving chemical DPO rules (Definition 6.14)
for 𝑃-species.
• Morphisms: composable sequences of DPO derivations in LGraph𝑃, taken up to
the congruence relations of a strict symmetric monoidal category (associativity and
unitality of composition, monoidal axioms, naturality of the symmetry).
• Monoidal product: disjoint union 𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2 of molecular graphs on objects; parallel
juxtaposition of DPO derivations on morphisms.
• Monoidal unit: the empty graph ∅.
That L4(𝑃) as defined is the free strict SMC on the generating DPO rules requires
verification on two fronts: that the concrete construction is well-defined as a strict SMC
(not just a category, since SMC structure includes symmetry and tensor coherence), and
that it satisfies the universal property of the free SMC on the chemical DPO signature. The
three properties of LGraph𝑃established in Section 6.2.3 are what make the SMC structure
hold concretely; the universal property then follows from the standard construction of free
SMCs on a directed signature.
Proposition 6.23 (L4(𝑃) is the free strict SMC on its generating DPO rules). The category
L4(𝑃) of Definition 6.22 is a free strict symmetric monoidal category over the signature of
valence-conserving DPO rules for 𝑃-species in LGraph𝑃.
Proof. The construction in Definition 6.22 presents L4(𝑃) concretely: morphisms are
equivalence classes of DPO derivation sequences in LGraph𝑃modulo the SMC congruence
(associativity, unitality, monoidal axioms, naturality of the symmetry). We verify that this
construction is the free strict SMC on the directed signature Σ of valence-conserving DPO
rules for 𝑃-species, in two parts: (a) the construction is a well-defined strict SMC, and (b)
it satisfies the universal property of the free SMC on Σ.
For (a), the three properties of LGraph𝑃from §6.2.3 establish that the SMC structure
holds concretely for derivation classes.
(i) Adhesivity makes derivations well-defined. Each generating rule 𝑝= (𝐿←𝐾→𝑅)
applied at a match 𝑚: 𝐿↩→𝐺has a unique gluing context 𝐷when the dangling condition
holds (Proposition 6.17); for well-posed chemical rules whose reaction centre is enclosed by
𝐿, the dangling condition is automatic (Section 6.3). The product 𝐻is therefore unique up
147


## Page 148


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
to isomorphism, and sequential composition of derivations is well-defined and associative
on derivation classes.
(ii) Local Church–Rosser realises commutativity of independent steps concretely.
The SMC’s interchange law and the naturality of the symmetry 𝜏together imply that
two independent generators applied to disjoint parts of an object commute up to SMC
congruence. What requires concrete verification is that this abstract commutativity is
faithfully realised on derivation classes. The Local Church–Rosser property (Theorem 7.7
of [136]) supplies it: two derivations 𝑑1, 𝑑2 at disjoint reaction centres in the same host
produce isomorphic products whether applied in either order.
(iii) Concurrency realises composition concretely. The Concurrency theorem (The-
orem 7.11 of [136]) supplies a single composite rule whose application produces the
same end product as the sequence. The composition of derivation classes is therefore
representable as a single-rule derivation, consistent with the abstract SMC composition.
For (b), freeness on Σ follows from the standard universal-property construction of the free
strict SMC on a directed signature [37, §XI.2], [145, §1]: the morphisms of L4(𝑃) are
finite formal composites of generators under sequential and monoidal composition, modulo
the SMC congruence, with two composites identified iff forced equal by the SMC axioms.
The DPO interpretation in LGraph𝑃, validated by (i)–(iii), contributes that each generator
can be applied at any chosen match in any host satisfying the gluing condition, witnessing
the formal morphism without introducing any non-SMC-congruent identifications.
□
L4(𝑃) as the free SMC: a tower-language derivation
The free SMC structure of L4(𝑃) is automatic from the universal-property construction
of free SMCs on a directed signature [37, §XI.2]: given the signature Σ of valence-
conserving DPO rules, the free SMC has morphisms = equivalence classes of formal
composites under the SMC congruence (associativity, unitality, monoidal axioms,
naturality of the symmetry). What the three properties of LGraph𝑃from Section 6.2.3
contribute is the faithfulness of the semantic interpretation of these formal morphisms
as concrete DPO derivations.
Adhesivity ⇒semantic well-definedness. At L0(𝑃)–L3(𝑃), a morphism from
complex u to complex v is a stoichiometric transition: a pair (u, v) with no internal
structure. At L4(𝑃), a morphism is a DPO derivation 𝐺⇒𝑝,𝑚𝐻: the unique gluing
context 𝐷(guaranteed by adhesivity of LGraph𝑃) is the categorical bridge between 𝐿
and 𝑅, not in general a chemical intermediate (Remark 6.12). A chemical intermediate,
when present (e.g., the trigonal-bipyramidal phosphorus intermediate in stepwise
identity substitution, Section 6.1), is the molecular graph 𝐻output by one derivation
and serving as input to the next, distinct from any single rule’s gluing context 𝐷.
Local Church–Rosser ⇒semantic commutation of independent steps. The
free-SMC symmetry 𝜏𝐺1,𝐺2 : 𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2 →𝐺2 ⊔𝐺1 is automatic by construction.
What LCR provides is its semantic realisation: two derivations at disjoint reaction
centres commute as DPO operations, instantiating the abstract symmetry concretely.
Without LCR, the abstract symmetry would still hold formally in L4(𝑃), but the order
of derivations could matter in LGraph𝑃, leaving the abstract SMC symmetry without
a faithful LGraph𝑃-realisation.
148


## Page 149


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Concurrency ⇒semantic single-rule composites. The free-SMC composition is
automatic by construction. What the Concurrency theorem provides is a representation
result: any composite of independent derivations can be realised as a single composite
DPO rule whose pushout produces the same end product (Theorem 7.11 of [136]).
The abstract composite morphism in L4(𝑃) thus has a concrete single-rule realisation
in LGraph𝑃.
Summary.
Free SMC structure: by construction.
Semantic interpretation in
LGraph𝑃: well-defined derivations (adhesivity), independent commutation (Local
Church–Rosser), single-rule composites (Concurrency). The freeness comes from
category theory; the chemistry comes from the semantic faithfulness via LGraph𝑃.
The generating data are the chemical DPO rules of Definition 6.14; the elementary basis
{𝑔1, . . . , 𝑔6} together with pericyclic primitives (Sections 6.3, 6.3.4) is a conjectured
minimal subset (Remark 6.19).
Having established that L4(𝑃) is a free strict SMC, one can now state precisely how it
sits in the tower. The forgetful functor 𝑈4 : L4(𝑃) →L0(𝑃) (constructed in Section 6.6)
provides the downward connection: it sends each molecular graph to its species-count
vector and each DPO derivation to the corresponding stoichiometric transition. The
decorating functors 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, FP of the lower levels lift to L4(𝑃) via 𝑈4 (Proposition 6.32):
no new primitive numerical functor enters at L4 beyond those lifted from L3 via 𝑈4,
but the free SMC that carries them is genuinely new. The universal property of L4(𝑃)
(Proposition 6.25 below) is what makes this connection canonical: any interpretation of the
DPO generators in a target SMC — whether a chemical database, a retrosynthesis planner,
or a Para-level ML model — extends uniquely to a functor from L4(𝑃).
Remark 6.24 (The structural break stated precisely). At every previous level L0(𝑃) through
L3(𝑃), the underlying free SMC was L0(𝑃) = FreeSMC(𝑃), with objects in NS and
morphisms as stoichiometric transitions. New levels added functors 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, FP on top of
the same underlying category.
At L4(𝑃), the underlying category is genuinely new: objects are molecular graphs,
not species-count vectors; morphisms are DPO derivations, not abstract stoichiometric
transitions. L4(𝑃) is not the free SMC of 𝑃with additional decoration. It is a different
free SMC, generated by richer data, connected to the previous levels only via the forgetful
functor 𝑈4 of Section 6.6.
Proposition 6.25 (Universal property of L4(𝑃)). Let C be any strict SMC. An assignment of
the valence-conserving DPO rules of 𝑃-species to morphisms of C, compatible with source
and target molecular graphs, extends uniquely to a strict SMC functor 𝐹: L4(𝑃) →C.
Proof. By Proposition 6.23, L4(𝑃) is the free strict SMC on the generating DPO rules.
The universal property of a free SMC states precisely that any assignment of generators to
morphisms of any strict SMC C extends to a unique strict SMC functor. Existence: define
𝐹on generators by the given assignment and extend to composites and monoidal products
by the SMC axioms; the SMC congruence in L4(𝑃) ensures 𝐹is well-defined. Uniqueness:
every morphism of L4(𝑃) is, by freeness, a unique composite of generators up to SMC
congruence, so the value of 𝐹on generators determines 𝐹on all morphisms.
□

The tower updated: two qualitatively different extension types
The tower L0 ↩→L1 ↩→L2 ↩→L3 ↩→L4 now contains two qualitatively different
types of extension:
• Decorator extensions (L0 →L1, L1 →L2, L2 →L3): the same underlying
free SMC L0(𝑃) is retained; each new level adds exactly one new functor into
𝐵R or Stoch (or more precisely, 𝔤S). The universal property of L0(𝑃) does all
the work.
• Structural extension (L3 →L4): the underlying free SMC is replaced by a
new one, L4(𝑃), generated by DPO rules rather than stoichiometric transitions.
Previous decorations lift via 𝑈4. No new primitive numerical functor is added
beyond those inherited from L3 via pullback along 𝑈4; the new content is in the
morphisms themselves (DPO derivations rather than stoichiometric transitions).
The structural break is forced by the coker(𝜑4) obstruction of Section 6.1 and
cannot be resolved by any decorator extension.

Remark 6.28 (On the generator label). The generator label 𝛾(𝑝) is essential to making 𝑈4
well-defined on morphisms. Since L0(𝑃) = FreeSMC(𝑃) is not a thin category (Petri
nets may contain distinct generators 𝑟1, 𝑟2 ∈R with identical source and target complexes),
𝑈4(𝑑) cannot be defined as “the unique morphism from 𝑈4(𝐺) to 𝑈4(𝐻)”; there may

resolves the ambiguity: 𝑈4(𝑑) is the specific generator 𝛾(𝑝), not merely any morphism
with matching source and target. This matters precisely for the forcing pair of Section 6.1:
when the Petri net 𝑃contains two distinct generators 𝑟concerted, 𝑟stepwise ∈R that realise
the same identity substitution at phosphorus through mechanistically distinct routes,
the corresponding DPO rules 𝑝concerted and 𝑝stepwise carry distinct labels 𝛾(𝑝concerted) =
𝑟concerted and 𝛾(𝑝stepwise) = 𝑟stepwise. 𝑈4 projects them to these two parallel generators in
L0(𝑃) — distinct morphisms with identical source and target complexes — rather than
collapsing them to a single morphism. When 𝑃has only one generator per stoichiometry
(the generic case), the label is redundant and can be inferred from (𝑈4(𝐿),𝑈4(𝑅)).

What 𝑈4 forgets and retains
Retained: which Petri-net generator the DPO rule realises (via its label 𝛾), and
therefore which species are consumed and produced (stoichiometry).
Forgotten: the molecular graphs of reactants and products; which bonds formed or
broke; the sequence of elementary DPO steps; the identity of the reaction centre; the
presence or absence of intermediate molecular graphs in stepwise mechanisms; all
stereochemical information.
For the forcing pair of Section 6.1, the concerted-SN2-P DPO rule and the stepwise A–E
DPO rule (realising identity substitution at phosphorus through distinct mechanisms)
carry distinct Petri-net labels 𝑟concerted and 𝑟stepwise when both appear as parallel
generators of 𝑃. Their 𝑈4-images are different but parallel generators in L0(𝑃):
distinct morphisms sharing source and target complexes. 𝑈4 thus preserves the
information that the two mechanisms yield identical reactants and products, while
discarding the internal DPO structure that distinguishes them at L4 and justifies their
existence as separate generators in the first place. The existence of parallel generators
in 𝑃is unmotivated at L0–L3 (where it can be postulated only by fiat) and finds its
principled structural basis at L4 (where it reflects genuinely distinct DPO derivations).

enters the tower at L5 as the minimax of 𝑉along the IRC (Section 8).

§6.7. Layer 1 and Layer 2 at L4
The Layer 1/Layer 2 split established at L1–L3 recurs at L4, but with a structurally different
character. At L1–L3, the split distinguishes the free assignment of a numerical functor
(Layer 1) from the coherence condition that links it to lower tower levels (Layer 2). At
L4, no new primitive numerical functor enters: the decorating functors 𝐹(4)
𝐻, 𝐹(4)

are all lifted from below via 𝑈4 (Proposition 6.32), so they are already fixed. The split
instead constrains the choice of DPO rules: which bond-change patterns, together with
their Petri-net labelling, yield molecular graphs on which the lifted decorations remain
well-defined.

The progression from L1 to L4 reveals a shift in what Layer 2 constrains: at L1–L2 it
constrains the values of numerical functors on stoichiometric cycles; at L3 it constrains
ratios of rate constants on those cycles; at L4 it constrains the graph structure of the
product molecules themselves, via the lone-pair count condition of Definition 6.35. In each
case, the Layer 2 condition is precisely what is needed to keep the tower’s numerical data
well-defined on the new data introduced at that level.
§6.8. The forcing-pair derivations and their distinctness
Section 6.1 identified the L3 →L4 forcing pair: identity nucleophilic substitution at
phosphorus, realisable either by a single concerted SN2-P transition state or by stepwise

Both pathways carry the same source and target complexes in N|S| and (under steady-state
on the TBI) the same L3 propensity; what distinguishes them is the DPO-derivation
structure at L4. This subsection makes that distinction precise.
Throughout, P denotes the central phosphorus atom of the substrate methyl ethylphenyl-
phosphinate, written Et(Ph)P(= O)OMe. We write OMe for the leaving methoxide and
18OMe for the isotopically labelled incoming methoxide. The ethyl group, phenyl group,
and doubly-bonded oxygen retain their labels and their bonds to phosphorus throughout
every rule below, and sit in 𝐾together with phosphorus itself (Remark 6.15). The two
methoxides change charge between 𝐿and 𝑅(neutral when bonded to P, −1 when free), so
each appears outside 𝐾at any step where its bonded/free status changes.
Remark 6.37 (On hypervalent phosphorus). The pentacoordinate phosphorus in the TBI is
hypervalent: its incident bond-order sum is Í
𝑒𝑏(𝑒) = 6 (Et, Ph, P=O, plus two single P–O
bonds to the methoxides), giving ℓ(P) = (5 −0 −0 −6)/2 = −1/2 from the basic valence
formula of Definition 6.4. The basic formula assumes octet-like electron counting and
does not accommodate the three-centre four-electron bonding characteristic of hypervalent
main-group atoms. A standard remedy is to extend the formalism so that, at hypervalent
vertices, ℓis supplied as part of the vertex label rather than computed from (𝑣el, 𝑞, 𝜌, Í 𝑏);
the basic formula is then recovered as the special case where the supplied ℓmatches the
octet-derived value.

§6.9. Four mechanisms as distinct morphisms in L4(𝑃)
Section 6.1 established the forcing pair for L4: concerted vs stepwise mechanisms at a
single heteroatom centre (the phosphorus identity-substitution example), the only kind
of pair L3 genuinely conflates. The classical mechanism pairs SN1 vs SN2 and E1 vs
E2 are not forcing pairs in this sense — their different propensity forms (𝑣= 𝑘1[RX] vs
𝑣= 𝑘2[RX][Nu], and analogously for E1/E2) separate them already at L3. What L4 adds
for these familiar pairs is a structural account that complements the kinetic distinction at
L3: each mechanism becomes a specific DPO derivation, with intermediate molecular
graphs that appear (or fail to appear) according to whether the mechanism is concerted
or stepwise. This section constructs explicit DPO derivations in LGraph𝑃for all four
mechanisms and verifies pairwise distinctness in L4(𝑃).
Throughout, atoms are labelled by (el, 𝑞, 𝜌) and bonds by their order 𝑏. The Layer 2
valence check at each step verifies that every atom of the product graph 𝑅satisfies ℓ(𝑣) ∈N
(Definition 6.4). For consistency with Remark 6.15, atoms whose label (el, 𝑞, 𝜌) changes
between 𝐿and 𝑅appear in 𝐿\ 𝑙(𝐾) and 𝑅\ 𝑟(𝐾) separately; only atoms with unchanged
labels sit in 𝐾.
6.9.1. Substitution pair: SN1 and SN2
Both mechanisms realise the same net transformation
R−X + Nu−−→R−Nu + X−,
and carry the same reactants and products in N|S|. They are distinguished at L3 by their
propensity forms (𝑣= 𝑘1 [RX] for SN1, 𝑣= 𝑘2 [RX][Nu] for SN2). The DPO derivations
below show why the propensities differ: the two mechanisms have different DPO-level
structure, with SN1 passing through an intermediate molecular graph that SN2 does not.
Example 6.41 (SN2 as a single concerted DPO rule). In the substrate, the electrophilic
carbon C bears label (C, 0, 0) with four bonds: to R (1), two H (2), and X (1) — total
𝑏C = 4, giving ℓ(C) = 0 (no lone pairs). The leaving group X has (el𝑋, 0, 0) in the
substrate and becomes (el𝑋, −1, 0) as X−. The nucleophile Nu has (elNu, −1, 0) as Nu−
and becomes (elNu, 0, 0) bonded to C. The carbon label (C, 0, 0) is unchanged; X and Nu
change charge and therefore cannot sit in 𝐾.
The DPO rule is a concerted composite of generators 𝑔2 (heterolytic C–X cleavage) and 𝑔1
(heterolytic C–Nu bond formation), applied as a single rule:

𝑅: C bonded to Nu (𝑏= 1); Nu: (elNu, 0, 0); X−: (el𝑋, −1, 0) isolated.

6.9.3. All four mechanisms are distinct in L4(𝑃)
Proposition 6.45 (Four mechanisms as distinct morphisms). In L4(𝑃), the DPO derivations
of Examples 6.41–6.44 are pairwise distinct morphisms.
(i) The SN2 derivation (Example 6.41) and the SN1 derivation (Example 6.42) are distinct
morphisms in L4(𝑃) and project to distinct morphisms in L0(𝑃): 𝑈4(SN2) = 𝑟SN2
a single generator, 𝑈4(SN1) = 𝛾(𝑝2) ◦𝛾(𝑝1) a 2-step composite, parallel to the
postulated generator 𝑟SN1 ∈R but distinct from it. All have shared source RX + Nu−
and target RNu + X−.
(ii) The E2 derivation (Example 6.43) and the E1 derivation (Example 6.44) are distinct
morphisms in L4(𝑃); 𝑈4(E2) = 𝑟E2 a single generator, 𝑈4(E1) = 𝛾(𝑝2) ◦𝛾(𝑝1) a
2-step composite at L0(𝑃), parallel to the postulated generator 𝑟E1 ∈R but distinct
from it.
(iii) No substitution morphism coincides with any elimination morphism: the four are
pairwise distinct in L4(𝑃) and project to four pairwise distinct morphisms in L0(𝑃).
Proof. (i) Substitution pair. The SN2 derivation is a single DPO step whose intermediate
graph 𝐷contains neither a carbocation nor any other chemically distinguished non-
substrate vertex. The SN1 derivation is the sequential composite 𝑝2 ◦𝑝1 passing through
the intermediate molecular graph 𝐺1, which contains a vertex with label (C, +1, 0) — the
carbocation. In L4(𝑃), a morphism is an equivalence class of DPO derivations under
SMC congruence (associativity, unitality, symmetry); no SMC congruence can collapse a
derivation passing through a (C, +1, 0) vertex to one that never visits such a vertex. Hence
the two derivations represent distinct morphisms.
By Definitions 6.14 and 6.27, 𝑈4(SN2) = 𝛾(𝑝SN2) = 𝑟SN2 is a single L0 generator, while
𝑈4(SN1) = 𝛾(𝑝2)◦𝛾(𝑝1) is the 2-step composite of the elementary heterolytic-cleavage and
-capture generators (by functoriality of 𝑈4). A single generator and a 2-step composite of
distinct generators are distinct morphisms in the free SMC L0(𝑃), so 𝑈4(SN2) ≠𝑈4(SN1)
even though both share source RX + Nu−and target RNu + X−in N|S|. The composite
𝑈4(SN1) is parallel to the postulated generator 𝑟SN1 ∈R but distinct from it: 𝑟SN1 has no
single-span L4 realisation.
(ii) Elimination pair. Analogous: the E2 derivation has no intermediate graph, while
the E1 derivation passes through the carbocation vertex (C, +1, 0). The two are distinct
in L4(𝑃); 𝑈4(E2) = 𝑟E2 is a single generator, while 𝑈4(E1) = 𝛾(𝑝2) ◦𝛾(𝑝1) is a 2-step
composite, parallel to the postulated 𝑟E1 ∈R but distinct from it.
(iii) Cross-class distinctness. The substitution generators and the elimination generators
have distinct source and target complexes in N|S|: substitution consumes RX + Nu−and
produces RNu+X−, while elimination consumes RX+B−and produces alkene+BH+X−.
In particular, the number of species produced differs. Thus no substitution morphism
coincides with any elimination morphism at L0, and since 𝑈4 is well-defined on L4

What L4 expresses that L3 cannot
The proposition shows how the four classical mechanism types are pairwise distin-
guished as morphisms in L4(𝑃). This is not the forcing argument of Section 6.1
(which concerns the L3-indistinguishable phosphorus pair); rather, it demonstrates
that the same DPO machinery automatically separates mechanism types that L3 also
distinguishes kinetically. In each case, L3 already distinguishes the two mechanisms
numerically via their different propensity forms, but L3 supplies no structural account.
L4 supplies that account: the two mechanisms correspond to DPO derivations with
genuinely different internal structure — one single-step without intermediate graphs,
the other two-step passing through a carbocation vertex (C, +1, 0).
Substitution. At L3: 𝑟SN1 and 𝑟SN2 are distinct generators with propensity values
𝑘1𝑥RX and 𝑘2𝑥RX𝑥Nu respectively. These propensity forms suffice to separate the
two morphisms in L3 but give no structural reason for the difference. At L4: the
propensity difference is explained by the different DPO derivation structures — SN2
as a single concerted rule, SN1 as a composite through the carbocation intermediate
graph. The structural distinction has familiar downstream consequences (Walden
inversion for SN2; partial racemisation for SN1 via planar carbocation attack from
either face), but these stereochemical consequences require three-dimensional data
and enter the tower at L4.5 rather than at L4.
Elimination. At L3: 𝑟E1 and 𝑟E2 are distinct generators with propensities 𝑘1𝑥RX and
𝑘2𝑥RX𝑥B, which separate them numerically but again give no structural account. At
L4: the difference is explained by the DPO derivation structures — E2 as a single
concerted rule with cyclic reaction-centre topology, E1 as a composite through the
same carbocation intermediate graph as SN1. The stereochemical consequences (E2’s
required anti-periplanar geometry, absent in E1) again live at L4.5.
Summary. L4 explains why the Petri net carries parallel generators that L3 distin-
guishes only by their propensity values. The explanation is structural: two DPO
derivations with different intermediate graphs. Three-dimensional consequences of
this structure (stereochemistry, orbital-symmetry selection rules) are the content of
L4.5 (Section 7).
6.9.4. L4 in action: the Briggs–Rauscher oscillating reaction
The examples of Section 6.9 involved pairs of mechanisms competing for a single substrate.
The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) oscillating reaction shows a richer phenomenon: a network in
which two categorically different mechanism types compete and switch roles periodically,
producing macroscopic colour oscillations visible to the naked eye. It illustrates how
mechanism-level information — the structural data of L4 — governs the topology of
reaction networks in ways that rate constants alone do not encode, and provides the first
case in this monograph where a global property of a reaction network (the structural origin
of oscillation) is exhibited as an L4-level predicate.

The Briggs–Rauscher reaction thus illustrates a general principle that the tower makes
precise: the structural origin of oscillation is an L4 predicate: it requires that the network
contain morphisms from at least two distinct mechanism families that compose into a cyclic
trajectory. A kinetic model at L3 can fit the oscillation period and amplitude to data once
the reaction network is supplied, but only L4 provides the structural account of why the
network admits oscillatory dynamics in the first place.
§6.10. What L4 cannot express: forcing of L4.5
The mechanistic level L4(𝑃) was forced by the concerted versus stepwise pathway at
phosphorus: two reactions sharing source, target, and (under steady-state on the TBI)
L3 propensity, distinguishable only at the level of DPO derivations (Sections 6.1, 6.8).
The same machinery applies to the analogous mechanism pairs of carbon chemistry —
SN1 versus SN2, E1 versus E2, and ionic versus radical pathways in oscillating networks
— though for these L3 already provides kinetic separation; what L4 contributes is the
structural account (Section 6.9). It does so by replacing stoichiometric transitions with
DPO derivations: objects are molecular graphs, morphisms encode the sequence of bond
changes, and mechanistically distinct reactions are distinct morphisms.
Yet L4(𝑃) remains blind to spatial orientation. The label set (el, 𝑞, 𝜌) records element
type, formal charge, and radical count; bond-order labels record connectivity. None of
these encode the three-dimensional arrangement of substituents around a stereocentre.
Two molecules that are mirror images of each other are graph-isomorphic in LGraph𝑃
— identical vertex labels, identical edge labels, identical adjacency structure — and are
therefore identified by L4(𝑃), which sees nothing beyond graph isomorphism. Any DPO
rule that applies to one applies identically to the other. The following forcing pair makes
this concrete.

The type of extension L4 →L4.5. The extensions L0 →L1 →L2 →L3 were
decorator extensions: the underlying free SMC L0(𝑃) was retained and a new numerical
functor was appended at each step. The extension L3 →L4 was a structural extension:
the underlying free SMC was replaced by a new one generated by DPO rules, with no
new numerical functor. The extension L4 →L4.5 is of a third type: an equivariant
extension. The free SMC of DPO derivations is retained; no new numerical functor
is added. Instead, the category is equipped with an action of a group encoding spatial
orientation, and morphisms are required to be equivariant with respect to that action.
Chirality, stereochemical descriptors, and orbital-symmetry selection rules are then the
orbit structure and representation theory of this equivariant extension. The construction is
developed in the following chapter.

§7. L4.5: The Stereochemical Level
§7.1. Forcing the extension: what L4 cannot express
Section 6.10 introduced the enantiomer swap as the forcing pair motivating L4.5: the same
DPO rule applied to (𝑅)- and (𝑆)-substrates produces different physical products that L4
cannot distinguish. This section develops that forcing rigorously and introduces a second
independent forcing pair — the conrotatory / disrotatory distinction in pericyclic ring closure
— which manifests the same L4 blindness in a different chemical setting. Both pairs are then
resolved by a single discrete algebraic datum: a chirality label 𝜎: Stereo(𝐺) →{+1, −1} at
each stereocentre (see Definition 7.6), augmenting the molecular graph without introducing
3D coordinates. Throughout, 𝜑4.5 denotes the restriction map Aut(L4.5) →Aut(L4) in
the automorphism exact sequence of the tower.
Remark 7.1 (Why L4.5: a symmetry layer over L4). The fractional index 4.5 is not
a notational convenience. It encodes the mathematical relationship between this level
and its predecessor: L4.5(𝑃) is L4(𝑃) seen through a symmetry filter. The objects are
augmented molecular graphs — the same combinatorial kind as L4, decorated with chirality
labels — and the morphisms remain DPO derivations; but now only the 𝐺∗-equivariant
derivations are admitted. L4.5(𝑃) is a category over L4(𝑃) via the forgetful functor
𝑈4.5 : L4.5(𝑃) →L4(𝑃) that drops the chirality labels: its morphisms are 𝐺∗-equivariant
DPO derivations on chirality-labelled graphs, with the same DPO machinery as L4(𝑃). It
is not a sub-SMC of L4(𝑃) in the literal sense — its objects are augmented graphs (𝐺, 𝜎),
not bare graphs — but neither is it a new category built from scratch: the underlying
combinatorics and rewriting machinery are inherited from L4.
This places L4.5 in contrast with the two surrounding transitions. The extension L3 →L4
was a structural break: L4 introduced an entirely new class of morphisms (DPO derivations
in LGraph𝑃) that L3 had no access to. The forthcoming extension L4.5 →L5 will be
a geometric break: L5 introduces genuinely continuous and geometric data — 3D atom
positions and the continuous potential energy landscape they define — a qualitatively new
mathematical structure.
By contrast, L4 →L4.5 is a symmetry enrichment: the same DPO framework, restricted to
its 𝐺∗-equivariant part. No new numerical functor is added; the underlying free SMC is
not rebuilt. The fractional index 4.5 records exactly this: we are still in the L4 world, but
looking at the part of it that respects a discrete symmetry group. Separating L4.5 from
L5 honours the bottom-up forcing principle: each level is the unique minimal extension
resolving a specific pair of reactions, and the two forcing pairs of this section are resolved
by the discrete 𝐺∗-datum alone.
Two forcing pairs for L4.5
Forcing pair 1: enantiomers under SN2.
Consider the bimolecular substitution of 2-bromobutane (stereocentre at C2, bonded
to four distinct substituents: CH3, C2H5, H, Br) by hydroxide, starting from each

Walden’s 1896 observation that nucleophilic substitution at a stereocentre proceeds with
inversion of configuration [148] was mechanistically explained in the 1930s: Hughes
and Ingold [149] identified back-side attack as the SN2 mechanism, and Cowdrey,
Hughes, Ingold, Masterman, and Scott [150] established in 1937 that the clean
elementary SN2 step at a configurationally stable tetrahedral stereocentre proceeds with
complete inversion; mixed mechanisms involving SN1 contributions, neighbouring-
group participation, or ion-pair effects appear in the tower as compositions of multiple
L4.5-morphisms with L3-level rate weights, not as deviations from the elementary
SN2 rule. The question for the tower is whether this experimental fact is visible as a
theorem or only as an empirical constraint.
In LGraph𝑃, the molecular graphs of (𝑅)- and (𝑆)-2-bromobutane are isomorphic:
identical element types, formal charges, radical counts, bond orders, and adjacency.
No datum in (el, 𝑞, 𝜌, 𝑏) distinguishes left-handed from right-handed arrangements of
substituents around C2. This rests on a modelling convention: the L0 species set is not
pre-refined by stereodescriptors. Inserting (𝑅)- and (𝑆)- as primitive species labels
at L0 would build into the model the very distinction L4.5 is constructed to derive.
Under this convention, both reactions apply the same DPO rule (Example 6.41) to
graph-isomorphic substrates and produce graph-isomorphic products:
𝑟𝑅= 𝑟𝑆
as morphisms in L4(𝑃).
The permutation 𝜋𝜒that exchanges the two graph-isomorphic enantiomer copies
at the L4 level is an automorphism of L4(𝑃) identifying the two reactions — but
the physical reactions are distinct: their products differ in sign of optical rotation,
binding affinity to chiral receptors, and metabolism by enzymes. The entire field of
asymmetric synthesis rests on the distinction being real. Hence [𝜋𝜒] is a non-trivial
element of coker(𝜑4.5).

The two datums at L4.5
The minimal new structure at L4.5 consists of two datums, both discrete and algebraic:
• Chirality labels 𝜎: Stereo(𝐺) →{+1, −1} on each stereocentre, augmenting
the molecular graph. Six decades of asymmetric synthesis encoded as a sign.
• The chirality-symmetry group 𝐺∗= Aut(𝐺) ⋉Z𝑘
2 (Definition 7.5), acting
on chirality-labelled graphs by permuting atoms and flipping 𝜎at subsets
of stereocentres. The Woodward–Hoffmann selection rules are captured as
𝐺∗-equivariance of the DPO rules — no 3D geometry required.
Both datums are discrete and algebraic: the hallmark of the symmetry-enrichment
character of L4.5. Three-dimensional consequences (specific molecular geometries,
activation barriers, vibrational modes) are deferred to L5.
§7.2. The chirality symmetry group 𝐺∗
Section 7.1 showed that both forcing pairs for L4.5 — enantiomer substrates under SN2
and conrotatory/disrotatory electrocyclic closures — are resolved by equipping molecular
graphs with discrete chirality labels 𝜎: Stereo(𝐺) →{+1, −1} and by letting a finite
group 𝐺∗act on these labels. This section defines that group, identifies its two factors,
and verifies that it acts sensibly on chirality-labelled graphs. The 𝐺∗-action on L4.5(𝑃),
projected through the forgetful functor 𝑈4.5, makes the forcing cokernel classes [𝜋𝜒] and
[𝜋ec] in Aut(L4(𝑃)) visible as obstructions that the symmetry enrichment to L4.5 removes.
The group 𝐺∗has two factors. The first, Aut(𝐺), is the group of label-preserving graph
automorphisms of 𝐺: permutations of the vertex set 𝑉that fix the labelling functions 𝜆𝑉,
𝜆𝐸and the bond-order function 𝑏. These are the physically meaningful relabellings —
permutations of identical-nucleus atoms that also respect the bonding pattern — and form a
graph-theoretic restriction of the permutation part of the Longuet–Higgins framework [154],
namely those nuclear permutations expressible from the connectivity data L4 has made
available. The second factor encodes orientation flips at stereocentres. For a molecule

computable from 𝐺∈LGraph𝑃alone: atomic numbers are part of el, and topology is the
graph structure.

Definition 7.12 (Chirality-labelled molecular graph). A chirality-labelled molecular graph

every stereocentre. If Stereo(𝐺) = ∅, then 𝜎has empty domain and (𝐺, ∅) is achiral.

𝑃). The category LGraph𝐺∗

• Objects: chirality-labelled molecular graphs (𝐺, 𝜎).

• Monoidal unit: (∅, ∅).
Chemically: an object of LGraph𝐺∗

at each stereocentre, and a morphism is a molecular-graph inclusion that preserves those

§7.4. Definition of L4.5(𝑃)
Sections 7.2–7.3 assembled the two pieces needed to define L4.5(𝑃): the chirality symmetry
group 𝐺∗(𝐺) = Aut(𝐺) ⋉Z𝑘
2 and its action on the ambient rewriting category LGraph𝐺∗
𝑃
by auto-equivalences. This section imposes the 𝐺∗-equivariance condition on DPO rules,
defines L4.5(𝑃) as the free strict symmetric monoidal category those rules generate, and
records the universal property and tower coherence structure that follow. The stereochemical
theorems — Walden inversion, racemisation, Woodward–Hoffmann — are then obtained
in §7.5–7.6 as consequences of the equivariance condition imposed here.

𝐺∗-equivariant DPO rules together with their chirality lifts.

§7.5. Stereochemistry as theorems at L4.5
Sections 7.2–7.4 built L4.5(𝑃) to resolve the two forcing cokernel classes [𝜋𝜒] and [𝜋ec]
of §7.1. This section collects the payoff. Four classical results of stereochemistry —
Walden inversion (§7.5.1), racemisation via SN1 (§7.5.2), net retention via double inversion
(§7.5.3), and the categorical structure of enantiomers (§7.5.4) — become theorems at L4.5,
deducible from the 𝐺∗-equivariance condition and the DPO machinery alone. No quantum
mechanics, no 3D coordinates, and no experimental postulates beyond the chirality lift of
each rule and the graph-theoretic detection of stereocentres (Definition 7.6) are invoked.
The tower-level contribution of L4.5 is the orbit-uniformity of stereochemical outcome:
𝐺∗-equivariance propagates a given mechanism’s stereochemistry uniformly across every
chirality-labelled substrate in each 𝐺∗-orbit, with the mechanism’s directional choice
(inversion vs retention) supplied as an external input via the chirality lift. Solvent- and
temperature-invariance, where empirically observed, falls outside L4.5’s modelling scope;
the level provides the orbit-uniform shadow of those invariances, not their derivation.
7.5.1. Walden inversion
In 1896 Paul Walden observed that malic acid could be converted to chlorosuccinic acid and
back through a sequence of reagents, with the recovered malic acid displaying flipped optical
rotation: the configuration had been inverted somewhere in the cycle without any obvious
cause [148]. The mechanism remained contested for four decades. Hughes and Ingold’s
systematic kinetic work in the 1930s [149] established that bimolecular nucleophilic
substitution (SN2) proceeds by back-side attack: the nucleophile approaches from the face
opposite the leaving group, forcing a “Walden inversion” of the four substituents around the
reactive carbon. Cowdrey, Hughes, Ingold, Masterman, and Scott provided the definitive
stereochemical evidence in 1937 [150]: every SN2 reaction gives complete inversion of
configuration, on every substrate, in every solvent, at every temperature.
This empirical universality demands a structural explanation that is insensitive to the
continuous parameters L4.5 does not know about (solvent, temperature, conformer). At
L4.5, universality is a theorem.

Walden inversion: tower content and empirical universality
Theorem 7.27 explains the universality of Cowdrey et al.’s 1937 empirical observation
[150] once back-side attack is supplied as the mechanism-specific input. Its two inputs
are:
• the back-side-attack topology of SN2, encoded as the chirality lift 𝜎𝑅= −𝜎𝐿;
• 𝐺∗-equivariance, enforcing uniform behaviour across 𝐺∗-orbits of L4.5-
substrates.
The categorical content is the uniform 𝜎′( 𝑓(𝑣)) = −𝜎(𝑣) relation across every
chirality-compatible match. Solvent- and temperature-independence of the empirical
observation falls outside L4.5’s modelling scope (the level has no parameter for either),
so the theorem cannot directly establish it; what the theorem provides is the consistent
shadow at L4.5 of an empirically solvent- and temperature-independent phenomenon.
No solvent model, no potential energy surface, no quantum treatment of the transition
state is used — not because L4.5 proves their irrelevance, but because the universality
content visible at L4.5 is the orbit-uniform sign relation, and that content is solvent-
and temperature-agnostic.
Mechanisms violating universality — those whose stereochemical outcome depends
on solvent, temperature, or substrate type — are not single 𝐺∗-equivariant L4.5-
morphisms; they are mixtures of two or more L4.5-morphisms whose relative weights
require L3-level data (rate constants). The SN1 mechanism (next subsection) is an
example: it is not a single equivariant rule but two equivariant rules sharing an achiral
intermediate.
7.5.2. Racemisation via SN1
Remark 7.29 (Racemisation, for mathematicians). A racemic mixture is an equal-parts
mixture of the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule. It has zero net optical rotation because
the contributions of (𝐺, +1) and (𝐺, −1) cancel. Racemisation is a process that converts an
enantiomerically pure starting material into a racemic mixture; it destroys stereochemical
information. In tower language: racemisation is the passage from a non-𝐸∗-symmetric
state (pure enantiomer) to an 𝐸∗-symmetric state (racemic mixture). The SN1 mechanism
achieves this by passing through a planar intermediate in which the reactive carbon is no
longer a stereocentre.

7.5.3. Net retention via double inversion: neighbouring group participation
The previous two subsections treated single-step stereochemical events: SN2 preserves
and inverts the chirality label in one rule application (Theorem 7.27); SN1 destroys and
regenerates it across two rules (Theorem 7.30). A third case, due to Winstein [159],
combines two inversion steps to give net retention: the reaction proceeds with inverted
configuration at the intermediate and inverted again at the product, so the initial and final
configurations match. This mechanism is neighbouring group participation (NGP), also
called anchimeric assistance.
Remark 7.33 (Neighbouring group participation, for mathematicians). In NGP, the substrate
carries a nucleophilic heteroatom or 𝜋-bond positioned close to the reactive carbon — for
example, a 𝛽-acetoxy group on a cyclohexyl tosylate, Winstein’s classical system. When
the leaving group departs, the neighbouring nucleophile attacks the reactive carbon from
the opposite face, forming a bridged intermediate (in Winstein’s case, a five-membered
acyloxonium ring). The reactive carbon remains four-coordinated throughout: it loses
the bond to the leaving group but immediately forms a bond to the bridging nucleophile,
hence is a stereocentre in the bridged intermediate. An external nucleophile then attacks
the bridged intermediate, again from the opposite face, opening the ring and giving the
final product. The classical experimental observation is that the reaction gives complete
retention of configuration at the reactive carbon, despite involving two nucleophilic attack
steps [159]. Historically this was puzzling because neither step individually retains: each
inverts. Two inversions give retention.
Theorem 7.34 (Net retention via double inversion at L4.5). Let (𝐺, 𝜎) be a chirality-
labelled substrate with stereocentre 𝑣, and let 𝑟1, 𝑟2 be 𝐺∗-equivariant DPO derivations
such that:
• 𝑟1 has the inverting chirality lift at 𝑣(back-side attack by the neighbouring nucle-
ophile);
• 𝑟2 has the inverting chirality lift at 𝑣(back-side attack by the external nucleophile on
the bridged intermediate).
Then the composition 𝑟2 ◦𝑟1 satisfies
𝜎final(𝑣) = 𝜎(𝑣),
i.e. the net stereochemical outcome at 𝑣is retention of configuration.

What the theorem says about NGP chemistry
Theorem 7.34 recovers, in two lines, a result that historically required careful
experimental design to establish. Winstein’s evidence [159] included: rate acceleration
(the neighbouring group assists the ionisation, giving first-order kinetics despite formal
bimolecular reactants), racemisation in the absence of external nucleophile (the bridged
intermediate can open from either face, analogous to Theorem 7.30(ii)), and complete
retention when the external nucleophile is present in excess (the two sequential
back-side attacks dominate the kinetics).
At L4.5, the argument is structural and does not require the ion-pair analysis that made
Winstein’s original treatment subtle. Two 𝐺∗-equivariant back-side-attack DPO rules
compose to a rule that preserves the chirality label at 𝑣. The bridged intermediate
is a valid object in L4.5(𝑃) because the reactive carbon remains four-coordinated
throughout — the bond to the leaving group is replaced by the bond to the bridging
nucleophile — so the carbon is still a stereocentre in the intermediate, with its chirality
label inverted by the first step.
The theorem generalises immediately to longer sequences: any sequence of 2𝑛back-
side-attack steps at 𝑣gives net retention; any sequence of 2𝑛+ 1 gives net inversion.
This is the L4.5-level parity rule for nucleophilic substitution sequences, recovered
from Theorem 7.27 by composition.

Enantiomers: the tower account
Properties (i)–(v) together reproduce, from the tower construction, the full chemical
concept of a pair of enantiomers.
Property (ii) encodes why enantiomers have identical achiral physical properties:
same boiling point, same melting point, same NMR spectrum in an achiral solvent,
same reaction rates with achiral reagents. All of these are L𝑘-level data for 𝑘< 4.5,
and they are identical for the two enantiomers because 𝑈4.5 collapses the pair to a
single object.
Property (iv) encodes the categorical statement that within L4.5, no morphism flips the
chirality label at a bond-graph stereocentre while leaving the underlying graph fixed.
This captures the chemistry of configurational chirality at tetrahedral stereocentres —
the case where four distinct substituents at 𝑠𝑝3 carbon define the chirality datum.
Several real interconversion mechanisms fall outside this framework because they
are not visible at L4.5: amine inversion (umbrella flipping at nitrogen via a planar
transition state), atropisomer interconversion (rotation around a single bond), and
helical inversion in helicenes all interchange “enantiomeric” stereoisomers without
breaking the bond graph. These phenomena require 3D-coordinate data (transition-
state planarity), barrier heights (whether the inversion is thermally accessible at room
temperature), or both — inputs that enter the tower only at L5 and above. Property (iv)
is the L4.5-level shadow of configurational chirality specifically; the broader physical
concept of “stereochemical interconvertibility” lives at higher levels.
Property (v) encodes the central principle of asymmetric synthesis. A 𝐺∗-equivariant
reaction treats both enantiomers uniformly, producing enantiomeric products in equal
amounts. To produce one enantiomer preferentially, a reaction must break the 𝐺∗-
symmetry — by using a chiral catalyst or reagent modelled as a fixed object (𝐶, 𝜎𝐶)
in the reaction network. When the catalyst appears explicitly with a fixed chirality

The four theorems of this section — Walden inversion, racemisation, net retention via

§7.6. Pericyclic stereochemistry at L4.5: a theorem and a Woodward–Hoffmann
conjecture
The stereochemical theorems of §7.5 treated reactions at a single stereocentre. The present
section takes up the second forcing obligation of §7.1 — the electrocyclic forcing pair
[𝜋ec] — and asks what L4.5 can say about the pericyclic selection rules more generally.
The answer has two parts: a theorem providing the categorical content (𝛼-equivariance
selects one chirality lift from two), and a conjecture identifying the equivariant lift with
the thermally allowed Woodward–Hoffmann product. The theorem is established here;
the conjecture is accompanied by verification in the principal case (electrocyclic) and a
discussion of its scope and limitations.
7.6.1. Background
A pericyclic reaction is a concerted reaction — bond-making and bond-breaking occur
simultaneously, with no ionic intermediate — whose transition state has a cyclic arrangement
of the participating atoms and bonds, allowing electron reorganisation around a closed
loop [15]. At L4(𝑃), pericyclic reactions are DPO rules whose reaction centre 𝐿\ 𝐾
together with 𝑅\ 𝐾traces a cyclic subgraph topology [142]. The three principal families
are electrocyclic ring closures/openings, cycloadditions, and sigmatropic shifts.
Woodward and Hoffmann discovered in 1965 [151, 15] that the stereochemical outcome of
every pericyclic reaction is governed by a single principle: the symmetry of the molecular
orbitals must be conserved along the reaction path. For ground-state (thermal) reactions,
this means the orbitals of the reactant must flow continuously into those of the product
without crossing a symmetry-imposed barrier. Reactions that satisfy this are thermally
allowed; reactions that would require a barrier crossing are thermally forbidden (but
photochemically allowed, since the barrier vanishes upon electron promotion).
The resulting selection rules depend only on electron count:

Conrotatory means the two terminal groups rotate in the same direction; disrotatory means
they rotate in opposite directions. Suprafacial (supra) means the new bond forms on the

same face of the 𝜋system; antarafacial (antara) means it forms on the opposite face. The
work earned Hoffmann the 1981 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared with Fukui for related
frontier-orbital analysis [153, 152]; Woodward had died in 1979 and the prize could not be
awarded posthumously.
Pericyclic reactions are about stereochemistry — which product isomer is produced and
through which transition-state geometry — and this is exactly the content that lives at
L4.5 as chirality labels and nowhere lower in the tower. At L4, the thermally allowed
and thermally forbidden outcomes of a pericyclic reaction share the same bond-graph
DPO rule (𝐿←𝐾→𝑅); the distinction between them is purely stereochemical (which
face of the 𝜋-system the new bond forms on, and the resulting relative configuration of
the new stereocentres) and invisible until L4.5. At L3, the rate constants of allowed and
forbidden processes are different in practice (forbidden reactions face higher activation
barriers), but L3 does not explain why they differ; the structural reason — 𝛼-equivariance
or its failure at the chirality lift — is a L4.5 fact. L4.5 is thus the first tower level where
the allowed/forbidden distinction can be stated structurally, not merely registered as a
numerical rate difference.
7.6.2. The categorical theorem
The connection between WH and L4.5 rests on a single graph-theoretic observation.
A pericyclic reaction centre is a cyclic subgraph, and cyclic graphs admit non-trivial
automorphisms — specifically, the reflections that swap pairs of stereogenic terminal atoms.
These automorphisms project from the 3D symmetry elements (𝐶2 axes, 𝜎𝑣planes) of
the transition state to the graph level, where they act on the vertex set by permuting the
reaction-centre atoms. Call such an automorphism a reaction-centre automorphism of the
rule.
Theorem 7.37 (𝛼-equivariance distinguishes pericyclic product lifts (ring-closure direc-
tion)). Let 𝑝0 be a pericyclic ring-closure DPO rule in LGraph𝑃— a rule whose reactant
side 𝐿has the participating atoms in an open-chain 𝜋-system (sp2 hybridisation at the
termini) and whose product side 𝑅has the new 𝜎-bond closing those termini into a ring
(sp3 at the new stereogenic positions). Let 𝛼be a reaction-centre automorphism of 𝑝0 —
that is, an involutive graph automorphism 𝛼∈Aut(𝐿) ∩Aut(𝑅) that exchanges a pair of
stereocentres {𝑣1, 𝑣2} ⊂Stereo(𝑅). Then:
(i) 𝑝0 admits exactly two chirality lifts ˜𝑝+, ˜𝑝−distinguished by the relative sign of
𝜎𝑅(𝑣1) and 𝜎𝑅(𝑣2):
˜𝑝+ : 𝜎𝑅(𝑣1) = 𝜎𝑅(𝑣2),
˜𝑝−: 𝜎𝑅(𝑣1) = −𝜎𝑅(𝑣2).
(ii) Exactly one of the two lifts is 𝛼-equivariant: ˜𝑝+ is 𝛼-equivariant and ˜𝑝−is not.
Proof. (i). The reaction produces the two stereocentres 𝑣1, 𝑣2 ∈Stereo(𝑅) from sp2 atoms
in 𝐿(hence 𝑣1, 𝑣2 ∉Stereo(𝐿): at the 𝐿-side these vertices have three neighbours each,
failing condition (i) of Definition 7.6). A chirality lift of 𝑝0 is therefore a choice of
(𝜎𝑅(𝑣1), 𝜎𝑅(𝑣2)) ∈{+1, −1}2 at the product side — four options in total. Identifying lifts
related by the 𝐸∗action (𝜎𝑅↦→−𝜎𝑅), which produces the enantiomeric product and hence
the same stereochemical content up to overall enantiomer choice, the four options collapse
into two equivalence classes:

(ii). The 𝛼-equivariance square (Definition 7.18) for ˜𝑝± with 𝛼acting on chirality functions

Remark 7.38 (What the theorem says, tower-natively). Theorem 7.37 separates a pericyclic
rule into two chirality-lift classes defined by the relative sign pattern at the new stereocentres.
At L4, both lifts collapse under 𝑈4.5 to the same bond-graph rule: the distinction is
L4-invisible. At L4.5, the reaction-centre automorphism 𝛼is a non-trivial element of
Aut(𝐺) ≤𝐺∗(𝐺), and 𝛼-equivariance singles out exactly one of the two lifts. The tower
contribution is the classification of pericyclic product lifts by 𝛼-parity, not the identification
of which class is thermally allowed — that identification is the content of the conjecture
below.
7.6.3. The Woodward–Hoffmann identification conjecture
Theorem 7.37 gives the combinatorial skeleton: for every pericyclic reaction with a
reaction-centre automorphism 𝛼, one of two chirality lifts is 𝛼-equivariant. The question
this section poses is whether that combinatorial skeleton tracks the Woodward–Hoffmann
selection rules.
Conjecture 7.39 (Woodward–Hoffmann identification at L4.5, electrocyclic case). Let
𝑝0 be an electrocyclic ring-closure rule with 𝑁𝜋-electrons in the reactant 𝜋-system, and
let 𝛼be its reaction-centre automorphism (the reflection exchanging the two terminal
stereocentres). Let ˜𝑝+, ˜𝑝−be the two chirality lifts of Theorem 7.37. Then the thermally
allowed Woodward–Hoffmann product corresponds to:
• the 𝛼-equivariant lift ˜𝑝+ when 𝑁≡0 (mod 4) (i.e., 4𝑛electrons);
• the non-𝛼-equivariant lift ˜𝑝−when 𝑁≡2 (mod 4) (i.e., 4𝑛+ 2 electrons).
The photochemically allowed product corresponds to the opposite lift in each case.
Remark 7.40 (What the conjecture claims). Theorem 7.37 is a combinatorial theorem: it
classifies product lifts by 𝛼-parity. Conjecture 7.39 adds empirical content: it identifies
which 𝛼-parity corresponds to the thermally allowed outcome, with an alternation governed
by 𝑁mod 4. The alternation itself — the hallmark of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules
— is the conjecture’s substantive claim. Below L4.5, the alternation is invisible because
chirality labels are absent; at L4.5, it is expressible but not derivable from categorical
axioms alone. The identification between 𝛼-parity and thermal allowedness requires input
from the orbital-symmetry analysis of Woodward and Hoffmann, and this input is not
currently derivable from the tower structure below L6 (where the full electronic Hilbert
bundle becomes available).

𝛼-equivariant) and 4𝑛+ 2 (thermal ↔non-𝛼-equivariant) is the WH hallmark.
Cycloadditions and sigmatropic shifts. The categorical theorem (Theorem 7.37) extends
to cycloadditions and sigmatropic shifts whenever the reaction centre admits an involutive
graph automorphism exchanging new stereocentres. The Diels–Alder [4+2] cycloaddition,
for instance, has reaction centre {C1, . . . , C6} (four from the diene, two from the dienophile)
and a natural 𝐶2 automorphism of the 6-membered transition-state ring. For substrates with
the requisite substitution pattern to produce stereocentres at the new 𝜎-bond termini, the
𝛼-parity of the chirality lift distinguishes the two possible cycloadduct stereochemistries.
Substrates without such substitution (unsubstituted butadiene plus ethylene) produce a
cyclohexene with no stereocentres, making the 𝜎-analysis vacuous. The general WH
identification for cycloadditions follows the same (4𝑛) vs. (4𝑛+ 2) alternation as the
electrocyclic case; the conjecture extends accordingly but verification requires case-by-case
substrate choice.
7.6.7. Scope and limitations
Remark 7.41 (What L4.5 can and cannot distinguish). Theorem 7.37 and Conjecture 7.39
together express the L4.5-visible content of the Woodward–Hoffmann rules. Two scope
boundaries should be made explicit.
Product-level vs. motion-level distinctions. The reaction-centre automorphism 𝛼is a
graph-level object: it permutes vertices without reference to 3D geometry. A single graph
automorphism 𝛼can be the shadow of either a 𝐶2 rotation axis (as in conrotatory motion)
or a 𝜎𝑣mirror plane (as in disrotatory motion); both act identically on the vertex set.
Consequently, L4.5 distinguishes the two products (trans vs. cis, supra-supra vs. supra-
antara) but not the two transition-state motions (conrotatory vs. disrotatory, axial vs. planar).
The motion-level WH content — which orbital symmetry element is preserved during
the continuous reaction path — requires the 3D geometry introduced at L5, where the
Euclidean group 𝐸(3) acts on configurations. At L5, the distinction between 𝐶2-preserving

Theorem content. Every pericyclic rule with a reaction-centre automorphism 𝛼
exchanging new stereocentres decomposes into exactly two chirality lifts, distinguished
by whether 𝜎𝑅is 𝛼-invariant or 𝛼-anti-invariant. The 𝛼-invariant lift ( ˜𝑝+) is 𝛼-

Conjecture content.
The Woodward–Hoffmann (WH) rules assert an empirical
identification: the 𝛼-equivariant lift is the thermally allowed product for 4𝑛electrons,
and the non-equivariant lift is thermally allowed for 4𝑛+ 2 electrons. The alternation

disrotatory closure of hexa-2,4-diene is a perfectly valid morphism of L4(𝑃). Its
L4.5 chirality lift to the cis product, however, is not 𝛼-equivariant (Theorem 7.37),
hence not 𝐺∗-equivariant, hence not a generator of L4.5(𝑃). The cis product itself is
a perfectly valid object of L4.5(𝑃) — it exists as a real molecule with a well-defined

at L4.5. This is the categorical incarnation of WH at L4.5: the inadmissibility of
the forbidden pericyclic rule, not of its product, is the failure of the chirality lift to
be 𝐺∗-equivariant. The orbital-symmetry conservation argument of Woodward and
Hoffmann supplies the 3D geometric justification for why 𝛼-equivariance should
correspond to thermal allowedness — this justification operates at L5 (3D geometry)
and fully at L6 (electronic structure), both beyond the present chapter.

and C−D bending vibrations change character at the SN2 transition state. The reactive
carbon passes through a nearly pentacoordinate geometry (bipyramidal around the central
carbon, with the leaving group and nucleophile at the apical positions and the three
remaining substituents on an equatorial plane), and one bending mode at the reactive carbon
softens significantly between the reactant (tetrahedral, bending frequency ≈1340 cm−1)
and the TS (bending frequency ≈1150 cm−1). The resulting zero-point-energy shift differs
between H and D by a small amount that, accumulated over all three hydrogens at the
reactive carbon, produces a rate ratio near 1.3 [161]. A careful derivation requires the
bending-mode frequencies at both the reactant and the transition-state geometries; the
transition-state geometry is the saddle point of the potential energy surface 𝑉: C𝑒(𝐺) →R,
a L5-level datum.
The starker case:
primary KIE. When the C−H bond is directly broken in the
rate-determining step — as in base-catalysed proton abstraction from a carbonyl 𝛼-
carbon — the isotope effect is much larger: 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷≈5–7 at 25 ◦C, with a semi-
classical maximum 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷≈7 [24].

3D geometry ⇒TS geometry ⇒activation barrier 𝐸𝑎⇒rate constant 𝑘.
None of the arrows can be reversed from L4.5-level data. L5 closes the chain by introducing
three new objects, together constituting the tower’s first geometric break:

To a chemist: molecules now have shapes, and shapes determine how fast reactions

7.7.2. The 3D realisation of chirality labels
The passage to L5 also completes a deliberate deferral from L4.5. At L4.5, the enantiomers
(𝐺, +1) and (𝐺, −1) were declared distinct objects, but the sign 𝜎∈{+1, −1} was abstract:
the category recognised the two as different yet could not say which 3D arrangement
corresponded to which sign. The Cahn–Ingold–Prelog convention for identifying 𝜎with
(𝑅)/(𝑆) (Remark 7.7) was an external labelling convention, not derivable within L4.5.
At L5, the Born–Oppenheimer PES 𝑉on C𝑒(𝐺) for a chiral molecule with a configurational
stereocentre at carbon has two distinct minima separated by a high racemisation barrier (the
energy cost of inverting the stereocentre, typically much larger than 𝑘𝐵𝑇for tetrahedral
carbon). The configuration orbifold C𝑒(𝐺) itself remains connected as a topological space,
but its low-energy region — the union of basins of attraction of the local minima at thermally
accessible energy — decomposes into two disjoint basins, one for each enantiomer. The
abstract parity 𝐸∗∈𝐺∗(𝐺) from §7.2 acquires a geometric realisation as the involution
exchanging the two basins, physically effectable only by traversing the racemisation barrier.
The chirality label 𝜎(𝑣) ∈{+1, −1} then admits a canonical geometric interpretation: it is
the basin label on C𝑒(𝐺), recording which low-energy basin the molecule inhabits.

This completes the geometric picture of stereochemistry. At L4.5, 𝜎was a discrete sign

The L4.5-theorems of §7.5 translate into L5-geometric statements; below,
C𝑒(𝐺joint) denotes the configuration orbifold for the joint set of atoms participating in the
reaction (substrate plus reagents), with bond-graph changes treated as transitions between
PES regions in the standard reactive-PES sense:
• Walden inversion (Theorem 7.27) is a reaction path on C𝑒(𝐺joint) connecting the
substrate basin to a product basin of opposite chirality, with the back-side-attack TS
geometry interpolating between them.
• Racemisation (Theorem 7.30) is a path that visits the planar SN1 carbocation TS —
a saddle point lying equidistant (in barrier height) from both enantiomer basins —
and descends with equal probability into either basin, matching the racemic outcome
at L4.5.
• Net retention via double inversion (Theorem 7.34) is a path that crosses the inversion
saddle twice (substrate →bridged intermediate →product), with the two basin
crossings composing to a path that returns to the starting basin’s chirality class.
The passage from L4.5 to L5 is thus not only the addition of new content (PES, rates,
barriers); it is also the geometric realisation of content already established at L4.5 as
discrete combinatorial data. Chapter 8 develops this realisation in full.

§8. L5: The Geometric Level
§8.1. Forcing the extension: geometry from the kinetic isotope effect
Section 7.7 closed with the forcing pair: CH3Br and CD3Br undergoing the same SN2
reaction are structurally identical at L4.5(𝑃) (isomorphic graphs, identical DPO rule,
no stereocentre) yet react at different speeds, with 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷≈1.3 recorded empirically
as a L3-decoration. This section develops the forcing argument rigorously, identifies
the minimal new structure the rate difference demands, and explains what this structure
fundamentally represents.
The central claim is simple: the rate difference requires knowing where the transition state
is in 3D space — a geometric datum that does not exist anywhere in the tower below L5.
This forces not just a configuration space, but a full Riemannian geometric structure on
that space, together with a real-valued function (the potential energy surface) on it.
Forcing pair for L5: same symmetry, different activation barrier

𝑟𝐷: CD3Br + OH−→CD3OH + Br−,

Both at 298 K in water [160]; 𝑘𝐷is not independently measured here but derived from

Structural indistinguishability at L4.5. At every level of the tower constructed so
far, the two systems share their entire categorical structure. H and D carry the same
element label (atomic number 1), so CH3Br and CD3Br are isomorphic as objects
in LGraph𝐺∗

accompanies every C–H→C–D substitution at the reactive carbon, in every solvent, at
every temperature in the harmonic-thermal window, points to a structural feature the
tower has not yet named.
The chemist’s intuition supplies the answer immediately. The deuterium atom is twice
as heavy as the protium it replaces, the C–D bond therefore vibrates more slowly than
C–H, and the lower zero-point energy of C–D shifts the activation barrier upward
by a small amount that accumulates over three substitutions and twice across the
reactant-to-TS geometry change. Every clause of this explanation invokes structure
that does not exist below L5: 3D positions for the carbon and its substituents, a

The fourth type of tower extension
The tower has so far exhibited three types of extension (Remark 7.24): decorator
(L0 →L3), structural (L3 →L4), and symmetry enrichment (L4 →L4.5).
The extension L4.5 →L5 introduces a fourth type: geometric decoration. The
new functor 𝐹𝑉assigns to each species not a single real number (as at L1–L3) but a
smooth function on a continuous space: an infinite-dimensional datum.
This is a genuine structural break in the tower. At L1–L3, specifying a reaction means
giving one or two real numbers per generator (e.g. Δ𝐻and 𝑘). At L5, specifying a
reaction means giving the full shape of 𝑉along the reaction path — in principle, a
function on all of C𝑒(𝐺). This data can only be obtained by:
• First-principles computation: solving the electronic Schrödinger equation at
each geometry (quantum chemistry: HF, DFT, CCSD(T), etc.), exact but
expensive;
• Experimental measurement: spectroscopy, crystallography, and kinetics data
constrain 𝑉at specific geometries; or
• Machine-learning approximation: a Para-level model 𝐹Θ
𝑉in 𝐿Para
5
trained on
quantum chemical reference data.
All three approaches converge towards the exact Born–Oppenheimer surface, with first-
principles computation exact in the complete-basis-set, full-CI limit and approximate
in any practical truncation, while measurement and machine-learning approaches are
intrinsically approximate. The categorical framework records what datum is needed
(𝐹𝑉as a functor into OrbMorse) without specifying how to obtain it.
Why L5 is genuinely new: a narrative.
The tower from L0 to L4.5 is entirely shape-independent. Stoichiometry, thermodynamics,
kinetics, bond-graph mechanisms, and stereochemical outcomes are all properties of how
atoms are connected (and with what orientation) — but not of where they sit in 3D space.
An organic chemist can write every mechanism in this thesis using only topology and
signed graphs, without ever drawing a 3D picture.
L5 is where 3D pictures become indispensable. It is the level of the tower at which the
following phenomena first have a mathematical home:
• Steric effects: the activation barrier of a reaction increases when bulky substituents

§8.2. The configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺)
Standing assumption: the Born–Oppenheimer framework. Throughout this section,
all geometric and energetic content is understood within the Born–Oppenheimer (BO)
approximation [164]: electronic and nuclear motion decouple at leading order in the small
parameter 𝜀= (𝑚𝑒/𝑀)1/2, where 𝑚𝑒is the electron mass and 𝑀a typical nuclear mass
(𝜀≈10−2 for light molecules). At this order, electrons relax adiabatically to the ground
state for each fixed nuclear geometry R, and nuclei move on the resulting ground-state
potential energy surface 𝑉(R). This separation produces two well-defined objects — the
configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) defined below, and the PES 𝑉: 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) →R defined in §8.3 —
which together (with the mass-weighted metric 𝑔) constitute the Morse triple (𝐶𝑒(𝐺),𝑉, 𝑔)
that the categorical functor 𝐹𝑉: L4.5(𝑃) →OrbMorse assigns to each molecular graph at
the L5 level.
The BO approximation is accurate for the vast majority of ground-state thermal chemistry:
away from degeneracies, the error introduced by the adiabatic decoupling is of order
𝜀= (𝑚𝑒/𝑀)1/2 [165], and exponentially small in 1/𝜀whenever the ground and first excited
states are separated by a uniform spectral gap [166]. For typical molecules (𝜀≈10−2) in the
regime of ordinary ground-state thermal chemistry, BO corrections are usually smaller than
the dominant electronic-structure and solvation errors of practical computational methods,
so bond lengths, vibrational frequencies, and reaction barriers computed on the ground-state
adiabatic surface are reliable to within chemical accuracy [164, 167]. BO corrections
become non-negligible in high-resolution spectroscopy, light-atom isotope shifts, precision
thermochemistry, and near non-adiabatic regions; the leading mass-dependent corrections
