— the diagonal Born–Oppenheimer corrections (DBOC) — lie outside the scope of the
leading L5 analysis and enter as higher-order refinements.
Its limitations arise at conical intersections (CIs): geometries where the ground and first
excited states become degenerate so the spectral gap closes, the adiabatic decoupling
breaks down, and nuclear motion couples the two surfaces [154, 168, 169]. That failure is
precisely the phenomenon that forces L6 (§8.7); by construction, the entire L5 framework
operates in the open dense subset of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) where the spectral gap is positive.
8.2.1. Construction
Having accepted the BO separation, nuclear configurations R = (r1, . . . , r𝑛) ∈R3𝑛become
the fundamental geometric objects. Two configurations represent the same molecular
shape if they differ only by an overall rigid-body motion (translation or rotation of the
entire molecule) or by a permutation of nuclei that are physically identical. The natural
mathematical object encoding this identification is not a manifold but an orbifold: the
quotient of R3𝑛by the combined group of these equivalences has non-trivial stabilisers at
symmetric configurations, and fixed-point quotients produce orbifold singularities rather
than manifold charts. The definition records this quotient precisely.

8.2.2. Point groups as isotropy subgroups
Molecular point groups are one of the most practically useful concepts in chemistry. Every
undergraduate learns to classify a molecule by its symmetry elements (rotation axes 𝐶𝑛,
mirror planes 𝜎, improper rotations 𝑆𝑛, and inversion 𝑖), assign it to a point group (𝐶2𝑣,
𝑇𝑑, 𝐷6ℎ, etc.), and then read off selection rules for spectroscopy and orbital interactions
from the corresponding character table [171, 172]. This is almost always presented as a
classification procedure: examine the molecule, list its symmetry operations, identify the
group.
What is less often made explicit is that these symmetry operations have a dynamical origin.
A symmetry operation of a molecule at geometry R is precisely a rigid-body motion
(rotation or improper rotation) that, combined with a permutation of identical nuclei,
maps R to itself. This is the definition of the permutation-inversion group introduced by
Longuet-Higgins [173] and developed into a comprehensive spectroscopic framework by

categorical statement below identifies molecular point groups as the isotropy subgroups of
the 𝐺∗-action on 𝐶𝑒(𝐺). While the permutation-inversion framework itself is standard,
its expression as 𝐺∗-isotropy within a tower extension—and the consequent derivation of

operation, and 𝜎records on which side of 𝐸∗a given stereoisomer sits at each stereocentre.

The question deferred at L4.5 is: what does this discrete label correspond to geometrically?
The answer is supplied by the topology of the potential energy surface. The idea has
precursors in the literature on molecular topology: Woolley [174] argued that molecular
structure itself is not a purely quantum-mechanical concept but requires appeal to the PES,
and Amann [175] formalised chirality as a superselection rule arising from the topology
of the molecular state space. The following proposition makes the relevant topological
invariant explicit as the connected-component structure of the accessible region of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺).
The single-stereocentre case is stated below for clarity, with the general case deferred to a
remark.

Remark 8.11 (Pyramidal-inversion energetics). For a tetrahedral carbon stereocentre bonded
to four distinct substituents, 𝐸inv is very large: direct pyramidal inversion requires an
essentially planar tetracoordinate carbon—four substituents coplanar with the central atom,
retaining all four bonds—which is geometrically strained and costs hundreds of kJ/mol.
In practice, stereocentre interconversion of such centres occurs only via bond-breaking
pathways (e.g., SN1 through a planar carbocation, or base-catalysed enolisation), which
are not single-surface processes on the starting substrate’s 𝑉. Under normal chemical
conditions (𝑇≈300 K, accessible thermal energies ≲𝑘𝐵𝑇≈2.5 kJ/mol above the ground
state), the accessible region 𝐶𝑒acc(𝐺) consists of two entirely disconnected components,
making 𝜎a robust topological invariant of the molecular state.
The contrast with nitrogen stereocentres (e.g., NH3, amines) is instructive: nitrogen
inversion through a planar tricoordinate TS has a barrier of only ∼24 kJ/mol, well within
thermal access, so nitrogen stereocentres are typically not resolvable as distinct enantiomers
under standard conditions. This difference in barrier heights is itself an L5 datum: the
same abstract group-theoretic structure at L4.5 yields different topological consequences
depending on the PES landscape, which only L5 sees.
The chirality bridge between L4.5 and L5
Proposition 8.8 closes the explanatory gap opened at L4.5: the abstract label 𝜎∈
{+1, −1} was promised a geometric realisation, and here it is.
The key conceptual point is that 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) itself is topologically trivial (path-connected):
the two stereoisomers are not distinguished by any topological property of configuration
space alone. What distinguishes them is the energetic structure of 𝑉—specifically,
the existence of a large inversion barrier that partitions the accessible region into two
components. Chirality is therefore not a topological invariant of the molecular graph
(an L4 or L4.5 statement) but a topological invariant of the accessible PES (an L5
statement). The L4.5 label 𝜎is the shadow of this PES topology projected back onto
the graph level.

8.3.1. The electronic Hilbert bundle
At each level L𝑘(𝑃) for 𝑘≤4.5, the objects of the tower are molecular graphs (𝐺, 𝜎) with
various discrete decorations (Δ𝐻, 𝑘𝑟, DPO mechanisms, chirality labels), but no information
about where atoms sit in 3D space. The BO approximation (§8.2, standing assumption)
assigns to each nuclear geometry R ∈𝐶𝑒(𝐺) a well-posed quantum-mechanical eigenvalue
problem: find the ground state of the electronic Hamiltonian ˆ𝐻el(R). The electronic
Hilbert bundle is the geometric object that packages this family of eigenvalue problems
into a single structure over 𝐶𝑒(𝐺).
This construction has a multi-layered history in the molecular and mathematical-physics
literature. Mead and Truhlar [168] introduced the molecular vector potential in the BO
approximation, recognising that the R-dependence of the electronic wavefunction produces
an effective gauge field entering the nuclear Hamiltonian. The fiber-bundle interpretation
of this geometric phase — with the Berry connection identified as a 𝑈(1) connection
on a line bundle over parameter space — was developed by Simon [176] following
Berry [177]. The rigorous adiabatic-theoretic foundation, justifying the decomposition of
Hel into adiabatic sub-bundles and controlling the errors, was established by Teufel and
Panati–Spohn–Teufel [178, 179]. All of this machinery is what L5 inherits.

8.3.2. The Born–Oppenheimer section and PES
The Hilbert bundle provides the arena; the BO section selects the physically relevant state
in each fiber. At each geometry R, the electronic Hamiltonian ˆ𝐻el(R) has an isolated
ground-state eigenvalue 𝐸0(R) at the bottom of its spectrum (existence of bound states
for neutral molecules is a consequence of Zhislin’s theorem [181] and is standard for
chemically relevant geometries), with 𝜎0(R) the corresponding unique (up to phase)
normalised eigenstate. Varying R smoothly while tracking this ground state defines the
BO section.

Layer 1 and Layer 2 for 𝐹𝑉at L5
Layer 1: any smooth function 𝑉: 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) →R on the configuration orbifold. There is
no “one real per generator” universal property: 𝑉requires specifying its value at every
point of the (3𝑛−6)-dimensional orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), an infinite-dimensional datum.
Layer 1 asserts that such a function must exist and be smooth on the non-degenerate
(CI-free) subset of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺).
Layer 2: two additional conditions tying 𝑉to the physics of ˆ𝐻el.
(a) BO derivation: 𝑉(R) = ⟨𝜎0(R)| ˆ𝐻el(R)|𝜎0(R)⟩+ 𝑉nn(R). The PES is not an
arbitrary smooth function but the sum of the ground-state electronic eigenvalue
and the nuclear–nuclear Coulomb repulsion.
(b) Global existence of 𝜎0: the ground state is non-degenerate on the relevant open
subset of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), so 𝜎0 is a smooth section of Hel →𝐶𝑒(𝐺) over that subset.
Condition (b) is the Born–Oppenheimer approximation proper. It fails at conical inter-
sections where 𝐸0(R) = 𝐸1(R) (ground and first excited states become degenerate):
𝜎0 is undefined at such geometries, and the global section fails to exist. That failure
forces L6 (§8.7).
Using 𝑉in the tower. Layer 2(a) makes 𝑉computable from first principles. Layer 2(b)
ensures the ground-state line bundle 𝐿0 := span{𝜎0(R)}R is globally trivial (§8.3.4),
which in turn means the Berry connection 𝐴0 vanishes identically (Proposition 8.21).
Together, conditions (a)–(b) also underpin the TST coherence condition (§8.5): the
rate constant 𝑘𝑟at L3 is derived from the saddle-point value of 𝑉at L5.
8.3.3. Critical points of 𝑉and the IRC
With 𝑉and 𝑔in hand, a central task of computational chemistry becomes precise: navigate
the landscape of 𝑉to identify stable geometries, reaction pathways, and barriers. The
mathematical language for this navigation is Morse theory — the study of smooth functions
via their critical points and gradient flows.
In practice:
• Geometry optimisation is gradient descent on (𝑉, 𝑔) to find local minima — the
stable molecular structures. Every structure deposited in the Cambridge Structural

Database or the NIST WebBook corresponds to a minimum of 𝑉.
• Transition-state (TS) search is finding index-1 saddle points — configurations where
the energy is stationary but has one direction of descent (the reaction mode) and all
other directions of ascent. Methods such as QST2/QST3 and eigenvector-following
locate these points by following the negative Hessian eigenvector uphill.
• IRC calculation follows the gradient flow from the TS downhill (in the mass-weighted
metric 𝑔) to identify the reactant and product connected to that TS. The IRC in
mass-weighted coordinates was formalised by Fukui [162] and given its modern
treatment by Miller, Handy and Adams [163].
In categorical terms, this entire computational toolkit is the exploration of the Morse
structure of 𝐹𝑉: the functor 𝐹𝑉: L4.5(𝑃) →OrbMorse assigns to each molecular graph
the Morse triple (𝐶𝑒(𝐺),𝑉, 𝑔), and its critical-point data are precisely what OrbMorse-
morphisms must preserve.

8.3.4. The Berry connection
The BO section 𝜎0(R) is a wavefunction, hence defined only up to an overall complex
phase 𝑒𝑖𝜙at each geometry. The question of how this phase choice changes as the nuclei
traverse a closed loop 𝛾in 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) is not a gauge artefact: the holonomy of the phase (the
total accumulated phase around 𝛾) is a gauge-invariant observable. This holonomy is the
geometric phase or Berry phase [177, 176], identified in the molecular context by Mead
and Truhlar [168].
The physical significance is direct: a nuclear wavepacket that traverses a loop in 𝐶𝑒(𝐺)
returns to its starting point with a modified electronic phase. If this phase is −1 (a
sign change of the electronic wavefunction), the nuclear wavepacket acquires destructive
interference with itself, producing observable spectroscopic consequences [154]. This is
the molecular Aharonov–Bohm effect. In the tower language:

loops (Proposition 8.21 below).
• At L6, conical intersections are the sources of non-trivial Berry holonomy: a loop
encircling exactly one CI acquires phase −1. This non-trivial holonomy is precisely
the datum that L5 cannot encode and L6 must introduce.
The Berry connection is therefore the bridge datum between L5 and L6 in the tower.

Remark 8.22 (Simple connectivity of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) and the L5 vs. L6 boundary). The real-gauge
argument of Proposition 8.21 works locally on any simply-connected open subset of
𝐶𝑒(𝐺), and extends globally provided 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) itself is simply connected. When 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) has
non-trivial topology — in particular, when conical intersections form a codimension-2
submanifold 𝑋CI ⊂𝐶𝑒(𝐺) (codimension 2 because CIs of a real-symmetric Hamiltonian
satisfy two real conditions on the 2 × 2 effective block) — the complement 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) \ 𝑋CI
has non-trivial 𝜋1 (loops encircling 𝑋CI cannot be contracted), and the global real-gauge
extension can fail around such loops. The standard example is the H3 system, where the
𝐷3ℎconical intersection creates a loop with Z2 holonomy (Berry phase 𝜋): the ground-state
wavefunction changes sign under a traversal of this loop [154, 168]. That failure is precisely
the L5 →L6 transition: L5 operates on simply-connected, CI-free regions where all
holonomies are trivial; L6 admits CI-induced holonomies in coker(𝜑6).
The spinless assumption in the proposition is likewise standard in BO theory for ground-
state thermal chemistry. For electrons with spin-orbit coupling, time-reversal is T 2 = −1
(Kramers) and the analysis changes: additional Z2 structure enters the Berry connection.
These effects become relevant at L6 and beyond and are not treated here.
Remark 8.23 (What the proposition establishes in the tower). Proposition 8.21 has three
distinct consequences for the tower, each at a different level of abstraction.
Physical consequence. The electronic wavefunction accumulates no geometric phase as
the nuclei traverse any loop in 𝐶𝑒(𝐺). Nuclear dynamics on the ground-state BO surface is
self-consistent: the electronic subsystem does not distinguish one traversal of a nuclear loop
from another, and there is no quantum interference between paths with different winding
histories. This is the regime of adiabatic thermal chemistry — the regime in which all of
organic chemistry, most of thermodynamics, and most of kinetics operates.

§8.4. Definition of L5(𝑃)
The two preceding sections established the raw materials: the configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺)
(§8.2) and the four-layer structure of (𝑉, 𝑔, 𝜎0, 𝐴0) (§8.3). This section assembles them
into the categorical objects that define L5(𝑃), proves that these objects form a well-defined
category, and situates L5(𝑃) coherently in the tower.
The plan is a two-step construction:
(I) Build the target category OrbMorse (§8.4.1): the symmetric monoidal category that
receives the geometric decoration.
(II) Construct the geometric functor 𝐹𝑉: L4.5(𝑃) →OrbMorse (§8.4.2), which assigns
to each molecular graph the Morse triple of its configuration space, PES, and
mass-weighted metric, and to each DPO derivation its intrinsic reaction coordinate.
Together these yield L5(𝑃) := (L4.5(𝑃), 𝐹𝑉) (§8.4.3), a 𝐺∗-equivariant SMC decorated by
a lax monoidal functor to OrbMorse.

8.4.1. The target category OrbMorse
The geometric decoration at L5 targets a category whose objects are the configuration
orbifolds of molecules equipped with a PES and a metric. This category must be constructed
carefully: its morphism structure must capture the physical notion of a reaction as a gradient-
flow path from a reactant minimum to a product minimum through a transition state, and
its monoidal product must encode the combination of non-interacting molecular systems.
Classical Morse theory provides the necessary ingredient. Initiated by Morse [182], it
assigns to each smooth function 𝑉: 𝑀→R a critical-point structure (non-degenerate
critical points with integer indices) from which global topological properties of 𝑀can be
recovered. In our setting 𝑀= 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) is not a manifold but an orbifold — a topological
space locally modelled on R𝑘/Γ for finite groups Γ [183]. The relevant Morse theory for
orbifolds, developed for our purposes below, is a direct extension: one works on the smooth
stratum (where 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) is a manifold) and tracks the orbifold strata as additional structure.
Two key structural features determine the correct morphism definition. First, chemical
reactions are atom-conserving: the total multiset of nuclei is unchanged between reactants
and products (no nuclear transmutation under ordinary chemical conditions). For an
elementary reaction from reactant system 𝐺to product system 𝐻with the same atom
set, the appropriate domain for the intrinsic reaction coordinate is the joint configuration
orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺⊔𝐻) introduced in §8.3.3: the configuration orbifold of the combined
reactive complex, large enough to contain both reactant and product geometries as local
minima and the transition state between them as a saddle point. Second, the full interacting
PES 𝑉full on this joint orbifold is a single smooth function — not two separate PESs glued
at the TS. An elementary morphism in OrbMorse is therefore a triple (𝑉full, RTS, 𝛾) where
the gradient flow 𝛾on 𝑉full connects a reactant minimum (encoding the source object) to a
product minimum (encoding the target object) through the distinguished saddle point RTS.
General morphisms of OrbMorse, encoding multi-step mechanisms, are compositions of
elementary morphisms in the free-category sense made precise in Definition 8.24 below.
Definition 8.24 (The category OrbMorse). The symmetric monoidal category OrbMorse is
defined as follows.
Objects. Triples (O,𝑉, 𝑔) where:
• O is a smooth Riemannian orbifold (locally modelled on R𝑘/Γ for finite groups
Γ [183]);
• 𝑉: O →R is a smooth function, Morse on the open subset of chemically accessible,
CI-free, non-coalescence geometries (all critical points in that region are non-
degenerate);
• 𝑔is the Riemannian metric on O.
A distinguished minimum Rmin(O) ∈O marks the reference geometry (the equilibrium
structure).
Elementary morphisms (geometric channels). For objects (𝐶𝑒(𝐺),𝑉𝐺, 𝑔𝐺) and (𝐶𝑒(𝐻),𝑉𝐻, 𝑔𝐻)
with 𝐺and 𝐻sharing an underlying atom multiset, an elementary geometric channel is a

Proposition 8.25 (OrbMorse is a strict SMC). With the structure of Definition 8.24, OrbMorse
is a strict symmetric monoidal category.
Proof. Category. Morphisms are finite strings of elementary geometric channels; identity
at each object is the empty string; composition is concatenation of strings. Both associativity
of composition and the unit laws hold strictly by definition of string concatenation (i.e.,
OrbMorse is the free category on its generating graph of elementary channels).
Strict monoidal. The three structural isomorphisms are all identities. Associativity:
(O1 × O2) × O3 = O1 × (O2 × O3) as product orbifolds; (𝑉1 + 𝑉2) + 𝑉3 = 𝑉1 + (𝑉2 + 𝑉3)
in 𝐶∞; (𝑔1 ⊕𝑔2) ⊕𝑔3 = 𝑔1 ⊕(𝑔2 ⊕𝑔3) as block metrics. Left/right unit: {∗} × O = O,
0 + 𝑉= 𝑉, and 0 ⊕𝑔= 𝑔.
Symmetric. The swap isomorphism 𝜏12 : (O1 × O2,𝑉1 + 𝑉2, 𝑔1 ⊕𝑔2) →(O2 × O1,𝑉2 +
𝑉1, 𝑔2 ⊕𝑔1) is the coordinate swap; hexagon axioms hold by commutativity of + and ⊕.

Remark 8.26 (Monoidal product vs. joint orbifold: Layer 1 and Layer 2). The categorical
monoidal product (O1 × O2, 𝑉1 + 𝑉2, 𝑔1 ⊕𝑔2) approximates the asymptotic structure of
the joint configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2) at infinite fragment separation. The two
spaces differ in two ways: 𝐶𝑒(𝐺1) × 𝐶𝑒(𝐺2) has dimension dim 𝐶𝑒(𝐺1) + dim 𝐶𝑒(𝐺2) =
3(𝑛1 + 𝑛2) −12 (two 𝑆𝐸(3) quotients), while 𝐶𝑒(𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2) has dimension 3(𝑛1 + 𝑛2) −6
(one 𝑆𝐸(3) quotient), containing three additional relative-motion coordinates; and the

non-zero at finite separation. Explicitly:
𝑉full(R1, R2, s) = 𝑉1(R1) + 𝑉2(R2) + 𝑉int(R1, R2, s),
where s denotes the relative-separation coordinates and 𝑉int →0 as |s| →∞.

• Layer 1 (strict product): 𝑉full = 𝑉1 + 𝑉2. The two subsystems do not interact; no
barrier, no IRC, no reaction. Sufficient for isolated-fragment properties (𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆of

• Layer 2 (lax product): 𝑉full = 𝑉1 +𝑉2 +𝑉int on 𝐶𝑒(𝐺1 ⊔𝐺2). The interaction creates

witnesses the interaction correction.
The interaction term: the ion-dipole complex in SN2
The interaction term 𝑉int is not a mathematical abstraction but a physical observable
with direct chemical consequences.
The SN2 PES. For the reaction CH3Cl + OH−→CH3OH + Cl−, the non-interacting
Layer 1 approximation gives the PES as the sum of the isolated reactant PESs: a flat
surface with a single minimum at the CH3Cl equilibrium geometry and no barrier.
The Layer 1 PES predicts no reaction pathway, no TS, and no product formation.
The full Layer 2 PES adds 𝑉int, which includes the long-range ion-dipole Coulomb
attraction between OH−and CH3Cl. This attraction creates:
(i) An ion-dipole complex [CH3Cl · · · OH−]: a shallow well (≈−40 kJ/mol below
separated reactants) appearing at intermediate C· · · O distance ≈3.5 Å. This
minimum is entirely due to 𝑉int and is invisible at Layer 1.
(ii) The transition state [HO · · · CH3 · · · Cl]‡ at shorter C· · · O and C· · · Cl distances:
the saddle point of the full Layer 2 surface.
(iii) An analogous product complex [CH3OH · · · Cl−] on the exit channel.
The full Layer 2 PES profile is a characteristic double-well potential with two
intermediate complexes flanking the central TS — a well-established feature of
gas-phase SN2 reactions whose shape is entirely due to 𝑉int [167].
In OrbMorse language: the monoidal product object (𝐶𝑒(CH3Cl) ×𝐶𝑒(OH−),𝑉CH3Cl +
𝑉OH−, 𝑔) has no morphism to the product object at Layer 1. The morphism exists
only at Layer 2, where 𝑉int provides the gradient-flow cobordism (the IRC from the
ion-dipole complex through the TS to the product complex on 𝐶𝑒(CH3Cl ⊔OH−)).

Remark 8.31 (Why 𝐹𝑉is lax, not strict). The critical distinction from all lower-level
decorator functors (𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, 𝐹𝑃) is that 𝐹𝑉is lax monoidal.
At L1–L3, the decorator functors are strict monoidal: 𝐹𝐻(𝐺⊗𝐻) = 𝐹𝐻(𝐺) + 𝐹𝐻(𝐻)
(the enthalpy of a combined system is the sum of the parts) because 𝐹𝐻reads off global
conserved quantities unaffected by intermolecular interactions.
At L5, strictness would require 𝐹𝑉(𝐺⊗𝐻) = 𝐹𝑉(𝐺) ⊗𝐹𝑉(𝐻), i.e., the full PES equals
𝑉𝐺+𝑉𝐻on the nose. But this is the non-interacting approximation (Layer 1), which cannot
produce a transition state. The Layer 2 BO PES has 𝑉full = 𝑉𝐺+ 𝑉𝐻+ 𝑉int whenever
fragments interact; the laxator 𝜙𝐺,𝐻is the physical correction witnessing this interaction.
In terms of the tower structure: the laxator is the first occurrence in the tower of a non-trivial
structural morphism witnessing the breakdown of additivity. 𝐹𝑉is the first functor in the
tower whose monoidal structure is genuinely lax.

Remark 8.32 (What computational methods provide 𝐹𝑉, and their position in OrbMorse).
Unlike 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆, and FP, the functor 𝐹𝑉cannot be specified by a finite list of numbers:
𝑉𝐺: 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) →R is an infinite-dimensional datum. In practice it is approximated by one
of four progressively coarser methods, each occupying a well-defined position relative to
OrbMorse.
(i) Exact BO PES (full CI): the ground-state PES defined by 𝑉(R) = 𝐸0(R) + 𝑉nn(R),
where 𝐸0 is the lowest eigenvalue of the exact electronic Hamiltonian and 𝑉nn is
the nuclear–nuclear Coulomb repulsion. This is the Layer 2 datum. For fixed lift
choices (electronic-structure theory, conformer, TS, IRC branch) it is well-defined
(Theorem 8.33 below), but computationally inaccessible for all but the smallest
systems. It defines the exact object of OrbMorse that 𝐹𝑉targets.
(ii) Coupled-cluster CCSD(T): an approximation ˜𝑉CC ≈𝑉that truncates the cluster
expansion at doubles with perturbative triples [167]. This is the “gold standard”
of computational chemistry, recovering > 99.9% of the correlation energy for
most closed-shell molecules. Its critical-point structure (minima, saddle points)
agrees with the exact PES to within the triples error. In OrbMorse: ˜𝑉CC defines an
approximate Morse triple that is a perturbation of the exact Layer 2 object; the Morse
structure (and hence the IRC and 𝐸𝑎) is preserved up to the truncation error.
(iii) Density functional theory (DFT): ˜𝑉DFT = 𝐸Kohn-Sham, the energy functional
of an auxiliary non-interacting system with an approximate exchange-correlation
functional [167].
DFT is computationally efficient and typically accurate for
equilibrium geometries and moderate barriers; it can fail for dispersion-dominated
interactions (e.g. van der Waals complexes) and for open-shell transition metals. In
OrbMorse: ˜𝑉DFT is an approximate object in which the Morse structure may differ
qualitatively from the exact PES when the exchange-correlation functional is poor
near saddle points.
(iv) Classical force fields (GAFF [184], FF19SB [185], CHARMM [186], OPLS [187,
188]): an analytic approximation ˜𝑉FF = Í

Remark 8.34 (Morse genericity). The Morse condition on 𝑉𝐺(non-degenerate critical
points) is not guaranteed by the BO construction but holds for all chemically relevant
molecular systems at all chemically relevant geometries. Non-Morse critical points do occur
in molecular physics — notably at catastrophe geometries where two critical points merge
(fold catastrophe) or a saddle degenerates (cusp catastrophe), and at conical intersections
themselves — but these are non-generic under parameter variation and belong to higher
tower levels (L6 for CIs, L7 for anharmonic and tunneling phenomena that probe non-Morse
regions). For all critical points on the accessible region 𝐶𝑒acc(𝐺) under standard thermal
conditions, Morseness holds.

in the pointed-set sense made precise in §8.1.

Reading the diagram: the decorator chain L0 →L3 adds one scalar functor per step
(all strict monoidal). The structural extension L3 →L4 replaces the underlying

The four extension types are, in order: decorator (L0 →L3), structural (L3 →L4),
symmetry enrichment (L4 →L4.5), and geometric decoration (L4.5 →L5, lax).

Remark 8.39 (Status of the two conditions). The naive condition (18) essentially never holds
exactly. The full condition (19) holds up to anharmonic and deep-tunneling corrections
for essentially all elementary reactions where the BO approximation itself holds, and
becomes exact in the limit of a classical harmonic BO PES with no recrossing and no
tunneling [195, 196]. The decomposition (17) attributes the residual to a prefactor part
(ln 𝑄‡/𝑄reac: ZPE plus entropy plus rotational/translational ratios) and a transmission part
(ln 𝜅: recrossing plus semiclassical tunneling). Both parts are L5-computable. A genuine
L7 signal — a residual not explained by PES-derived semiclassics — arises only when
multidimensional nuclear-wavefunction effects dominate; see Remark 8.41 and §8.7.
Three inter-level coherence conditions in the tower
The tower contains three conditions linking data at non-adjacent levels. Each condition
is a statement that a lower-level datum (at level 𝑗) is constrained by higher-level data
(at level 𝑘> 𝑗), not that the lower datum is “derivable from” the lower level.

All three conditions reside at L5 or below: the constrained lower-level data are
re-expressible in terms of higher-level structural data. The L2–L3 condition fails
for driven non-equilibrium systems (detailed balance violated at the network level).
The L1–L5 condition fails when anharmonic or non-RRHO contributions to ZPE or
thermal energy dominate (floppy molecules, low-frequency torsions, high 𝑇). The
L3–L5 condition fails for (18) routinely but holds for (19) with L5-computable
corrections for essentially all reactions where the BO approximation itself holds. A
genuine L7 signal — a residual not explained by L5 semiclassics — is addressed in
§8.7.

Remark 8.41 (Tower attribution of tunneling: the L5/L7 boundary is sharper than textbook
pedagogy suggests). Proposition 8.40 establishes the secondary KIE as an L5 theorem. For
primary KIEs — including the anomalously large values observed in enzymatic hydrogen-
transfer reactions — the tower attribution requires care: textbook treatments identify
“quantum tunneling” with “nuclear wavefunctions on the BO surface” and conclude L7 is
needed. This identification is incorrect. The L5/L7 boundary is drawn by the dimensionality
of the nuclear wavefunction required, not by the mere presence of quantum effects:
The tower criterion. L5 admits quantum information at fixed geometry or along low-
dimensional reaction paths: harmonic ZPEs (Hessian spectra at critical points), 1-D
anharmonic proton vibrational states in PES slices (vibrationally adiabatic potential cuts),
semiclassical tunneling actions along instantons or corner-cutting paths, and ring-polymer
imaginary-time quantum statistics.
L7 is reserved for the multidimensional nuclear
wavefunction on the full nuclear configuration space: states on the full nuclear Hilbert
space Hnuc, not restrictions to 1-D slices or frozen environments.
Semiclassical tunneling is L5. All standard tunneling corrections — Wigner, Bell,
Eckart, small-curvature tunneling (SCT), large-curvature tunneling (LCT), microcanonical
optimised multidimensional tunneling (𝜇OMT) [195, 198] — require only the PES,
Hessians along the MEP, and (for LCT) off-MEP PES data for corner-cutting paths.
No nuclear wavefunction is constructed. Ring-polymer instanton theory (RPI) [202]
computes the dominant tunneling trajectory as an imaginary-time classical orbit on the
inverted PES — a stationary-phase saddle of the path integral — requiring only the PES.
Perturbative corrections to RPI [203] achieve few-percent agreement with exact nuclear
QM on benchmark systems using only PES and its derivatives.
Enzymatic KIEs of 20–700 are L5. Soybean lipoxygenase wild type shows 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷≈80
at 25 ◦C [204]; the L546A/L754A double mutant reaches 𝑘𝐻/𝑘𝐷≈540–700 [205],
several orders of magnitude above the 298 K semiclassical ZPE ceiling of ∼7–9. These
values are quantitatively reproduced by vibronically nonadiabatic proton-coupled electron
transfer (PCET) models [206, 207] and by ensemble-averaged variational TST with
𝜇OMT tunneling corrections (EA-VTST/𝜇OMT, [208]). Both frameworks construct the
rate from 1-D proton vibrational wavefunctions in frozen active-site geometries plus

What forces L7. Genuine L7 phenomena are those requiring the multidimensional nuclear
wavefunction on the full nuclear configuration space as a primary object. These include:
• MCTDH wavepacket propagation for reactive scattering (full nuclear Schrödinger

• Colbert–Miller DVR for full quantum reaction rates on small systems;
• exact nuclear diagonalisation for tunneling splittings in highly symmetric systems,
below the instanton-validity crossover temperature where perturbative RPI fails to
converge;
• ortho/para nuclear-spin statistics, which requires the full nuclear wavefunction to
enforce Bose/Fermi symmetry under the 𝐺∗-action of L4.5 (the symmetry group
exists at L4.5; its consequences for the total nuclear-spin-symmetrised wavefunction
live at L7);
• the superselection-sector structure of molecular identity (see Chapter ??).
In the tower, L7 is forced by phenomena that cannot be reduced to L5 data plus semiclassical
corrections — not merely by the presence of large KIE values or strong quantum behaviour.
The forcing argument for L5 ⇒L7 (§8.7) is grounded in such phenomena.

Remark 8.44 (Hess’s law and BO/RRHO are logically independent). The distinction made
in Step 5 of the proof deserves emphasis: Hess’s law and the BO/RRHO decomposition
are statements of different kinds at different tower levels.
• Hess’s law = L1-functoriality of 𝐹𝐻on reaction networks. Content: composition law
𝐹𝐻(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) = 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2) + 𝐹𝐻(𝑟1), established at L1 from the state-function character
of enthalpy [53], and therefore automatically independent of L5 data (BO, RRHO,
geometry). It survives in systems where BO fails — conical intersections, non-
adiabatic dynamics, ultrafast photochemistry — because its derivation does not use
BO.
• BO/RRHO decomposition = object-level (pointwise) representation of 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) via L5
data. Content: for each reaction 𝑟, the real number 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) decomposes as (23). This is
a cross-level consistency statement (L1 ↔L5) about pointwise values, presupposing
BO and the RRHO factorisation of the molecular partition function.
In a categorical presentation the two can be conflated (both involve “the enthalpy functor”),
but they are distinct statements and must be cited distinctly: Hess [53] and the state-function
treatment of enthalpy for the former; Ochterski [199] and the RRHO thermochemistry
treatment of Helgaker–Jørgensen–Olsen for the latter.
Remark 8.45 (The tower is coherent: higher levels constrain lower ones pointwise).
Proposition 8.43 exemplifies a general pattern: the pointwise values of every lower-level
functor in the tower admit a BO/RRHO-type representation in terms of L5 data (𝐹𝑉, 𝑔) in
the appropriate approximation.
• 𝐹𝐻(𝑟) ≈Δ𝑉elec(𝑟) + Δ𝐸ZPE(𝑟) (from 𝐹𝑉at minima and Hessians; this section).
• 𝐹𝑆(𝑟): partition-function ratio at Rmin, requiring the full Hessian spectrum — an L5
datum.
• 𝐹𝑃(𝑟) = 𝜅(𝑘𝐵𝑇/ℎ)(𝑄‡/𝑄reac)𝑒−𝑉‡/𝑘𝐵𝑇: full TST from 𝐹𝑉, Hessians at RTS and
Rmin, plus semiclassical corrections for 𝜅— all L5 data.
The composite forgetful functor 𝑈5→𝑘(for 𝑘= 1, 2, 3) therefore corresponds to a projection
from the L5 geometric level onto its thermochemical (𝑘= 1), equilibrium (𝑘= 2), or
kinetic (𝑘= 3) shadow at the level of pointwise values.
Crucially, this pointwise coherence does not reduce the composition laws (Hess’s law,
detailed balance, the chemical master equation) to L5: these are functoriality statements
established at their own levels from level-specific physics, and they survive replacements
of the L5 representation of individual values. The tower is a coherent filtration pointwise,
not a tower in which each level is derived from the next one up.

§8.7. What L5 cannot express: forcing of L6
The entire L5 framework rests on Layer 2(b) of §8.3: the ground-state section 𝜎0 is a
smooth section of Hel on the relevant CI-free open subset of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), equivalently, no conical
intersection (CI) between 𝑉0 and 𝑉1 lies in the chemically accessible region traversed
by the IRC and its low-energy basins. Within this restriction L5 completely describes
ground-state thermal chemistry via the Morse triple (𝐶𝑒(𝐺),𝑉0, 𝑔). But Layer 2(b) is not
permanent. It fails for a large class of chemically important processes, and the failure is
not a matter of approximation quality: it is a topological obstruction invisible to 𝑉0.
The key point is that L5 records only the ground-state PES function 𝑉0, not the electronic
bundle that fibres over it. A CI is a geometric feature of 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) where 𝑉0(R) = 𝑉1(R). At

This idealised pair is hypothetical — two real molecular systems with pointwise-
identical 𝑉0 but different CI topology are not generically realised in nature. The forcing
argument is a categorical test of expressive power: it asks whether the L5 datum
(𝐶𝑒(𝐺),𝑉0, 𝑔) contains enough information to distinguish system A from system B,
and the answer is no. In actual chemistry, the A vs B distinction manifests as the
difference between reactions whose accessible nuclear region encloses a CI (e.g. H +
HD reactive scattering at high collision energies) and those whose region does not
(e.g. ground-state SN2 at thermal conditions).

The extension L5 →L6 differs in character from every previous extension in the tower.
All lower extensions add structure on the configuration orbifold — a PES function, a metric,
a Morse structure, DPO rules, 𝐺∗-equivariance. The L5 →L6 extension adds structure
over 𝐶𝑒(𝐺): the topology of the Hilbert bundle Hel →𝐶𝑒(𝐺) whose fibres carry the
electronic wavefunctions.

triviality; for systems with broken time-reversal symmetry (external magnetic fields,
spin-orbit coupling), 𝑐1 becomes informative and the codimension-3 Berry-monopole
regime applies. L6 accommodates both regimes; the molecular Aharonov–Bohm forcing

§9. L6: The Electronic Structure Level
§9.1. Forcing the extension: half-integer pseudorotation quanta in Na3
The vibrational spectrum of Na3 in its 22𝐸′ excited electronic state, measured by Delacré-
taz, Grant, Whetten, Wöste, and Zwanziger [215], is the canonical molecular example
of fractional pseudorotational quantisation. In the ideal free-pseudorotor model, an ordi-
nary single-valued scalar nuclear wavefunction on the pseudorotation circle has integer
angular quantum numbers 𝑗= 0, ±1, ±2, . . .. The Jahn–Teller Berry sign changes the
boundary condition to 𝜓(𝜙+ 2𝜋) = −𝜓(𝜙), so the allowed quantum numbers become
𝑗= ±1/2, ±3/2, ±5/2, . . .. The lowest pseudorotational level lies at ℏ2/(8𝐼ps) above the
trough minimum in this limit, with no 𝑗= 0 level in the topological sector.1
This observation forces the passage from the scalar geometric level L5 to the electronic-
bundle level L6. The L5 projection retains only the lower adiabatic surface 𝑉−and the
mass-weighted metric 𝑔; if the associated nuclear wavefunction is treated as an ordinary

Why Z2-valuedness matters chemically
𝑤1(𝐿R
0 ) is a topologically protected property of a molecule’s electronic structure,
unlike 𝑉‡ or Δ𝐺which vary continuously with substitution, solvent, or temperature.
Along any closed loop of configurations 𝑤1 takes the value 0 (no CI enclosed) or 1
(odd number of CI components enclosed); there is no “half a conical intersection”.
Continuous perturbations cannot turn a CI on or off gradually — the gap either
closes along the path (𝑤1 flips) or it does not. This discreteness makes CI topology
experimentally certifiable: a ± outcome on each loop-resolved measurement, not a
continuous number to fit.

Scattering corroboration in H + HD
The same 𝑤1 ≠0 bundle structure appears in reactive scattering. H3 shares the 𝐷3ℎ
Jahn–Teller 𝐸⊗𝑒structure of Na3, with a codim-2 CI seam at equilateral-triangle
geometries. At collision energies above the CI (𝐸coll ≈2.77 eV), crossed-beam imaging
experiments resolve forward-scattering oscillations in (𝑣′, 𝑗′)-resolved differential
cross sections of H + HD →H2 + D [223]; the analogous effect below the CI was
reported in [224]. Single-surface L5 scattering on the ground-state PES [225] predicts
smooth angular distributions; including the Mead–Truhlar vector potential, or imposing
𝑤1 = 1 boundary conditions on loops linking the CI seam, reproduces the oscillations
quantitatively [214]. The topological sign comes from the electronic CI of the H3
system; the H/D substitution makes product channels experimentally distinguishable
and changes the scattering kinematics, but the geometric-phase mechanism itself is
the Z2 holonomy associated with loops around the H3 CI. Bound-state spectroscopy
of Na3 and reactive scattering of H + HD are two manifestations of the same 𝑤1
holonomy in different observable channels.

Remark 9.18 (The BO approximation at L6). The single-surface Born–Oppenheimer
approximation is justified asymptotically on regions where the relevant electronic state
is isolated by a uniform gap and nuclear motion is sufficiently slow; the small parameter
𝜀separating electronic and nuclear timescales is fixed once in Chapter 10 [178]. The
single-surface BO approximation breaks down at X01 and may also become inaccurate near
small gaps or strong derivative-coupling regions, where multi-state treatment of the active
bundle is required.
The L5 shadow (Ω,𝑉0, 𝑔) does not record the eigenline topology, and quantising it with
single-valued nuclear wavefunctions assigns trivial sign holonomies. At L6, the bundle
E(𝑁), its Berry connection, X01, and 𝜂𝐵are retained. The sign holonomy (−1)⟨𝜂𝐵,[𝛾]⟩
enters the adiabatic nuclear equation as a Mead–Truhlar vector potential or as antiperiodic
boundary conditions on loops linking X01 [168]. It is the electronic-bundle datum that the
scalar L5 description forgets, not strictly a non-BO quantity.
What L6 means in practice
The L5/L6 distinction is about what datum the computation targets, not which method
is used.

supplies the 𝐹𝑉data: minima, saddles, IRC, barriers, vibrational frequencies.
L6 data. Locating X01 and evaluating 𝜂𝐵on loops in Ω◦is a multi-state question: one

multireference or state-averaged methods such as CASSCF, MRCI, NEVPT2, and
MC-PDFT are the standard tools [226].
The forgetful functor 𝑈6 is the operation of extracting only the ground-state PES
from a multi-state calculation: it compresses (E(𝑁), 𝐴, X01, 𝜂𝐵) down to 𝑉0 alone.
If the relevant dynamics remains on a single smooth isolated adiabatic surface
and the real eigenline is topologically trivial on the explored region, the L5 scalar
description may be sufficient. 𝜂𝐵= 0 is not by itself a guarantee that L6 data are
unnecessary: photoisomerisation, internal conversion, photodissociation, spin-orbit-
mediated intersystem crossing, and charge-transfer dynamics all require L6 data —
multiple electronic surfaces, derivative couplings, seam geometry, and (when relevant)
the topological sign — and are not determined by 𝑉0 alone.

The sign change in the laboratory
The sign −1 has two standard experimental manifestations.
Quantum interference in reactive scattering. When a nuclear wavepacket reaches
a product channel by two paths — one winding around the CI, one not — the two
amplitudes acquire a relative sign −1. Wherever both paths contribute coherently to
the same product, this yields destructive interference that redistributes the angular
distribution of products relative to a scalar single-surface calculation on the same
ground-state PES that omits the geometric-phase boundary condition. The effect was
predicted by Mead and Truhlar [168], quantitatively modelled for the H+H2 →H2+H
system by Juanes-Marcos, Althorpe, and Wrede [214], and observed experimentally
for the isotopic analogue H + HD →H2 + D by Yuan et al. above the CI energy [223]
and below it [224]. Measured differential cross sections agree with geometric-phase-
inclusive scattering calculations on the ground-state PES and disagree with calculations
on the same PES that omit the phase. This is the cleanest laboratory signature to date
of a topological (L6) effect in a simple chemical reaction.
Anti-periodic boundary condition on nuclear motion encircling X01. For a nuclear
coordinate 𝜙parametrising a loop that links X01 in the course of a photochemical
pathway, the electronic sign change imposes an anti-periodic boundary condition on
the nuclear wavefunction:
𝜒nuc(𝜙+ 2𝜋) = −𝜒nuc(𝜙),
enforcing single-valuedness of the total vibronic wavefunction Ψ = 𝜒nuc 𝜎0. Physically,
this shifts the allowed pseudorotational quantum numbers from integers to half-integers:
𝑗∈Z
⇝
𝑗∈Z + 1
2.
The same mechanism produces the half-integer pseudorotation quantum numbers in
Na3 established in §9.1; it is also used in ultrafast spectroscopy to detect and characterise
CIs through the rearrangement of vibronic spacings near a CI funnel [226]. The effect
operates only on nuclear motion that genuinely encircles X01; ground-state dynamics
along a path that remains in a simply connected gapped region and does not link the
CI seam does not realise it.
In both cases the observable effect is controlled by the discrete class 𝜂𝐵= 𝑤1(𝐿R
0 ). A
scalar calculation on the ground-state PES that omits the geometric-phase boundary
condition gives the trivial sign sector; the physical L6 lift assigns sign holonomy −1
to loops linking the CI seam. The topological class itself cannot change continuously:
changing the sign sector requires the relevant loop to pass through a degeneracy, or
the gapped real eigenline description to break down on the loop.

9.6.2. The Landau–Zener formula as a non-adiabatic scalar estimator

plane, and the standard two-state LZ formula is no longer exact. It survives only as a local

locally diabatised two-state model near the branching region. The path-level matrix-valued

coupling, and local slopes.

makes product channels experimentally distinguishable, but the electronic geometric phase
is inherited from the conical-intersection topology of the underlying H3 electronic problem.

§9.7. What L6 cannot express: forcing of L7
Up to L6, the molecular graph 𝐺and the associated nuclear configuration space are taken
as input data: the object (𝐺, 𝜎) comes first, and ˆ𝐻el(R), 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), and the adiabatic bundle
Hel(𝑁) are built over a region of that configuration space. Nuclear permutations may appear
as geometric or orbifold symmetries, but the nuclei themselves are not yet quantised as
identical particles. In particular, L6 does not impose the exchange symmetry of the nuclear
wavefunction, nor does it derive molecular graph structure from the all-particle Coulomb
Hamiltonian.
L7 is forced by two observations L6 cannot accommodate:
(1) Nuclear indistinguishability: identical nuclei carry exchange statistics — antisym-
metry under exchange for half-integer-spin nuclei, symmetry for integer-spin nuclei.
Protons give the cleanest forcing example as spin-1
2 fermions.
(2) Molecular identity: despite this indistinguishability, molecular structure appears
as a stable effective sector or correlation pattern in the quantum description. The
emergence of “this molecule” rather than “a superposition over graphs” must be
281

derived, not postulated.
Both observations concern particle statistics and identity, not reaction rates. Large kinetic
isotope effects and tunnelling corrections are not, by themselves, clean forcing examples
for L7: many such effects can be modelled semiclassically as corrections on an L5-level
potential-energy or free-energy surface (see Remark 8.41 of §8.5). They force L7 only
when the nuclear wavefunction, nuclear spin symmetry, or identical-particle exchange
structure becomes part of the state description rather than a correction functional on a
classical PES.
9.7.1. First forcing pair: nuclear indistinguishability

First forcing pair for L7: identical-nucleus statistics
At every level up to L6, nuclei are treated as distinguishable: each occupies a
position R𝑖on 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), which is modelled on its regular strata as the quotient of
R3𝑛by SE(3) ⋊Aut𝜇(𝐺), with Aut𝜇(𝐺) relabelling graph vertices while preserving
labels and masses. This treats nuclear permutations as a geometric symmetry of
configuration space; it does not impose antisymmetry on the nuclear wavefunction.
The fully quantum treatment requires the total molecular wavefunction to transform as
the correct sign representation under exchange of any pair of identical nuclei, giving
observably different predictions.
Paradigm: ortho/para H2. For ground-state H2, the electronic and vibrational factors
are symmetric under proton exchange, and the rotational wavefunction has parity
(−1)𝐽. Since the two protons are identical fermions, the total wavefunction must be
antisymmetric under exchange. Hence the nuclear-spin singlet 𝐼= 0 (antisymmetric)
pairs with even 𝐽to give para-H2, while the nuclear-spin triplet 𝐼= 1 (symmetric)
pairs with odd 𝐽to give ortho-H2. The two spin isomers have different rotational
partition functions and therefore different low-temperature thermodynamic behaviour,
and the interconversion is symmetry-forbidden in an isolated molecule. In the absence
of efficient paramagnetic, surface, or impurity-mediated conversion channels, ortho–
para interconversion is slow on laboratory timescales, a metastability that underpins
contemporary hyperpolarisation methods such as PHIP and SABRE [230].
What L6 cannot express. The L6 electronic data
(Hel(𝑁), 𝐴, X01, 𝜂𝐵)
are built over a classical nuclear configuration space. They do not include the nuclear
spin Hilbert space, nor the representation of the identical-proton permutation group.
Hence the distinction between

Unlike the ortho/para example above, the second example is not a completed forcing

to a deeper limitation of L6: the molecular graph 𝐺is still input data, whereas in an
all-particle quantum treatment molecular structure should emerge from correlations,

symmetry breaking, and sector selection rather than being postulated.
A species in L5(𝑃) is a pair (𝐺, 𝜎), and the L6 electronic lift presupposes 𝐺:
the active bundle Hel(𝑁) →Ω ⊂𝐶𝑒(𝐺) is built over the configuration region
associated with that graph. Given only the Coulomb Hamiltonian for a collection
of identical nuclei and electrons, why does a definite molecular structure — such
as a triangular D+
3 configuration — emerge from a totally permutation-symmetric
all-particle wavefunction?
Exact bound eigenstates of the all-particle Coulomb
Hamiltonian inherit the symmetries of the Hamiltonian, so molecular shape is
not represented as a literal fixed nuclear framework in the naive eigenfunction
picture [174, 231]. It must be recovered from correlations, sector structure, symmetry
breaking, or suitable classical/semiclassical limits. In the Primas–Amann framework,
molecular structure is proposed to emerge as a superselection sector of the full
quantum description in the mass-ratio limit 𝜀= (𝑚𝑒/𝑀)1/2 →0 [232, 175]; a general
theorem identifying arbitrary chemical graphs 𝐺with such sectors remains an open
problem.
Recent numerical work by Lang, Cezar, Adamowicz, and Pedersen [233] provides
a concrete demonstration of structural emergence for D+
3: Markov-chain Monte
Carlo sampling of a totally permutation-symmetric pre-BO wavefunction recovers an
unambiguous equilateral-triangular structure. A general theorem for arbitrary graphs
𝐺remains open and is treated in §10.7.
What L6 cannot express. At L6, two molecular graphs correspond to different
input objects and there is no operation internal to the theory that derives one graph
sector from the all-particle Hilbert space. In the full quantum description, by contrast,
identical nuclei live in a single permutation-symmetric framework, and graph-like
molecular structures must emerge as effective sectors or correlation patterns. This
motivates L7, but the general sector theorem for arbitrary chemical graphs remains
open: the present discussion identifies the structural task that L7 must eventually
solve, namely deriving graph-like molecular sectors from the all-particle quantum
theory rather than assuming 𝐺as input.

L7 as the strictly quantum tower level
The tower L0 →· · · →L6 built chemistry from combinatorics through topology-
decorated fibre structure over smooth configuration orbifolds, with nuclei classical
throughout. L7 is the strictly quantum cap: nuclei become quantum identical particles,
the BO approximation appears as an asymptotic effective theory in the 𝜀→0
regime, compatible with the classical fibre of the deformation-quantisation picture,
and molecular identity is to be derived rather than postulated.
The next chapter develops L7 in this spirit, necessarily more speculative than its
predecessors: the four open constructions (continuous field for molecules, groupoid
C*-algebra encoding nuclear statistics, possible K-theoretic or real-bundle refinements
of the Z/2 Berry-sign class, superselection-sector theorem for arbitrary 𝐺) are
surveyed with explicit state-of-the-art attributions and open-problem formulations.
The ortho/para H2 forcing example establishes the physical necessity of adding
nuclear quantum statistics; the molecular-identity discussion motivates the broader
L7 programme. The mathematical framework is the subject of what follows.

§10. L7: The Full Quantum Level
§10.1. Forcing the full quantum level
Section 9.7 identified two reasons the tower must pass beyond L6, of different logical status.
The first is a clean forcing example: ortho- and para-H2, which share the same L6 electronic
shadow but differ by nuclear spin-statistical sector. The second is a programme-level
direction: the recovery of graph-like molecular structure from an all-particle quantum
theory, rather than taking 𝐺as primitive input.
(I) Clean forcing example: nuclear spin statistics. Ortho- and para-H2 share the
same scalar and electronic L6 shadow. Their distinction is not electronic; it is
nuclear spin-statistical. The distinction lies in the nuclear spin-statistical sector, an
object L6 does not carry. The two spin isomers have different allowed rotational
quantum numbers and hence different rotational partition functions, including the 1:3
nuclear-spin degeneracy of the para and ortho sectors, with correspondingly different
low-temperature thermodynamic behaviour. In the absence of efficient paramagnetic,
surface, or impurity-mediated conversion channels, ortho–para interconversion is
slow on laboratory timescales; the precise rate is strongly condition-dependent [238].
(II) Programme-level direction: molecular identity as an emergent sector. The molecular
graph 𝐺∈LGraph𝑃is given data at every level L4–L6: the DPO rules, the
stereochemical symmetry, the configuration region, the active electronic bundle, and
the Berry-sign data all presuppose a chosen graph. The Woolley–Primas–Sutcliffe
problem [174, 232, 231] asks whether such molecular structure can be recovered
from the all-particle Coulomb Hamiltonian rather than postulated. This is not a
completed forcing theorem in the present manuscript; it is the programme-level task
that motivates the general L7 construction.
The first example gives the clean forcing obstruction: L6 does not contain nuclear spin-
statistical sectors. The second points to the broader completion problem: 𝐺should
ultimately emerge from the all-particle quantum theory rather than remain primitive input.
Both motivate L7, but with different logical status.
At L6, nuclear positions are still treated through a classical configuration space. Permu-
tations may appear as geometric or orbifold symmetries, but there is no nuclear Hilbert
space and no imposed bosonic or fermionic exchange symmetry of the nuclear wavefunc-
tion. At L7 the nuclei become quantum particles whose algebra of observables carries
exchange-indistinguishability constraints, and from whose representation theory the graph
label 𝐺should be derivable as an effective sector rather than postulated.
Warning 10.1 (Programmatic character of this chapter). Unlike the earlier levels, where
the intended data and forgetful projections can be specified explicitly, L7 is introduced as
a mathematical programme. The level is defined by the conditions its data must satisfy,
while the full construction of morphisms and the operator-algebraic functorial structure
remains open.
The correct formulation is a forgetful obstruction rather than an automorphism cokernel.

The shape of Chapter 10
Section 10.2 develops the new physical content of L7 — the nuclear Schrödinger equa-
tion, the PST 𝜀-expansion, and the demarcation between L5 semiclassical tunnelling
and genuinely L7 phenomena. Sections 10.3 and 10.4 present the two mathematical
programmes closest to delivering C2: strict deformation quantisation (Rieffel, Lands-
man) and the Georgescu–Iftimovici 𝑁-body algebra. Section 10.5 formulates L7(𝑃)
as a category of L6-objects equipped with candidate full quantum/operator-algebraic
lifts, together with a forgetful projection
𝑈7 : L7(𝑃) →L6(𝑃).
Section 10.6 states four conjectures (the precise form of C1–C4) as the tower’s original
contribution at this level. Section 10.7 develops the Woolley–Primas problem as the
tower statement of C4. Section 10.8 closes with the complete tower, the corrected list
of forgetful extensions, and the three inter-level coherence conditions.
§10.2. Quantum nuclear dynamics: the new physical content of L7
The forcing arguments of §10.1 identified two structures absent from L6: a wavefunction
for the nuclei (with the indistinguishability it carries) and the programme of recovering
molecular identity as an effective superselection or correlation-sector label. This section
develops the first physical content that L7 delivers: the nuclear Schrödinger equation on the
BO surface, the space-adiabatic 𝜀-expansion that recovers the Born–Oppenheimer approxi-
mation as a controlled asymptotic, and its semiclassical tunnelling regime. Section 10.2.3
returns to the forcing content with the ortho/para example.
Warning 10.3 (What this section does not claim). Anomalous primary kinetic isotope
effects — including values of 55 ± 6 [245] and 661 ± 27 [246] in enzymatic hydrogen
transfer — are frequently cited as evidence for a quantum-mechanical treatment of nuclei.
They are not evidence for L7 specifically. Large KIEs are not, by themselves, clean forcing
examples for L7. Many such effects can be estimated using semiclassical or path-integral
approximations built from L5-level geometric data: a PES, a mass metric, Hessians, and
barrier geometry. These methods can account for many large KIEs in model-dependent
settings, but they do not by themselves force the full L7 structure. What L7 adds is the
nuclear Hilbert-space and operator-algebraic framework in which such approximations
are derived, together with nuclear exchange-statistical sectors that no scalar semiclassical
correction can express.

approximate. The L7 novelty lies not in the tunnelling estimate itself but in the Hilbert-
space/𝐶∗-algebraic setting in which such estimates become theorems, together with the
exchange-statistical sectors developed in §10.2.3.

10.2.3. Ortho and para-hydrogen: the forcing content of L7
The tunnelling content of §10.2.2 is reproduced by L5 semiclassical methods; it sharpens
but does not force L7. Ortho- and para-hydrogen, by contrast, are distinguished by a
structure no level below L7 carries: the symmetry of the nuclear wavefunction under
proton exchange. This is forcing pair (I) of §10.1 in concrete form.
Example 10.9 (Ortho/para-H2). The proton is a spin-1
2 fermion. Pauli antisymmetry
requires the total H2 wavefunction Ψ = 𝜓spatial ⊗𝜒spin to be antisymmetric under proton
exchange 𝜋12. Since 𝜋12𝜓𝐽= (−1)𝐽𝜓𝐽on rotational states with quantum number 𝐽,
nuclear-spin states split into:
• para-H2: singlet spin (𝐼= 0, antisymmetric under 𝜋12), paired with even 𝐽. Ground
state 𝐽= 0.
• ortho-H2: triplet spin (𝐼= 1, symmetric under 𝜋12), paired with odd 𝐽. Lowest state
𝐽= 1, roughly 14.7 meV above para.
At thermal equilibrium, the 3:1 nuclear-spin degeneracy gives ortho:para = 3 : 1 at high 𝑇
and pure para as 𝑇→0. In the ordinary isolated, spin-independent approximation, the
spatial and nuclear-spin sectors are separately preserved, so ortho and para subspaces are
invariant. Conversion requires weak spin-dependent, magnetic, surface, impurity-mediated,
or other environmental interactions.
In the absence of efficient such channels, ortho–para conversion is slow on laboratory
timescales; the precise rate is condition-dependent. The two spin isomers have different
rotational partition functions and therefore different low-temperature thermodynamic
behaviour. The lowest ortho level 𝐽=1 lies above the para ground level 𝐽=0 by 2𝐵, where
𝐸𝐽= 𝐵𝐽(𝐽+ 1); for H2, this is about 14.7 meV, and ortho-to-para conversion releases
approximately this gap per converted molecule upon liquefaction.

Forcing vs content at L7
Sections 10.2.1–10.2.2 developed content that L7 makes rigorous: the nuclear
Schrödinger equation, its 𝜀-expansion with Berry/geometric corrections, and the
Agmon–Helffer–Sjöstrand tunnelling asymptotic. Many of its leading semiclassical
consequences can be estimated from L5-level data; the L7 claim is on the Hilbert-space
and 𝐶∗-algebraic framework (§10.3–§10.5). Section 10.2.3 developed the content
that forces L7: nuclear exchange symmetry, nuclear spin-statistical sectors, and the
resulting ortho/para superselection decomposition.
No scalar L5-level semiclassical correction can produce the nuclear spin-statistical
sector decomposition itself; the symmetry of the nuclear wavefunction under proton
exchange is a genuinely L7 datum, and the metastable ortho/para populations — with
distinct rotational partition functions, slow condition-dependent interconversion in
the absence of efficient catalysts, and the 𝐽=1 →0 energy release in ortho-to-para
conversion — are its laboratory signatures.

unspecified. That connection is the substance of space-adiabatic perturbation theory
(PST) [179, 178]: it shows how the Berry connection and related geometric terms from
the chosen L6 electronic lift enter the effective nuclear Hamiltonian in the semiclassical
expansion, as Layer 2(b) requires, and provides the Hilbert-space error estimate that
underlies the 𝐶∗-algebraic Born–Oppenheimer statement (Conjecture 10.36).
At the clamped-nuclei electronic level, isotopologues such as H2 and D2 share the
same electronic surface and active electronic data (𝜎𝑗, 𝐴, 𝜂𝐵). Their leading dynamical
differences enter through the nuclear masses in the effective Hamiltonian, with the
underlying compact-operator fibre abstractly isomorphic (by Remark 10.12) but carrying
different Hamiltonian elements. In addition, their nuclear spin-statistical sectors differ at L7:
protons are fermions and deuterons are bosons, so the total wavefunction is antisymmetric
under proton exchange and symmetric under deuteron exchange, with correspondingly
different spin-rotational sector decompositions (see §10.2.3). Nuclear-mass data already
belong to L5 (Mathbox 10.2.1).

§10.4. The Georgescu 𝑁-body algebra: ingredients for Layer 2(a)
Construction C2 is the pair (Layer 1 + Layer 2). Section 10.3.1 supplied Layer 1 via the
Landsman tangent-groupoid construction: an abstract continuous field with the correct
fibre algebra but no connection to molecular physics. This section develops the ingredients
for Layer 2(a) — the identification of 𝐴𝐺
𝜀as a specific algebra to which the nuclear-
effective Hamiltonian 𝐻𝜀is affiliated, rather than only an abstract 𝐶∗-algebra satisfying
the SDQ axioms. The tool is the Georgescu–Iftimovici graded crossed-product algebra
𝔄(𝑋) [242, 253], a 𝐶∗-algebra on 𝐿2(𝑋) providing a 𝐶∗-algebraic framework in which a
large class of 𝑁-body Hamiltonians with admissible decaying pair interactions — including
Coulomb-type interactions under the Georgescu–Iftimovici affiliation hypotheses — have
affiliated resolvents. The algebra’s graded ideal structure encodes a particle-cluster partition
lattice, reproducing the HVZ theorem as a purely algebraic fact.
Warning 10.18 (Layer 2(a) ingredients vs. Layer 2(a) completed). Throughout this section,
𝑋denotes a nuclear configuration vector space and 𝔄(𝑋) the corresponding 𝑁-body
algebra on 𝐿2(𝑋), before any Euclidean or exchange quotient. The Layer 2(a) condition
of Open Problem 10.3.4 is the identification of 𝐴𝐺
𝜀on the quotient/sector Hilbert space

Oppenheimer electron–nuclear Hamiltonian, by contrast, lives on 𝐿2(R3(𝑁nuc+𝑁el)) (modulo
centre-of-mass and exchange) and would require applying the 𝑁-body machinery to the
full particle configuration space — outside the scope of this section. What is established
on 𝐿2(𝑋) is developed below: 𝔄(𝑋) as an ambient algebra for nuclear effective 𝑁-body
Hamiltonians, the affiliation of 𝐻𝜀, and the HVZ theorem as an algebraic consequence.
The Georgescu algebra in the tower
(i) What 𝔄(𝑋) provides. A specific 𝐶∗-algebra on 𝐿2(𝑋) to which the nuclear-
effective Hamiltonian 𝐻𝜀= −(𝜀2/2)Δ + 𝑉(R) is affiliated, where 𝑉is the BO
eigenvalue selected at L6 (Remark 10.20). The SDQ axioms of Definition 10.10
specify the abstract structure of 𝐹7(𝐺); 𝔄(𝑋) names a concrete algebra to which the
correct Hamiltonian is affiliated.
(ii) The graded structure tracks particle-cluster asymptotics. ℜ(𝑋) is graded by a
semilattice S of linear subspaces of 𝑋describing the relative-coordinate quotients
of the system — equivalently, by particle-cluster partitions. This lattice is related
to, but not identical with, the L0 stoichiometric bookkeeping: L0 records species
and reaction balances, whereas ℜ(𝑋) records asymptotic cluster decompositions of a
fixed 𝑁-body Hamiltonian. Chemical dissociation channels emerge by interpreting
certain cluster partitions as molecular fragments. The HVZ theorem (Theorem 10.23)

the algebraic location of the bound-state spectrum. Inside K(𝐿2(𝑋)), 𝔄(𝑋) does

What the Georgescu algebra means for chemistry
An ambient algebra for the nuclear 𝑁-body problem. The standard class of
nuclear-effective Hamiltonians 𝐻𝜀= −(𝜀2/2)ΔR + 𝑉(R) with admissible decaying
pair interactions is affiliated to 𝔄(𝑋) under the Georgescu–Iftimovici hypotheses.
This class includes Coulomb-type pair interactions, which are not in 𝐶0(𝑋/𝑊𝑖𝑗) (they
are singular on the collision set) but are admissible unbounded affiliated potentials
(Remark 10.20). 𝔄(𝑋) is not a particular approximate Hamiltonian model; it is a
canonical ambient 𝐶∗-algebraic framework to which the relevant Hamiltonians are
affiliated, with graded structure capturing the particle-cluster partition lattice.
The dissociation ladder. For water H2O (labelled atoms {H1, H2, O}) there are
𝐵(3) = 5 set partitions: {H1H2O}, {H1} | {H2O}, {H2} | {H1O}, {O} | {H1, H2}, and
{H1} | {H2} | {O}. After identifying the two hydrogen labels, these five partitions
reduce to four symmetry orbits: the undissociated channel and three dissociation
channels — H+OH, O+ {H, H}, and H+H+O. Whether the {H, H} cluster supports
a bound H2 state is spectral information of the corresponding cluster Hamiltonian, not
part of the partition lattice itself.
HVZ as the quantum dissociation threshold. The bottom of 𝜎ess(𝐻H2O) is the
minimum cluster threshold across non-minimal partitions: the quantum-mechanical
dissociation threshold of the chosen Schrödinger Hamiltonian. After adding zero-point
and electronic corrections, this threshold is the spectral analogue of the dissociation
energies organised at L1 by Hess-law bookkeeping — now derived as an algebraic
consequence of the ideal structure of 𝔄(𝑋).

10.4.2. HVZ and Mourre: spectral structure from the ideal lattice
The two foundational spectral results of 𝑁-body quantum mechanics are algebraic statements

Remark 10.24 (HVZ across the tower: L0 →L7). The union in Theorem 10.23 runs over a
particle-cluster partition lattice, related to but distinct from L0 stoichiometric bookkeeping:
L0 records species and reaction balances, whereas 𝔄(𝑋) records asymptotic cluster decom-
positions of a fixed 𝑁-body Hamiltonian. Chemical dissociation channels are obtained by
interpreting certain cluster partitions as molecular fragments. Algebraic HVZ is therefore
a 𝐶∗-algebraic computation of a quantum dissociation threshold whose thermochemical
analogue is the Hess-law L1 dissociation energy, mediated by the appropriate zero-point
and electronic corrections: the cluster lattice, invisible in the electronic structure at L6,
reappears at L7 as the ideal lattice of 𝔄(𝑋).

10.4.3. Channels vs species: the gap to Construction C4
What 𝔄(𝑋) encodes, and what remains for C4
What is encoded. The graded structure of ℜ(𝑋) tracks asymptotic cluster behaviour:
which atoms separate as |R| →∞, and at which thresholds. HVZ and Mourre follow
from this structure, and every affiliated 𝑁-body Hamiltonian inherits its spectral
framework.
What is not encoded. Within K(𝐿2(𝑋)), 𝔄(𝑋) does not distinguish which bound
configuration is occupied: bound ground and excited states, and weakly bound van
der Waals states, are all represented in the compact/localised part. Resonances —
non-𝐿2 poles of the resolvent — require separate scattering/resonance theory and
are not located in K(𝐿2(𝑋)) at all. In tower terms: 𝔄(𝑋) encodes the asymptotic
cluster channels but not the molecular identity (the L4 graph 𝐺) that must emerge
algebraically at L7.
Two steps to close the gap.
(i) 𝐺∗-equivariant restriction and descent (L4.5 data). Two related operations are re-
quired: restricting to 𝔄(𝑋)𝐺∗(the subalgebra commuting with the permutation-
inversion group 𝐺∗), and descending to an algebra on the quotient/sector
Hilbert space associated with 𝐶𝑒(𝐺), compatible with the Landsman fibre
K(𝐿2(𝐶𝑒(𝐺))) of Theorem 10.11. Ammann–Mougel–Nistor [254] identify
Georgescu’s 𝐶∗-algebraic compactification of 𝑋with Vasy’s blowup compactifi-
cation; this is the geometric scaffold on which the 𝐺∗-action can be implemented
equivariantly. The explicit molecular construction has not been carried out.
(ii) Molecular species identification (Construction C4). Equip the descended algebra
with an observable subalgebra, symmetry, or representation structure whose
sectors are labelled by graph-like molecular structures. The compact ideal
supplies the localised spectral regime, but the graph labels require additional
superselection/observable data, since K(H) is simple as a 𝐶∗-algebra and
admits no bare ideal decomposition. This is the content of Conjecture 10.42(a)
and the subject of §10.7; it is logically downstream of step (i).
§10.5. The full quantum level L7(𝑃): object-level specification
Sections 10.2–10.4 developed the three mathematical strands that make the full quantum
level a candidate for formal definition: the nuclear Schrödinger equation on the BO surface
(C1 at the Hilbert-space level), strict deformation quantisation and the space-adiabatic
𝜀-expansion (the ingredients of C2), and the Georgescu 𝑁-body algebra (Layer 2(a)
ingredients of C2). This section specifies the object-level data required of an L7-lift over
an L6-object, defines the target category C∗Algcont, and records the conditions that a future
functorial construction 𝐹7 would have to satisfy.

on morphisms is not given here and is part of the open programme of Constructions C2–C4
(Remark 10.30). Every statement below is a statement about what the specification commits

Where the four contents show up in the laboratory
C1 (dynamics): solving 𝐻𝜀
eff on 𝐿2(𝐶𝑒reg(𝐺)) gives vibrational spectra, zero-point
energies, and tunnelling amplitudes. Most standard electronic-structure workflows
(DFT, CCSD(T)) provide clamped-nuclei BO surfaces; force-field methods supply
approximations to them; both feed the classical/effective nuclear models at lower
tower levels. The size of BO/non-adiabatic error is property- and system-dependent
and breaks down near CI seams; no universal percentage estimate follows from 𝜀𝐺
alone.
C2 (existence): the 𝐶∗-algebraic status of every claim below.
C3 (topology): geometric-phase effects in reactions such as H + HD →H2 + D
associated with the H3 conical-intersection topology [258] and analogous cold-
reaction measurements [259] are laboratory manifestations of non-trivial Berry-sign
data 𝜂𝐵, with large channel- and energy-dependent modifications of state-resolved
observables; conjecturally, they correspond to a non-trivial 𝐾𝑂-theory class of the

Remark 10.40 (Real vs. complex Berry structure). The framework above uses real line
bundles and 𝐾𝑂-theory because non-relativistic molecular Hamiltonians with 𝑇2 = +1
yield real eigenstates with Z2-valued holonomies (§9.3). For spin–orbit-coupled systems
(𝑇2 = −1, outside the monograph’s scope in §10.8.4), the eigenstates are Kramers pairs,
the eigenbundle is complex, and the analogous obstruction lives in complex 𝐾-theory with
integer Chern class; Hawkins [244] provides the template there. Conjecture 10.39 is the
real analog of Hawkins’ result, which has not been worked out for real line bundles over
molecular configuration orbifolds.
Chemistry. The sign flip of the real adiabatic eigensection around any loop encircling
a CI seam is directly observable in scattering experiments: Yuan et al. [258] provide the
experimental observation of the geometric-phase effect in the H + HD →H2 + D reaction
associated with the H3 conical-intersection topology, and Kendrick, Hazra, and Balakr-
ishnan [259] predict large channel- and energy-dependent modifications of state-resolved
rate coefficients in the O + OH →H + O2 reaction through quantum interference between
direct and CI-encircling pathways. Conjecture 10.39 says this laboratory observation
has a 𝐾𝑂-theoretic shadow: the same 𝜂𝐵that modifies state-resolved scattering observ-
ables also requires a twisted/local-system quantisation of {𝐴𝐺

seam X01 is present, the single-band gap condition fails at the seam and requires a separate
resolution (Conjecture 10.45, §10.6.4).

§10.7. Molecular identity as superselection sector: the Woolley–Primas problem in
the tower
Construction C4 — the representation-theoretic content layer of the object-level lift
𝐹obj
7
(𝐺) identified in Mathbox 10.5.5 — is the tower’s answer to a question that quantum
chemistry has carried since the 1970s: how does the notion of a definite molecular species,
assumed throughout L0–L6, emerge from the symmetric full-quantum theory? This section
develops that answer in detail, placing the historical Woolley–Primas problem in tower
language, identifying the stabilisation mechanisms required for Conjecture 10.42 — exact
spin-statistical, metastable semiclassical, and environmental — and recording the evidence
that supports each.
Section structure
§10.7.1: the Woolley–Primas problem as a tower statement. §10.7.2: stabilisation
mechanisms in the tower, with the (a1) exact spin-statistical regime, the (a2) metastable
semiclassical regime, and the (b) environment-induced regime distinguished. §10.7.3:
three cases addressed in the literature — (A) exact 𝑆2 exchange via Pauli for ortho/para
H2 (theorem); (B) Pfeifer–Amann chirality mechanism in a spin–boson model (model-
specific); (C) Lang et al. numerical illustration for a system with nontrivial 𝑆3
permutation symmetry, D+
3. §10.7.4: the tower’s conjectural formal resolution.
10.7.1. The Woolley–Primas problem as a tower statement
Woolley [174] observed that the eigenstates of the full Coulomb Hamiltonian ˆ𝐻Coul for
an assembly of electrons and nuclei transform as irreducible representations of the full
symmetry group (spatial rotations, translations, and nuclear permutations); in isolation
they carry no definite nuclear geometry, bond angles, or molecular structure. Primas [232]
elevated the observation into a critique of chemical reductionism: molecular structure, he
argued, is not derivable from quantum mechanics but is a classical concept imposed from
outside. Sutcliffe and Woolley [231] reiterated that the Born–Oppenheimer approximation
itself presupposes an empirically chosen molecular frame not determined by the theory.
The issue remains active: recent work in Foundations of Chemistry by Scerri [267], a
comment by Woolley [268], and a pedagogical discussion by Agostini and Curchod [269]
returns the Born–Oppenheimer / molecular-structure debate to the foreground without
323


## Page 324


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
consensus ([231] remains the standard position and no rigorous resolution has appeared in
the nearly five decades since Woolley’s 1978 paper).
In the tower, Woolley’s observation is exact. The molecular graph 𝐺∈LGraph𝑃is given
data at every level L4–L6: the DPO rules of L4, the permutation-inversion group 𝐺∗of
L4.5, the configuration orbifold 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) of L5, the Hilbert bundle and Berry connection of
L6 — all presuppose that 𝐺has been fixed. In the corrected L7 language, the missing
datum is the nuclear exchange-statistical representation structure: it is invisible to the
scalar/electronic L6 description, which works over the sector-reduced configuration space
and does not yet retain the full labelled spin-statistical representation structure carried by
the 𝐺∗-action on 𝑄reg
lab(𝐺) and on the nuclear-spin Hilbert factor.
The tower resolves the problem not by philosophical argument but by identifying the precise
level and mechanism at which 𝐺must emerge. The level is L7: the quantum algebra
𝐴𝐺
𝜀carries the 𝐺∗-action from L4.5, and the labelled spin-spatial Hilbert space H𝐺

lab(𝐺)) ⊗S𝐺decomposes under this action into 𝐺∗-isotypic Hilbert components

components. The compact ideal K(H𝐺
lab) itself is simple as a 𝐶∗-algebra and does not, in
isolation, decompose into molecular-species sectors. The mechanism for sector stability has
three regimes — exact (spin-statistical invariance under 𝐺∗for identical-particle sectors),
kinematic (𝜀→0 Agmon suppression between metastable wells), and environmental
(Pfeifer–Amann-type bath-induced selection in the chiral/metastable case) — developed
in §10.7.2. For a fixed graph 𝐺, the 𝐺∗-representation theory organises the allowed
nuclear-spin/permutation sectors 𝜋∈c
𝐺∗(a given graph generally carries several, e.g. ortho
and para of H2). The broader C4 problem is to relate this sector structure, together with
localised spectral data — in the sense of the Georgescu 𝐶∗-algebraic compactification
of §10.4.3, which encodes asymptotic dissociation channels and the geometry of nuclear
localisation at spatial infinity — to graph-like molecular identity at L4; this is the content
of Conjecture 10.42.
Chemistry. The practical stakes of Woolley–Primas are concrete. Three familiar empirical
phenomena anchor the C4 question, and the tower assigns each to a different mechanism of
Conjecture 10.42:
• Ortho/para H2. Routinely observed spectroscopically, computed quantum-mechanically,
and stable over laboratory timescales without environmental intervention. This is
the cleanest empirical anchor: an exact identical-particle sector decomposition that
holds at every 𝜀from spin statistics alone (the (a1) regime).
• Chirality of pharmaceuticals. The two enantiomers of a chiral drug have identical
Coulomb Hamiltonians and identical eigenstates, yet pharmacology treats them as
distinct species over chemically relevant timescales. Thalidomide is the canonical
cautionary example — complicated by in-vivo racemisation, so it is not a clean
exact-superselection case but rather a long-lived metastable sector, captured by the
(a2) regime supplemented by environmental selection of Pfeifer–Amann type (the
(b) regime) in the chiral spin–boson model.
• Isotopic labelling through metabolism. Nuclear isotope identity is conserved through
ordinary chemical reactions, allowing tracer experiments to track molecular identity
through long synthetic and metabolic chains. This is a chemically robust phenomenon
but a separate mechanism from 𝐺∗-representation superselection: it relies on the

Without Construction C4, these phenomena are facts of chemistry imposed on a quantum

rather than collapsed.
10.7.2. Amann’s mechanism in the tower
Pfeifer [260] established a model-specific mechanism for the superselection picture in the
chiral case: a two-level system modelling the enantiomeric inversion of a chiral molecule,
coupled to a bosonic bath with ohmic spectral density, becomes effectively localised in
one chiral state in the 𝑊∗-algebraic limit of infinitely many bath modes; the framework
was developed by Amann [175, 263]. The result is model-specific (a spin–boson model of
chirality in a specifically constructed environment), not a general theorem, but its structure
makes the mechanism by which molecular identity can become effectively localised explicit.
Placed in the tower, it separates cleanly into distinct stabilisation claims.
Step 1: the isolated quantum system has no preferred sector. The molecular Hamiltonian
