Pfeifer and Amann’s specific spin–boson chirality model demonstrates this in detail: for E
a bosonic bath with ohmic spectral density, the 𝑊∗-limit of infinitely many bath modes
suppresses coherence between the two chiral states and produces an effectively localised
metastable sector — not by thermodynamic preference (the wells have equal free energy
when 𝐺∗is exact) but by environment-induced selection in the infinite-bath limit. The
selected sector is determined by the state in which the molecule was prepared, not by any
energetic criterion. This supplies a model for environmental sector selection, not a general
theorem for arbitrary 𝐺∗; the corresponding general claim is the dynamical content of
Conjecture 10.42(b).
Remark 10.47 (Two distinct stabilisation mechanisms). The mechanisms above involve
different limits and address different questions. The exact identical-particle case ((a1) of
Conjecture 10.42) requires no limit and no environment: spin statistics fixes the sectors at
every 𝜀. The metastable kinematic case (semiclassical Agmon limit 𝜀→0) suppresses
coherent tunnelling between wells but says nothing about which well the molecule was
prepared in. Amann’s environmental limit uses an infinite bath / thermodynamic limit
of environmental degrees of freedom; it breaks symmetry and selects a sector but says
nothing about kinematic barriers. Real molecules benefit from whichever mechanism
applies. For H2 with identical-proton exchange group 𝑆2  Z/2, stability is exact from
spin statistics: ortho and para isotypes are rigorously disjoint at every 𝜀, and neither an
𝜀-limit nor an environment is needed. For chirality, kinematic Agmon stabilisation is weak
(the racemisation Agmon distance through a planar transition state is only moderately
large), and environmental stabilisation of the Pfeifer–Amann type provides an additional
model-specific mechanism that makes optical activity practically permanent.

proof of the full sector-stability conjecture (Conjecture 10.42(a)).

10.7.4. The tower’s formal resolution
Assembling the pieces: the tower does not postulate molecular identity at L4 and rediscover
it at L7; it conjectures that the identity be recoverable at L7 from the 𝐺∗-representation
structure of the labelled spin-spatial Hilbert space H𝐺
lab, together with the invariant
observable algebra and additional localised spectral data, and outlines the mechanisms by
which the recovery is expected to proceed: exact spin-statistical invariance for identical-
particle sectors, kinematic Agmon suppression for metastable barrier-protected sectors,
and Amann-type environmental selection for the chiral/metastable case.

The Woolley–Primas problem, in this framing, is not a philosophical puzzle but
the concrete mathematical question of whether Construction C4 can be completed:

constructions of §10.6 describe what remains.

Remark 10.49 (On exhaustiveness). Types (T1)–(T6) account for all eight transitions of
the present tower. The natural extensions discussed in §10.8.4 below fit the taxonomy as
follows: relativistic corrections reinstantiate (T6) with a different base operator; nuclear
structure coupling likely (T1) or (T5); QED adds quantised radiation degrees of freedom
that do not match any of (T1)–(T6) and would constitute a new extension type. The
taxonomy is useful but descriptive: no theorem of the form “every categorical extension of
chemistry must be of one of these six types” is claimed, and none is proved.

The tower L0–L7 is the canonical categorical framework for a specific regime of molecular
chemistry. The boundary is a precise domain specification.
Within scope: non-relativistic, spin-unresolved, closed-system molecular quantum
chemistry.

• Relativistic effects (spin-orbit coupling, mass-velocity, Darwin term): significant for

𝜀with the Dirac or Pauli–Breit operator. Categorically a re-instantiation

• QED corrections (Lamb shift, anomalous magnetic moment, vacuum polarisation):
relevant at parts-per-billion in precision atomic spectroscopy; negligible for chemistry.
Extension: quantised radiation field adds degrees of freedom outside the present
categorical framework; a new extension type.
• Nuclear structure (finite size, magnetic and quadrupole moments): relevant for
hyperfine splittings and muonic atoms. Extension: a parallel nuclear-structure tower
coupled to the molecular tower at L7.

What the L7 chapter contributes
Three contributions distinguish the tower at L7.
Forcing-pair discipline. Table 4 records a concrete reaction pair justifying each
transition L𝑘−1 →L𝑘; the tower is built from the bottom upward by this discipline
rather than designed from the top downward. To our knowledge, no prior categorical
treatment of chemistry (Baez–Fong, Baez–Pollard, Coecke) proceeds by forcing pairs;

Open problems precisely formulated. The four conjectures of §10.6 give a precise
categorical formulation of what is needed to make the Born–Oppenheimer approxima-
tion, the topology of conical intersections, and the emergence of molecular identity
into rigorous theorems about a single categorical object L7(𝑃). The mathematical
tools exist in pieces (PST, Landsman, Georgescu, Renault, Amann); their assembly
into the constructions C1–C4 is the research programme.
The tower does not claim that quantum chemistry is solved at L7. It claims that a
precise mathematical object to carry quantum chemistry has been defined, its content
layers identified, and the constructions that would produce specific instances stated
precisely enough to be either completed or refuted.

§11. The Para Enrichment: Machine Learning Models and Categorical
Completeness
The exact tower L0(𝑃) ↩→· · · ↩→L7(𝑃) built in Chapters 2–10 is the structural
decomposition of chemistry developed in this monograph: species and stoichiometry at
L0, enthalpy additivity at L1, the dagger and detailed balance at L2, the chemical master
equation at L3, bond topology at L4, stereochemistry at L4.5, the Born–Oppenheimer
potential at L5, electronic structure at L6, and nuclear quantisation at L7. Each morphism
in the tower is an exact law. Each extension was forced by a reaction pair the level below
could not distinguish. Nothing in that construction was statistical; nothing was learned
from data.
This chapter turns the tower outward. The models used to compute chemistry in practice
today — MACE [271], NequIP [272], So3krates [273], SO3LR [192], QIM [34], and the
rest of the published molecular machine learning catalogue — are neural networks, trained
force fields, parametric surrogates. The question this chapter asks is what the tower, as a
completed structural object, tells us about these models: what their architectures already
commit to, what they can and cannot represent, which tower-coherence conditions they
silently respect or silently violate.
A direct answer is blocked by a categorical kind mismatch. A tower morphism at level 𝑘is
an exact map: one specific, deterministic morphism of L𝑘(𝑃), delivered once and for all
by the tower construction of Chapters 2–10. A MACE force field is a parametric family
{ 𝑓𝜃}𝜃∈Θ, one map per point in a weight space Θ that the training procedure selects from.
The two sit in different kinds of category: tower morphisms in hom-sets C(𝑋,𝑌), MACE
in something like Ý
Θ C(Θ ⊗𝑋,𝑌). Asking “which tower level does MACE occupy?” is a
category error in the literal sense; the tower and the MACE model are different kinds of
mathematical object and share no hom-set. To use the tower as a diagnostic for the ML
literature, we need a categorical setting in which parametric families and exact morphisms
both live, with the exact tower appearing as a distinguished sub-structure of the richer
whole.
The construction that does this is the Para 2-category of Gavranović et al. [33]. For
a symmetric monoidal category (C, ⊗, 𝐼), the 2-category Para(C) has the same objects
as C, but its 1-morphisms 𝑋→𝑌are pairs (Θ, 𝑓𝜃) with Θ ∈C a parameter space and
𝑓𝜃: Θ ⊗𝑋→𝑌a morphism of C. 2-morphisms are reparametrisations 𝑟: Θ′ →Θ,
encoding weight tying, fine-tuning, and transfer learning. Applied at each tower level, Para
produces a perpendicular enrichment LPara
𝑘
(𝑃): a 2-category of parametric morphisms
standing above the exact morphisms of L𝑘(𝑃), with a vertical embedding 𝛾𝑘placing each
exact law as its trivial-parameter (Θ = 𝐼) version. There is no canonical reverse functor
collapsing a parametric morphism back to a single exact one. Such a reverse would need
to canonically select a weight 𝑟: 𝐼→Θ for each (Θ, 𝑓𝜃), but the comonoid structure on
Θ provides no such section: the counit !Θ : Θ →𝐼goes the wrong way — it discards the
parameter object rather than naming a point in it — and no canonical 𝐼→Θ accompanies it.
If such a canonical section did exist it would name the trained model from the architecture
alone, making training unnecessary. The tower therefore appears in this enriched setting as
the trivial-parameter slice of a richer categorical object populated by the architectures that
are actually trained; the structural question an architecture poses to the tower is the one

categorical completeness below formalises — whether the set of morphisms its weight
space can realise lies in L𝑘(𝑃), and how much of L𝑘(𝑃) it covers.
Once the tower and the parametric literature share a categorical home, three structural
questions about any published ML architecture become precisely answerable, and none of
them is answerable by benchmark comparison alone.
Is the architecture’s equivariance a design choice or a theorem? Each level L𝑘carries a
canonical symmetry group 𝐺𝑘— species permutations at L0–L3, graph automorphisms
at L4, the permutation-inversion group at L4.5, rigid motions composed with graph
automorphisms 𝑆𝐸(3) ⋉Aut(𝐺) at L5, gauge transformations on the electronic bundle
at L6, particle exchange at L7. Membership in LPara
𝑘
(𝑃) is defined by requiring strict
𝐺𝑘-equivariance of the underlying map at every parameter setting. MACE’s Clebsch–
Gordan tensor contractions enforce the L5 symmetry 𝑆𝐸(3) ⋉Aut(𝐺) for all 𝜃, not just
the trained one; membership at LPara
5
is therefore a theorem about the MACE architecture,
not a fortunate property of training. An architecture whose symmetry is merely learned
through data augmentation fails the membership condition and is not, in structural terms, a
parametric morphism at that level.
What can the architecture represent, independent of its training data? An architecture
(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) is categorically complete at level 𝑘on a morphism 𝜑of L𝑘(𝑃) if some parameter
setting 𝑟: 𝐼→Θ instantiates 𝑓𝜃to 𝜑exactly — equivalently, if 𝜑lies in the architecture’s
function class 𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) ⊆L𝑘(𝑃)(𝑋,𝑌), the set of instantiations as 𝑟ranges over
C(𝐼, Θ) (Remark 11.4). Completeness is a property of the function class, not of the loss or
the training set. An architecture incomplete at level 𝑘will fail on every task requiring a
target morphism 𝜑absent from 𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, 𝑓𝜃), regardless of training-set size, because no
choice of weights realises 𝜑.
Which tower-coherence conditions does the architecture enforce? The tower’s forgetful
functors 𝑈𝑘: L𝑘(𝑃) →L𝑘−1(𝑃) connect adjacent levels; a model claiming content at
multiple levels must respect the relations𝑈𝑘imposes on joint content. Three such conditions
are unenforced across the published literature. The Eyring TST condition couples a learned
rate law to the activation barrier of the same model’s potential energy surface (L3 ↔L5).
The categorical Wegscheider condition couples forward and reverse rate constants through
the thermodynamic Δ𝐺◦(L2 ↔L3). The topological output-type condition demands a
Hilbert-bundle-valued output rather than a scalar energy to carry the Berry-phase invariant
[𝛾𝐵] ∈𝐻1(𝐶𝑒(𝐺) \ X01, Z2) near conical intersections (L5 →L6). The first two are
literature-wide architectural absences that new designs could close; the third is a theorem
about output type — no reparametrisation of a scalar-energy architecture yields a Berry
connection, regardless of training, body order, or receptive field.
These three questions are the analytical spine of the chapter. They organise what the
tower, read through the Para enrichment, reveals about ML molecular modelling: a precise
structural classification of every major architecture, a completeness diagnostic that is
architectural rather than empirical, and a catalogue of tower-coherence conditions the
current literature does not enforce.

The Para 2-category is a formal device that treats an entire parametric family { 𝑓𝜃: 𝑋→
𝑌}𝜃∈Θ as a single 1-morphism (Θ, 𝑓𝜃), distinct from any particular trained instance. This
is what lets us speak about what functions an architecture can represent across its whole
weight space, independently of any one training run.
Definition 11.1 (Para(C) [33]). The Para 2-category Para(C) has:
• Objects: the objects of C.
• 1-morphisms 𝑋→𝑌: pairs (Θ, 𝑓𝜃) with Θ an object of C (the parameter space)
and 𝑓𝜃: Θ ⊗𝑋→𝑌a morphism of C.
• 2-morphisms (Θ, 𝑓𝜃) ⇒(Θ′, 𝑓𝜃′): morphisms 𝑟: Θ′ →Θ in C (reparametrisations)
satisfying 𝑓𝜃◦(𝑟⊗id𝑋) = 𝑓𝜃′.
• Composition of (Θ, 𝑓𝜃) : 𝑋→𝑌and (𝑄, 𝑔𝜙) : 𝑌→𝑍:
(𝑄, 𝑔𝜙) ◦(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) := ␀𝑄⊗Θ, 𝑔𝜙◦(id𝑄⊗𝑓𝜃) ◦𝛼𝑄,Θ,𝑋
,
where the associator 𝛼𝑄,Θ,𝑋re-brackets (𝑄⊗Θ) ⊗𝑋as 𝑄⊗(Θ ⊗𝑋) so that id𝑄⊗𝑓𝜃
applies.
• Identity on 𝑋: (𝐼, 𝜆𝑋).
In the strict monoidal case (𝛼, 𝜆, 𝜌all identities), composition reduces to 𝑔𝜙◦(id𝑄⊗𝑓𝜃)
and the identity on 𝑋to (𝐼, id𝑋).

Why a comonoid on Θ, and why this particular one. The operations a parameter space
admits — duplicate a weight (for sharing across layers) and discard a weight (formally
forgetting the parameter object) — are exactly those of a comonoid in a symmetric monoidal
category. This is not a structure newly imported from [33] for the present chapter: Chapter 5
already uses the same (Δ, !) data, there as the copy–delete morphisms on every object of a
Markov category, where Δ copies a random sample and ! discards one. Here the formal
content is identical and the interpretation shifts: Δ routes a single weight into two layers
(rather than copying a sample to two outputs); ! records the parameter object as formally
discardable (the categorical counterpart of the discardable sample, not a weight-zeroing or
weight-ablation operation). We record (C𝑘) explicitly because weight-sharing discipline is
architectural data: two networks with the same underlying map 𝑓𝜃but different comonoid
structures on Θ are different architectures, and LPara
𝑘
(𝑃) must distinguish them.

Membership in LPara

The targets of applied interest are those produced by the exact tower constructions of earlier

intersection. In each case 𝜑is a specific morphism of the corresponding L𝑘(𝑃), identifiable
in the chapter where the tower construction was defined.

It is complete on a class S ⊆L𝑘(𝑃)(𝑋,𝑌) if complete on every 𝜑∈S, and complete at
level 𝑘if complete on every morphism of L𝑘(𝑃)(𝑋,𝑌).
Completeness is a property of the architecture — its parameter space, its forward map, its
closure under choice of weights — and is logically independent of any training procedure.
No training recovers a target absent from the function class.
ML molecular architectures are typically complete on physically meaningful subclasses. At
L5, for instance, MACE/NequIP completeness on a dense subclass of smooth BO potentials
is framed conditionally on universal-approximation hypotheses in Section 11.4. They
are not complete on all of L5(𝑃)(𝑋,𝑌), and at L6 they are incomplete in a structurally
topological way. Section 11.7 identifies three specific 𝜑— one at L6 structurally outside
the function class of every scalar-energy architecture, and two at L2/L3 outside the function
classes of the published kinetic and joint kinetic-energetic architectures — that are the
tower-coherence gaps the rest of the chapter analyses.
Completeness is architectural, not empirical

lies outside 𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) for every 𝑆𝐸(3)-equivariant scalar-energy force field. The

§11.2. External categorical frameworks in tower language
The Para enrichment LPara
𝑘
(𝑃) of Section 11.1 unifies, into a single nested hierarchy,
characterisations of the membership condition (E𝑘) of Definition 11.2 that were developed
independently — before this monograph’s tower — one level at a time. In detail: (E0) is
Meseguer–Montanari’s free-strict-SMC morphism condition [32]; (E3)’s Markov-kernel
core is, on the stochastic-kinetics side, Fritz’s Markov-category morphism condition [275]
(positivity, probability conservation), with species-permutation equivariance the additional
tower-specific component; and, on the composable-networks side, Baez and Pollard’s
gray-box functor condition on open reaction networks [31]; (E4) is de Haan, Cohen, and
Welling’s Natural Graph Networks naturality on molecular graphs [274] and Bonchi et al.’s
DPO-compatible string-diagram rewriting of mechanistic graphs [276]; (E5) is Clebsch–
Gordan-augmented NGN, as realised in NequIP [272], MACE [271], and So3krates [273].
Each of these four external frameworks characterises one tower level on its own terms
and goes no further. The Cruttwell–Gavranović framework of categorical gradient-based
learning [277], treated separately below, runs perpendicular to this enumeration: it does
not pair with a single tower level but supplies the 2-categorical backdrop for gradient-based
training of any LPara
𝑘
(𝑃) architecture (Section 11.2.3). What the tower adds, via the
forgetful functors 𝑈𝑘: L𝑘(𝑃) →L𝑘−1(𝑃) of Section 11.1, is nesting: the hierarchy
L0(𝑃) ←L1(𝑃) ←· · · ←L7(𝑃) makes each (E𝑘) strictly refine (E𝑘−1), so a model at
level 𝑘inherits every lower-level condition and can fail higher-level ones in locatable ways
— by naming the specific forgetful functor above which it falls.
For each of the four level-pairing frameworks, this section records three things: (a) the
tower level 𝑘at which (E𝑘) identifies with the framework; (b) a direct verification of the
identification against the hom-set characterisation L𝑘(𝑃)(𝑋,𝑌) ⊆C(𝑋,𝑌) of Section 11.1;
and (c) the forgetful functor above which the framework’s categorical vocabulary runs out.
The CGGWZ subsection follows a different template, since the framework has no (E𝑘)
to identify and no 𝑈𝑘above which its vocabulary runs out — both of these facts being
consequences of its perpendicularity. The resulting pairings feed every subsequent section

11.2.1. De Haan–Cohen–Welling at LPara
4
: graph naturality
Chemically: membership in LPara
4
asks a force field to produce the same output for any pair
of molecular graphs related by atom relabelling (same graph, same prediction regardless of
how atoms are numbered); membership in LPara
5
additionally asks the output to transform
correctly under physical rotations and translations of the geometry. The first condition is
Natural Graph Networks naturality (this subsection); the second is NGN augmented by
Clebsch–Gordan tensor products, realised by NequIP, MACE, and So3krates.
The Natural Graph Networks (NGN) framework of de Haan, Cohen, and Welling [274]
gives the categorical language for message-passing neural networks on graphs. Its central
objects are graph feature spaces: functors 𝜌: Graph →Vec from a groupoid of graphs
(with graph isomorphisms as morphisms) to vector spaces. A natural graph network layer
between two such feature spaces is a natural transformation 𝐾: 𝜌⇒𝜌′, a family of maps
𝐾𝐺: 𝜌(𝐺) →𝜌′(𝐺) commuting with every graph isomorphism. Naturality is exactly
equivariance under graph-level symmetries — that is, under Aut(𝐺).
Proposition 11.6 (NGN naturality is (𝐸4)). At tower level 𝑘= 4, where 𝐺4 = Aut(𝐺) acts
on the labelled-graph category LGraph𝑃of Chapter 6:
(i) Graph feature spaces 𝜌: Graph →Vec restricted to the objects of LGraph𝑃are
exactly the Aut(𝐺)-equivariant feature maps at L4(𝑃).
(ii) The NGN naturality condition of [274] is the membership condition (32) at 𝑘= 4:
𝑓𝜃(𝜎· 𝐺) = 𝐷(𝜎) 𝑓𝜃(𝐺)
for all 𝜎∈Aut(𝐺),
where 𝐷is the representation of Aut(𝐺) on the output feature channels.
(iii) Local-to-global: an architecture satisfying naturality at every message-passing edge
satisfies it globally on the molecular graph [274].

Part II of Bonchi, Gadducci,
Kissinger, Sobociński, and Zanasi’s String Diagram Rewrite Theory [276] establishes that
DPO rewriting of hypergraphs modulo symmetric monoidal category equations corresponds
to string-diagram rewriting in a free SMC. This is the categorical foundation on which
the tower’s L4(𝑃) is built (Chapter 6): the six DPO generators of Definition 6.18 —
heterolytic and homolytic cleavage, electron-pair migration, and their reverses — are the
string-diagram generators of the free SMC that controls bond rearrangements, and DPO
rewriting in the labelled-graph category LGraph𝑃is the operational semantics for their
composition.

similar sequence-to-sequence models implicitly approximate morphisms in this string-

captures 𝐻el(R) completely but freezes the 𝑈(𝑁) fibre gauge by fixing a basis, while
section-level captures a single gauge-covariant state 𝜎but not the full operator.

Stoichiometric-support encoders.
DrFP’s map 𝑟↦→fp(𝑟) composes SMILES tokenisa-
tion, Morgan-substructure extraction, symmetric set difference 𝑅△𝑃, and hashed bit-folding
to a vector in {0, 1}𝑑. Two distinct tower objects fail to lift through this pipeline. The free
commutative monoid N[S] is lost first: hashing maps distinct substructures to the same
bit, bit-folding projects to {0, 1} and erases counts, so 𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, fp) lands in a multiplicity-
forgetting quotient of N[S] strictly below the free-commutative-monoid structure L0(𝑃)
requires. The Hess functor 𝐹𝐻: L1(𝑃) →𝐵R fails consequently: fp(𝑟1 ◦𝑟2) bears no
R-additive relation to fp(𝑟1) ⊕fp(𝑟2), so (E1) cannot even be stated in the codomain fp
lives in. The identity fp(𝑟) = fp(𝑟†) produced by the symmetric difference is not evidence
of L2-membership: it trivialises the dagger by collapsing forward and reverse reactions to
the identity in the codomain, before (·)† has any oriented reaction morphism left to act on.
The ceiling is accordingly the first lossy step in the pipeline: N[S] is unrecoverable, and
every higher structure depending on it — 𝐹𝐻, ker(𝐹𝑇
𝐺), FP, the DPO span — is unreachable
as a matter of type, not training.

ChemNODE parametrises a vector field 𝑑Φ/𝑑𝑡= 𝑓𝜃(Φ) on a
fixed thermochemical state space R𝑁𝑠+1. No Sym(S)-action is defined on the index set —
species indices are distinguishable MLP channels — no positivity constraint is imposed on
the RHS, and no guarantee is made that mass or element conservation survives integration.
𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) therefore does not land in Stoch (probability is not conserved), nor in the
mass-action subcategory of L0(𝑃), nor even in the Sym(S)-equivariant part of L0(𝑃).

the base architecture. ChemNODE sits strictly below LPara

Reaction SMILES sequence models.
Molecular Transformer maps token sequences in
Σ∗to token sequences in Σ∗by autoregressive decoding. No graph object appears in its type
signature: the token stream need not parse to a molecular graph at all, and when it does,
the mapping from strings to objects of LGraph𝑃is partial and learned. Atom and charge
conservation, bond validity, and Aut(𝐺)-equivariance are all training-emergent rather than
architectural, with documented failures even on in-distribution benchmarks. The image
of 𝐹𝑢𝑛𝑐(Θ, 𝑓𝜃) does not lie in the DPO-span category forced by the L3 →L4 pair, so
there is no pushout complement on which to claim L4 membership; there is not even a
Sym(S)-action on the input side, since distinct SMILES orderings of the same reactant
multiset are distinct input sequences. The architectural ceiling is N[S] itself: conservation
of species multiplicities is not enforced by construction, and Molecular Transformer sits
strictly below LPara
0
(𝑃).
The LPara
5
(invariant) block.
All nine architectures in this block target a scalar potential
𝑉: 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) →R with forces recovered by autodifferentiation on the conservative head.

pairwise-distance-dependent filters. DimeNet enriches the message with 3-body angles;
GemNet extends to 4-body dihedrals with a universal-approximation guarantee for 𝑆𝐸(3)-
invariant continuous functions on 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) at the conservative head. In all these cases
the outputs are scalar: internal rotationally covariant features are discharged through
an invariant readout. ALIGNN takes the line-graph perspective to expose bond–bond
angles, again at invariant output. PaiNN is the sole borderline case: its 𝑙=0 and 𝑙=1

polarizabilities) exit OrbMorse — but they land in rank-≤2 tensor bundles over 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) that
are topologically trivial (no eigenvalue-crossing locus seeds a non-trivial Chern class), so
nothing here advances to the topologically non-trivial Hel(𝑁) →𝐶𝑒(𝐺) that L6 demands.

5
(equivariant) block.
NequIP, MACE, MACE-MP-0, Allegro, So3krates,
SO3LR, Equiformer, and eSEN all satisfy (E5) as an architectural guarantee. Their
internal features carry 𝑂(3) irrep labels with 𝑙≤𝑙max, composed via e3nn Clebsch–Gordan

MACE adds body-order via the atomic cluster expansion; a separate observation, developed

is MACE trained at foundation-model scale; its codomain is unchanged. Allegro replaces
atom-centred message passing with iterated pairwise tensor products, giving a receptive
field bounded by 𝑟cut regardless of depth. So3krates uses 𝑆𝐸(3)-equivariant self-attention in

Remark 11.8 (Comonoid structure on ΘMACE; and what it does not encode). Clause (ii) of
Definition 11.2 requires the parameter space of a Para 1-morphism to carry a comonoid
structure (Θ, Δ, !) in the ambient cartesian category. For MACE this is realised by the
canonical cartesian comonoid: Δ: ΘMACE →ΘMACE ⊗ΘMACE is the diagonal (duplicating
a parameter tensor), and !: ΘMACE →𝐼is the unique map to the terminal object (forgetting
parameter dependence, not setting parameters to any particular value). The terminal map !
carries no architecturally specific content beyond the cartesian structure; the non-trivial
ingredient is Δ.
The architectural role of Δ in MACE is the use of a single learned parameter tensor in
multiple places. The clearest example is element embeddings: a learned vector ℎ𝑍is
associated with each chemical element 𝑍and fed to every atom of element 𝑍in the
molecule, realised by Δ duplicating the stored tensor into as many copies as there are atoms
of type 𝑍. Within a single message-passing layer, architectural weight sharing across
atom-centred features is likewise implemented by Δ.
This comonoid structure is distinct from the separate expressiveness claim — the question
of which target morphisms the ACE body-order expansion can approximate, as the ACE
order and angular-momentum cutoff grow. The comonoid governs which parameter reuses
the architecture permits; expressiveness bounds what the composed features can represent.
Conflating the two has been a recurring error in informal discussions of MACE’s tower
coordinates.

11.5.2. SO3LR: physics-informed range separation within LPara
5
(𝑃)
Pure neural-network force fields with finite cutoffs — MACE, NequIP, So3krates in its
standard form — predict a PES by learning the full interatomic interaction from data, inside
a receptive field determined by the cutoff radius or the attention kernel’s support. For
isolated small molecules this is adequate: the relevant physics lives within a few Å of each
atom, and the neural component has enough capacity to represent the resulting short-range
interactions. Condensed-phase systems are another matter. Biomolecules in solvent,
liquids, molecular crystals, and extended interfaces have substantial energy contributions
from long-range Coulomb and dispersion interactions that fall off only polynomially
(1/𝑟and 1/𝑟6 respectively) and remain non-negligible far beyond any practical cutoff.
Pure-MPNN architectures address this either by extending the cutoff (computationally
expensive and data-hungry, since the network must learn 1/𝑟from scratch) or by ignoring
the tail (accepting errors that accumulate over simulations of sufficiently large systems).
SO3LR [192] takes a structurally different approach. Its total energy decomposes as
𝐸SO3LR(R) = 𝐸ZBL(R) + 𝐸So3k(R) + 𝐸Elec({𝑞𝑖}, R) + 𝐸Disp({𝛼𝑖}, R),
where 𝐸ZBL is the analytic Ziegler–Biersack–Littmark short-range repulsion, 𝐸So3k is the
semilocal neural energy of the So3krates backbone, 𝐸Elec = Í
𝑖<𝑗𝑞𝑖𝑞𝑗/𝑟𝑖𝑗is a pairwise
Coulomb term evaluated with learned atomic partial charges 𝑞𝑖(R), and 𝐸Disp is a pairwise
van der Waals dispersion term with learned atomic polarizabilities 𝛼𝑖(R). The short-range
neural component carries the many-body correlations that the network learns efficiently;
the analytic long-range components carry the physics whose functional form is known in
advance and whose pairwise additivity the architecture imposes as a structural constraint.

range separation: the functional form of the long-range tails is known analytically (Coulomb

the neural backbone to learn them. The structural gain is independence from training
coverage on the long-range axis. A pure neural model can be made more accurate on
distribution-covered configurations but retains no architectural guarantee about physics
beyond its cutoff; SO3LR has the correct 1/𝑟and 1/𝑟6 behaviour built in, so the long-range

from So3krates’s global attention, but it is a design axis within LPara

What the long-range sector buys SO3LR
For molecules in vacuum at a scale where long-range physics is negligible, SO3LR
and a pure neural force field like So3krates or MACE are structurally interchangeable:
the short-range neural component dominates the total energy and the analytic tail is
numerically small. The distinction emerges in condensed-phase systems. Consider two
subsystems 𝑆1, 𝑆2 at separation 𝑟≫𝑟cut. A pure MPNN with a 5 Å cutoff computes
𝐸(𝑆1 ∪𝑆2) = 𝐸(𝑆1) + 𝐸(𝑆2), missing the Coulomb contribution (∼1/𝑟) and the
dispersion contribution (∼1/𝑟6) between them entirely. SO3LR’s range-separated
architecture returns, at that separation, 𝐸(𝑆1)+𝐸(𝑆2)+𝐸Elec(𝑆1, 𝑆2)+𝐸Disp(𝑆1, 𝑆2) —
the physically correct long-range terms, supplied analytically with parameters (𝑞𝑖, 𝛼𝑖)
the neural backbone has learned.
The structural gain is that the functional form of the long-range terms does not depend
on training coverage. A pure neural model can be made more accurate on distribution-
covered configurations but retains no architectural guarantee about physics beyond its
cutoff; SO3LR has the Coulomb and dispersion tails built in, so their form is correct
even for atomic configurations the training set never saw. This is the practical face of
the physics-informed range separation discussed in Observation 11.13: the long-range
functional form is a structural architectural commitment, not an empirical fit, and is
independent of training coverage.
Two axes of architectural design at a single tower level
So3krates and SO3LR together illustrate that tower-level membership is a single
coordinate among several architectural ones.
Both are objects of LPara
5
(𝑃) and
both are categorically blocked from LPara
6
(𝑃) by the output-type obstruction of
Proposition 11.19. Within LPara
5
(𝑃) they differ along two independent axes.
The first axis is the architectural strategy for realising (E5). MACE contracts through
local Clebsch–Gordan tensor products; So3krates couples through 𝑆𝐸(3)-equivariant
attention on an SPHC basis. Both produce parametric 1-morphisms of LPara
5
(𝑃), and
the tower does not distinguish them at level 5. This is the lesson of Remark 11.12:
extending receptive field, swapping CG for attention, or adding more layers changes
the specific 1-morphism at LPara
5
(𝑃) but travels zero distance along the L5 →L6
direction of the tower.
The second axis is whether the architecture incorporates physics-informed structural
baselines. Pure-MPNN architectures (MACE, So3krates) ask the neural backbone to
learn the full interatomic interaction within its receptive field; their function classes
contain whatever the network can express, subject only to the 𝐸(3)-equivariance and

§11.7. Three incompleteness results
The classification in Section 11.3 identifies three architectural gaps separating current
Para-morphism practice from a hypothetical model that fully inhabits the tower. The three
results differ in both character and severity, and they are presented in order of increasing
severity — with the numbering reversed, so that Gap 1 names the deepest result and is
presented last:
• Gap 3 (structural, presented first): no architecture jointly enforces Eyring TST
coherence between LPara
3
rate-law output and LPara
5
PES output.
• Gap 2 (thermodynamic, presented second): no neural kinetic model with indepen-
dently parameterised forward and reverse rate constants enforces the Wegscheider
consistency condition.
• Gap 1 (topological, presented last): architectures with output type OrbMorse are
categorically blocked from LPara
6
(𝑃).
Gaps 3 and 2 are contingent on the state of the published literature: each records that no
current architecture enforces a given tower-coherence condition, but such an architecture

not been applied to this problem.
Why the gap matters for reactive simulations
Reactive molecular dynamics with an MLFF simulates trajectories on 𝑉0(R) and
reads off an effective rate constant from the observed crossing frequency. Nothing
guarantees that this emergent rate satisfies the Eyring equation relative to the model’s
own barrier, because the model’s energy function was not trained to produce barrier
heights consistent with any experimental rate. In a functorially coherent architecture,
the L3 rate would be derived from the L5 barrier via condition (TST), with the rate
and PES components sharing a single parameter space as the Para-enriched level
LPara
𝑘

architectural loss relating their outputs. No such architecture currently exists in the
published literature.

invariant under reparametrisation, and OrbMorse and HilbBund are distinct.
By construction, every 1-morphism of LPara
6
(𝑃) has output type HilbBund: at each
R ∈𝐶𝑒(𝐺), a full electronic-structure fibre — an orthonormal basis of 𝑁states, eigenvalues

the lowest eigenvalue and its gradient, discarding excited-state energies, off-diagonal
connection coefficients, and topological class — none of which appears in the OrbMorse
output of (Θ, 𝑓𝜃).
A reparametrisation 𝑟: 𝐼→Θ in Para(L5(𝑃)) specialises the architecture to a parameter

Proposition 11.19 is not a statement about training-set size, model capacity, or
distribution coverage. The Berry-phase class [𝛾𝐵] ∈𝐻1(𝐶𝑒(𝐺) \ X01, Z2) assigns a
Z2-value to each homology class of loops encircling X01; the analogous 𝑐1 ∈𝐻2(−, Z)
in the spin–orbit-coupled case is similarly a cohomology class. These are not pointwise
functions on 𝐶𝑒(𝐺) at all — they are global topological invariants of the eigenbundle.

§11.8. Synthesis: the tower as design specification
This chapter has done three things. It has located each major ML molecular architecture
as a parametric morphism in some LPara
𝑘

boundary) and two literature-survey observations (the Eyring TST coherence gap between

the Para enrichment provides a verifiable structural criterion for the question “what can
this model represent?”, replacing benchmark intuition with a statement about the model’s
function class.

Classical ML benchmarks measure
accuracy on held-out data at a fixed trained parameter setting. Definition 11.5 provides

conical-intersection dynamics — not because it was trained on too little data, but because
the relevant structure is not representable within the function class at all. The diagnostic
therefore distinguishes failure modes that more data can fix from those it cannot.
11.8.2. Three research targets forced by the tower
The tower is not only a classification of what exists.
Turned around, it is a design
specification: each level specifies, via its membership condition and forgetful functor
structure, what a model must do architecturally to represent the chemistry at that level
faithfully. The three gaps identified in Section 11.7 define three concrete research targets —
not aspirational goals, but consequences forced by the tower’s structure, in the same sense
that each tower level was forced bottom-up by reaction pairs the previous level could not
distinguish.
Target 1: topologically complete LPara
6

§12. The lower tower in executable form: Φop on the Briggs–Rauscher
oscillator
The preceding chapters have constructed a categorical tower that stratifies chemistry by level
of structure: stoichiometry at L0, thermodynamics at L1–L2, kinetics at L3, mechanism
at L4, with L4.5 stereochemistry and higher levels above. The tower’s content is not
mere vocabulary: at every level it delivers theorems. At L3, Feinberg’s Deficiency Zero
Theorem forces weakly-reversible mass-action networks with deficiency 𝛿= 0 to admit
a unique positive stationary measure per stoichiometric class — which is precisely why
oscillating networks like the Briggs–Rauscher reaction must have 𝛿> 0. At L4, the
parameter projection 𝜋4 (§12.8) constrains exactly which mechanism data can survive
into the L3 rate constants, making the gap between mechanism-resolved and rate-resolved
descriptions explicit rather than tacit. These are not modelling choices that could have
gone differently; they are categorical consequences of the tower’s construction. If the tower
is to be more than a formal scaffold, those consequences have to survive contact with an
executable implementation evaluated against a specific chemistry.
This chapter closes the tower at the bottom by constructing a functor

than asymptotically suppressed.
The framework provides three concrete deliverables beyond confirmed predictions. First,
an explicit vocabulary (§12.9) for separating simulator-output features into three categories:
essential (the oscillation onset itself, tied to L2 stoichiometric feedback topology and L3
Jacobian sign-pattern), tunable (period and spike amplitudes, set by L3 rate constants and 𝜋4-
coarse L4 data), and scale-dependent representational artifacts (the smooth ODE quiescent
floors, whose physical referent depends on 𝑉; the ∼15% SSA-vs-ODE period drift, a 𝛾ODE
residual that vanishes as 𝑉→∞). Second, a canonical model-comparison machinery
(§12.8, Proposition 12.30) embedding every BR network variant — broCODENetwork,
broCODE5VarNetwork, bufferedH, furrowLikePoolNetwork — into a single
BorelStoch comparison space via the same 𝐹◦Φop, with TV, Wasserstein-1, and relative-
entropy metrics available. Third, an honest record of what the L3 simulator cannot
see by construction (§12.8, Remark 12.31): kinetic isotope effects on the methylene
hydrogens of malonic acid, transition-state geometry, pressure dependence, solvent and
ionic-strength dependence beyond the reference conditions absorbed into rxnRate. These
are L4-strength data dropped by 𝜋4; a successor L4-resolved implementation would have
to recover them.

§12.1. The Briggs–Rauscher reaction as a forcing ladder
12.1.1. The empirical problem
The Briggs–Rauscher (BR) reaction [146] is the clock reaction in which an acidic batch
of iodate, hydrogen peroxide, malonic acid, and a manganese(II) catalyst oscillates
visibly between colourless, amber, and dark blue before settling into equilibrium. Its net
stoichiometry,
IO−
3 + 2 H2O2 + CH2(COOH)2 + H+ −→ICH(COOH)2 + 2 O2 + 3 H2O,
(38)
contains no information about the oscillation: it is L0 data, identical to that of a hypothetical
non-oscillating reaction with the same input and output complexes.
Two parallel skeleton mechanisms were proposed in 1982 by Noyes and Furrow [147]
and independently by De Kepper and Epstein [35] in the same volume of JACS. Both
decompose the dynamics into two pathways for hypoiodous-acid production: Process A
386


## Page 387


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
(ionic, dominant at high [I−]), through sequential heterolytic O–I bond formations via
HIO2 and I2 intermediates; and Process B (radical, dominant at low [I−]), through
homolytic IO−
3 + HIO2 →2 IO•
2 with Mn(II)/Mn(III) cycling supplying single-electron
transfer. Process A consumes I−; the iodination of malonic acid by I2 regenerates it. The
system switches between A and B across a threshold in [I−], and that switching is the
mechanical content of the oscillation. The implementation in BR.Mechanism (§12.3)
follows the De Kepper–Epstein variant with two explicit reverse channels (R3-rev and
R4-rev), giving twelve reactions in total.

§12.2. Target category: Hask and BorelStoch
A categorical interpretation of the simulation must fix a category for total Haskell — the
operational layer in which the program runs — and a target category for the stochastic
content of L3 — the denotational layer in which distributions live — and a functor
sending the first to the second. The payoff is concrete: every claim about the simulator’s
accuracy will attach to a specific morphism in one of these categories and to a specific
user-controllable parameter (§12.5 onwards). This section fixes the two categories; §12.7
builds the functor.
12.2.1. Why not naive Hask
The naive category with Haskell types as objects and all Haskell functions as morphisms
fails the identity law: Bauer [315] observes that 𝑠𝑒𝑞⊥() differs from 𝑠𝑒𝑞(⊥. 𝑖𝑑) (), so id
is not a categorical identity under composition. Danielsson, Hughes, Jansson, and Gibbons
[316] prove that the total fragment of a partial language forms a bicartesian closed category
in which equational reasoning is sound. By Hask in the rest of this chapter we mean that
total fragment.
Assumption 12.1 (Totality and purity of the simulation core). Every function in the
simulation core — the L0 invariants atomConservation, chargeConservation;
the constructors mkReaction, mkNetwork; the L3 realisations BR.ODE.simulate
with stepAdaptive, and BR.SSA.simulate with step — is total and pure on
its domain. Stochasticity in BR.SSA is supplied entirely by the vendored BR.PRNG
(a state-threaded SplitMix64), so the IO monad never appears in the call graph: no
System.Random, no unsafePerformIO, no FFI, no exceptions. File I/O is confined
to BR.Output, which acts only at the simulation boundary and is not invoked by any
function below it.
Remark 12.2 (Why no Kl(𝐼𝑂)). With BR.PRNG pure and explicit, both the ODE and SSA
realisations of L3 live in Hask, not in a Kleisli category of a probability monad in the sense
of monadic semantics for computational effects [317]. Introducing Kl(𝐼𝑂), the Kleisli
category of the Haskell IO monad, would therefore add no structure here: the simulator
would use only the pure Kleisli arrows
𝐴
𝑓−→𝐵
return
−−−−→𝐼𝑂𝐵,
i.e. the wide subcategory
{return ◦𝑓: 𝑓∈Hask(𝐴, 𝐵)} ⊆Kl(𝐼𝑂)(𝐴, 𝐵).
We therefore target Hask directly.
12.2.2. Two-layer semantics: operational and denotational
The stochastic content of L3 requires a Markov category.
Definition 12.3 (Markov category; BorelStoch [312]). A Markov category is a semicarte-
sian symmetric monoidal category (C, ⊗, 𝐼) in which every object 𝑋carries a natural
commutative comonoid (copy𝑋, del𝑋) and every morphism 𝑓is counital, del𝑌◦𝑓= del𝑋.
389

Categorification of Chemical Reactions
Equivalently, it is a category in which the algebra of probability — sampling, copying,
discarding, composing — is expressible as pure morphism manipulation, without making
measure-theoretic integrals part of the primary syntax. BorelStoch is the Markov category
whose objects are standard Borel spaces (measurable spaces arising from a Polish topology,
i.e. a complete separable metric — countable sets, R𝑛, and finite products thereof) and
whose morphisms are measurable Markov kernels. It is a Borel restriction of the Kleisli
category Kl(G) of the Giry monad G [318], the probability-measure monad sending each
measurable space to its space of probability measures.
Hask is Cartesian and deterministic: any morphism in Hask between standard Borel
spaces embeds into BorelStoch as a Dirac kernel — the degenerate Markov kernel placing
all mass on a single point, i.e. the embedding of a deterministic function as a distribution
concentrated at 𝑓(𝑎). All Haskell types appearing in this chapter (Word64, Double,
Map Species Int, lists thereof) are countable or Polish, so this restriction is automatic.
Two categories are necessary because the stochastic content lives in BorelStoch (where
one states theorems and accuracy bounds), but the simulator runs in Hask (where one
debugs, profiles, and extends). The functor 𝐹below keeps the two pictures in sync: the
seed-marginal of any executable Haskell program is the Markov kernel it samples from.

12.2.3. One genuine laxity: 𝛾
In an IO-based formulation of this story (a System.Random-style codebase), Φop would

of the three collapse for BR. In pure Hask, Cartesian product is strictly associative and
commutative on the nose, so the parallel composition of two seed-parameterised morphisms
is invariant under sequencing: 𝛽is strict, not lax. The unit cell 𝛼becomes the parameter-
tensor unit isomorphism of the Para bicategory Para(Hask), treated as canonical coherence
data (§12.6) rather than as a laxity of Φop. The only cell that remains is 𝛾:

PRNG- and floating-point-level numerical artifacts (no separate user knob); ODE’s

ODE branch (state-space metric). The implicit-midpoint integrator in BR.ODE

The two branches differ in both the form of 𝛾(effectively zero in distribution on SSA,
deterministic step-size error on ODE) and the metric in which it is measured (TV on
SSA, state-space on ODE). The asymmetry is structural: SSA’s exactness modulo
numerical artifacts is intrinsic to the Gibson–Bruck NRM (§12.5), whereas the ODE
branch carries a genuine numerical laxity controllable by odeRTol and odeATol.
Remark 12.6 (Para is base-portable). The Para construction applies over any symmetric
monoidal base category; varying the base gives different applications (Smooth for back-
propagation in machine learning, Hask here for executable simulation, BorelStoch for
fully probabilistic kernels). Capucci and Myers [320] show that all these incarnations are
instances of a single two-categorical pattern, so transferring techniques between them is
structural rather than ad hoc. The seed-marginalisation functor 𝐹above realises this bridge
from the Hask incarnation to a Markov-category target for our specific choice of uniform
seed distribution on 𝑊; other distributions would yield other functors with the same shape.
§12.3. L0 in Haskell: Multiset Species as free commutative monoid
Level L0 is the tower’s stoichiometric foundation. Its objects are elements of the free
commutative monoid N[S] on the finite species set S (Equation (1)); its morphisms
are stoichiometric changes (reaction vectors in ZS); its functorial invariants are the
combinatorial data (𝑛, ℓ, 𝑠) — the number of distinct complexes, the number of linkage
classes (connected components of the reaction graph), and the rank of the stoichiometric
matrix — and the deficiency 𝛿= 𝑛−ℓ−𝑠. Two L0 structural integrity tests — atom and
charge conservation — attach to every reaction and must pass before any L3 dynamics
are simulated. This section shows how the BR codebase realises each of these pieces
concretely.
12.3.1. The free commutative monoid in Haskell
The set N[S] of Equation (1) carries a commutative monoid structure under pointwise
addition with the universal property that any function 𝜑: S →𝑀to a commutative
monoid 𝑀extends uniquely to a homomorphism ¯𝜑: N[S] →𝑀. The BR implementation
realises both in a single newtype.
Proposition 12.7 (L0 implementation). The newtype Multiset Species of
BR.Multiset exactly implements N[S] as an object of L0:
(i) (Bijection.) The invariant that the underlying Map Species Int has no entries
with value ≤0, maintained by every smart constructor, puts Multiset Species
in bijection with N[S].
(ii) (Monoid.) munion is pointwise addition; empty is the identity.

A multiset 𝑟∈N[S] has only multiplicity data. Attaching it to a reaction 𝑟src →𝑟tgt as a
L0 morphism, two linear conditions on the reaction vector 𝑟tgt −𝑟src ∈ZS must hold for
the reaction to represent a physically meaningful elementary step: conservation of each
chemical element, and conservation of total formal charge.

(the 𝑎-coefficient of the species formula), and let 𝑞: S →Z be charge.

canonical monoid-homomorphism extensions to N[S] (Proposition 12.7(iii)) are denoted
¯𝜑𝑎: N[S] →N and ¯𝑞: N[S] →Z.

The deficiency 𝛿= 𝑛−ℓ−𝑠is entirely an L0 invariant: it is computed from the stoichiometric
matrix 𝝂∈ZS×R — the matrix of L0-morphism data — without reference to rate constants,
thermodynamics, or mechanism. Theorem 2.29 states the L0 consequence of 𝛿= 0;

Remark 12.9 (Cross-level structure of DZT). The hypotheses of Theorem 2.29 (weak
reversibility, 𝛿= 0) are pure L0 data; the conclusions become assertions about the mass-
action flow only once a rate functor FP is chosen, at which point the statement strengthens
to Theorem 5.26. This is the tower’s reading of the Feinberg programme: DZT and DOT
are L0 →L3 theorems whose content straddles the combinatorial and kinetic levels. A
fully categorical proof would make the straddling functorial; see §?? for the conjectured
homological route.
L0 data of the Briggs–Rauscher network
The De Kepper–Epstein implementation (BR.Mechanism.briggsRauscherDE,
§12.1) has |S| = 15 species and twelve reactions (the ten elementary steps R1–R10 plus
explicit reverses R3-rev, R4-rev). Hand enumeration of distinct source/target multisets
gives 𝑛= 20 complexes distributed over ℓ= 10 linkage classes (each elementary
forward/reverse pair occupies its own class, since no two elementary steps share a
source or target complex); the rank 𝑠of the stoichiometric matrix is computable
by Gaussian elimination but plays no role below. Running the L0 checks gives
atomConservation briggsRauscherDE == True (each of H, C, O, I, Mn
balanced in every reaction) and chargeConservation briggsRauscherDE
== True (net charge zero in every reaction), so the network is L0-integral in the
sense of Definition 12.8.
Why the deficiency theorems are silent on BR. Of the twelve reactions, only the two
pairs R3/R3-rev and R4/R4-rev carry explicit reverses; the remaining eight elementary
steps (R1, R2, R5–R10) are unidirectional in the implementation. The network is
therefore not weakly reversible, and the hypotheses of both Theorem 2.29 and the
Deficiency One Theorem fail regardless of the value of 𝛿. L0 alone cannot predict the
BR steady-state structure — and indeed, no steady state exists during the oscillatory
phase: the system is held far from equilibrium by the buffered substrate pool (IO−
3,
H2O2, MA, Mn2+) and cycles between Process A and Process B without converging.
This is the chapter’s first concrete demonstration that L0 data alone is insufficient: the
dynamical content lives strictly at L3 and requires the simulator built in subsequent
sections.

rxnProducts) and L3 kinetics (rxnRate, rxnRateActive, rxnSaturation),

Remark 12.10 (The Wegscheider residual is not a lax cell of Φop). The single lax cell 𝛾of
Φop (§12.2) measures the operational truncation error of the simulator. The Wegscheider
residual — the distance of a network’s rate constants from the equilibrium locus (39) —
is, by contrast, a property of which network the user constructs at L3, not a functorial
mismatch in Φop. Conflating the two would multiply the chapter’s laxity vocabulary
without corresponding functorial content. Wegscheider is a parameter constraint; 𝛾is a
truncation laxity.

§12.5. L3 in Hask: exact SSA and adaptive ODE as parallel operational realisations
The stochastic content of L3 is carried by a functor FP that sends each reaction network N
with rate constants to the 𝜏-indexed family of time-𝜏transition kernels of its continuous-time
Markov chain (CTMC) on population states. We write FP(N)𝜏∈BorelStoch for the
kernel at horizon 𝜏; it is this family that the operational arrows below realise. The BR
codebase implements two simulators in Hask: BR.SSA.simulate samples FP(N)𝜏
exactly (for 𝜏set as ssaTimeMax), and BR.ODE.simulate integrates the deterministic
large-volume shadow of FP.
• BR.SSA.simulate: an exact Gibson–Bruck next-reaction method (NRM) that
samples the CTMC at the molecule-count level.
Its denotational image, after
marginalising over the PRNG seed, is FP(N)𝜏exactly — modulo SplitMix PRNG
quality and floating-point precision; there is no step-budget or 𝜏-leap truncation.
• BR.ODE.simulate: an adaptive implicit-midpoint Newton integrator that pro-
duces the deterministic large-volume mass-action flow, the 𝑉→∞Kurtz limit of
the CTMC [106], with a local truncation error controlled by step-doubling.
Both arrows share their L0 + L3 input — a Network record (§12.4) plus an initial counts
or concentrations map — and both are purely functional: no IO, no global mutable state, no
impurity at the type level. The SSA threads its SplitMix64 PRNG through the ssaPRNG
field of SSAState; the ODE is deterministic and uses no PRNG. The 𝛾-cell of Φop
(§12.2) specialises here to zero in distribution for SSA and to the implicit-midpoint local
truncation error for ODE.

-- Equation eq:sim:propensity, plus rational saturation.
propensity :: Double →Reaction →(Species →Int) →Double
propensity volL rxn lookupCount =
let activeList
= MS.toList (rxnRateActive rxn)
totalOrder
= sum [m | (_, m) ←activeList]
volScaling
= if totalOrder ≤1
then 1
else (volL * avogadro) ** fromIntegral (1
- totalOrder)
hMu
= product
[ fallingFactorial (lookupCount s) m | (s, m) ←
activeList ]
unsaturated = rxnRate rxn * volScaling * hMu
nav
= avogadro
satDenom
= 1 + sum
[ cl * fromIntegral (lookupCount tl) / (volL * nav)
| (tl, cl) ←rxnSaturation rxn ]
in unsaturated / satDenom
where
fallingFactorial :: Int →Int →Double
fallingFactorial n k
| k ≤0
= 1
| n < k
= 0
| otherwise = product [fromIntegral (n - i) | i ←[0 ..
k - 1]]

Remark 12.13 (The 𝛾-cell of Φop, made concrete). The lax cell 𝛾of Φop (§12.2) is the
TV-metric laxity for the stochastic arrow and the state-space local truncation error for
the deterministic arrow. Theorem 12.12 states that for SSA the TV component of 𝛾
vanishes (up to qualifications (i)–(ii)): BR.SSA has no 𝜏-leap, no step-budget, and no
fixed-step-size approximation. The remaining content of 𝛾lives entirely on the ODE arrow:
the implicit-midpoint scheme with step-doubling control bounds the per-component local
truncation error in species 𝑠by odeATol + odeRTol · |𝑐𝑠| (BR.ODE uses a weighted
max-norm of these component errors as its step-control criterion), accumulated over the
trajectory; this is what Remark 12.15 below compares against the SSA’s exact samples.
Remark 12.14 (Pure-functional rather than Kleisli semantics). Most categorical-CRN
expositions treat the rate-equation ODE only (e.g. Baez–Pollard’s open dynamical systems
[31]); a Haskell-side stochastic treatment of the CME would naturally reach for a Kleisli
category of IO or a similar effect-type framework. The BR.SSA implementation chooses
neither: the PRNG state is a pure value in SSAState, and step and simulate are
total functions in Hask with no Kleisli or monadic structure visible at the type level. The
stochastic semantics enters only via the para-monoidal lift of §12.2, where the PRNG seed
becomes the parameter object 𝑊= {0, 1}64 and seed-marginalisation produces the Markov
kernel. This is operationally minimal: no IO taint propagates, replay is trivial (just store
the seed), and the type SSAState -> Maybe SSAState of step carries no effect
markers beyond the totality-signalling Maybe.

12.5.5. The two L3 arrows as parallel operational realisations
Remark 12.15 (SSA and ODE as parallel operational realisations of L3). BR.SSA.simulate
and BR.ODE.simulate are two Haskell functions running side-by-side over the same
L0+L3 input data — a Network record plus an initial counts or concentrations map —
though their precise source and target types differ (see the haskellbox signatures above;
the SSA takes one SSAState, the ODE takes a curried ODEConfig →ODEState
→Double). The SSA delivers a sampled trajectory of molecule counts, the ODE
delivers a deterministic trajectory of concentrations. Their denotational images differ: the
SSA’s (under the para-monoidal lift of §12.2) is FP(N)𝜏itself, by Theorem 12.12; the
ODE evaluates the deterministic large-volume shadow of FP, realised via the Kurtz limit
X/(𝑉𝑁𝐴) ⇝c. Both functions nonetheless read the rate constants, saturation data, and
stoichiometry from a single Network value without translation, and agree on observables
well-defined in the 𝑉→∞limit while disagreeing on finite-population fluctuations.

ssaVolumeL = 1e-15 (one femtolitre) is the default,

roughly ten orders of magnitude (R3 forward at 3.1×1012 down to R9 at 12.5
and R10 at 37, with R3-rev at 0.73 in different units). This forces BR.ODE
to use an implicit scheme: explicit Runge–Kutta would require step sizes too
small to integrate even one BR oscillation in reasonable wall-clock time. The
adaptive implicit-midpoint Newton method with step-doubling is the source of
the ODE component of 𝛾(Remark 12.13).

§12.6. The Para construction in Hask
The Para construction [277] formalises a morphism parameterised by an external object.
For BR, the parameter is the SplitMix64 seed ssaSeed ∈𝑊= {0, 1}64 that fixes
the SSA’s random trajectory, threaded purely through ssaPRNG (§12.5); for the ODE,
the parameter is empty. Para gives the categorical home for “a Haskell function plus
its stored parameter,” decoupling the parameter algebra (how seeds compose) from the
underlying-morphism algebra (how SSA and ODE trajectories compose). We give the
abstract definition, instantiate it over Hask, and verify the coherence laws — which here
separate cleanly into a strict underlying layer (function composition in Hask is on the nose)
and a bicategorical parameter-tensor layer (tuple-isomorphism coherence).
12.6.1. Abstract Para
Definition 12.16 (Para construction [277, Def. 3.1]). Let (C, ⊗, 𝐼) be a symmetric monoidal
category with a right actegory action M ↷C. The bicategory Para(C) has:
• Objects: those of C.
• 1-morphisms 𝐴→𝐵: pairs (𝑃, 𝑓) with 𝑃∈M a parameter object and 𝑓: 𝑃⊗𝐴→
𝐵a morphism of C.
• Composition: (𝑄, 𝑔) ◦(𝑃, 𝑓) = (𝑃⊗𝑄, 𝑔◦(id𝑄⊗𝑓)); parameter objects compose
by tensor.
• 2-morphisms (𝑃, 𝑓) ⇒(𝑄, 𝑔): reparameterisations 𝑟: 𝑃→𝑄in M such that
𝑔◦(𝑟⊗id𝐴) = 𝑓.
• Identity: (𝐼, 𝜂𝐴) with 𝜂𝐴: 𝐼⊗𝐴→𝐴the left unitor of the actegory.
The bicategorical coherence data (associator, left/right unitors for composition) are inherited
from (M, ⊗, 𝐼) and the actegory action.
For BR’s pure-functional simulation, we take both C and M to be Hask (the total fragment,
following Assumption 12.1 in §12.2), with Cartesian product as tensor and the actegory
action 𝑃⊗𝐴= (𝑃, 𝐴) (tuple type). A 1-morphism (𝑃, 𝑓) : 𝐴→𝐵then corresponds, by
currying, to a pair (a stored parameter value of type 𝑃, a pure Haskell function of type
𝑃→𝐴→𝐵). The distinction from the operationally-effectful target one might naturally
reach for in a Haskell-side stochastic treatment (Para over Kl(𝐼𝑂)) is exactly the distinction
articulated in Remark 12.14: BR.SSA carries its PRNG state as pure data, not as an IO
effect.

12.6.2. The Para wrapper at the type level
The Para shape is a wrapper around any pure Haskell function plus its stored parameter. The
BR codebase does not introduce a named ParaMorphism type — BR.SSA.simulate
and BR.ODE.simulate are written as plain Haskell functions — but each fits the Para
shape once we identify the parameter explicitly. For pedagogical clarity we display the
wrapper that makes the Para structure explicit:
The Para shape over Hask (categorical view; not a BR module)

--
pmParams stores the parameter value of type P;
--
pmApply
is the curried Haskell function f : P →A →B.

{ pmParams :: !p
, pmApply
:: !(p →a →b)
}
-- Sequential composition in Para(Hask):
--
(Q, g) o (P, f) = (P x Q, (p, q) a →g q (f p a)).
-- Parameter spaces compose by Cartesian product (= tensor in
Hask).
paraThen :: ParaMorphism p a b
→ParaMorphism q b c
→ParaMorphism (p, q) a c
paraThen f g = ParaMorphism
{ pmParams = (pmParams f, pmParams g)
, pmApply
= (p, q) a →pmApply g q (pmApply f p a)

-- Para identity: ((), 𝜆_ a →a), the trivial parameter space

Para 1-morphism.
liftToPara :: (a →b) →ParaMorphism () a b

-- Forget the parameter by evaluating at the stored value.
forgetParams :: ParaMorphism p a b →a →b
forgetParams pm = pmApply pm (pmParams pm)

Corollary 12.25 (Para applied to chemical reaction simulation). The construction above
exhibits the Para construction (Definition 12.16) applied to a chemical reaction simulation:

construction include machine learning [277, 322], compositional game theory [313], and
active inference [314]; to our knowledge no prior treatment applies it to chemical reaction
simulation.
§12.8. L4 →L3 projection: rate constants as scalar coarse-grainings and model
variants as comparable reductions
The most conceptually delicate aspect of the simulation functor of §12.7 is that L4
mechanism data appears inside the L3 parameter space. At first sight this violates the
tower’s level stratification — L4 bond-level information is supposed to be invisible at
L3. This section shows that the appearance is a parameter projection: the BR simulation
retains only the part of L4 data that survives as scalar rate constants and, for channels
with rate-limiting intermediates, the saturation form of the rate law. The chapter’s several
BR network variants are correspondingly different L3 reductions of the same underlying
mechanism, comparable in BorelStoch via the construction of §12.2.
12.8.1. The L4 content of BR’s rate constants
Level L4 is the category of open reaction networks with full bond-level mechanism
data: a morphism at L4 specifies the elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form and
break), the transition-state geometry, and the parameters determining kinetic isotope effects,
temperature dependence, and solvent dependence [158].
The BR mechanism in BR.Mechanism encodes the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton [35]
as briggsRauscherDE (10 elementary steps plus two explicit reverses; 12 channels).
Each channel is recorded as a Reaction value (§12.4) carrying three pieces of data
relevant to the L4 →L3 projection:
• rxnRate ::
Double — the scalar rate constant used by both BR.SSA and
BR.ODE.
• rxnSaturation ::
[(Species, Double)] — an optional rational de-

12.8.3. Model variants as comparable L3 reductions
BR.Mechanism provides several network variants beyond briggsRauscherDE:
bufferedH (with H+ pooled), broCODENetwork (the BROCODE 2025 reduction),
broCODE5VarNetwork (a five-dynamical-variable reduction designed for Hopf bi-
furcation analysis), and furrowLikePoolNetwork (a Furrow-style variant pooling
several intermediates). Each variant is obtained from briggsRauscherDE by some
combination of (i) restricting the channel set R, and (ii) enlarging netPoolSpecies
(the set of species held constant during simulation; ssaCounts for these species are
frozen, per the pool-species convention of §12.5).

via (47). The embedding is canonical in the sense that the same 𝐹◦Φop applies to all
variants; comparison of variants is therefore comparison of Markov kernels in a single
category, with metric choices (total variation, Wasserstein-1, relative entropy) available
once the variants are embedded in a common dynamical state space (extending each
variant’s kernel by Dirac mass on its pooled coordinates).

Embedding into a common state space (union of dynamical species sets) is by extension

L3 reductions: predicted invariance and drift
The categorical framework predicts which BR observables should be invariant under
which L3 reductions:
• Onset preservation.
Oscillation onset (the Hopf bifurcation) depends on
both the network’s L2 stoichiometric topology and the sign-pattern of L3
Jacobian eigenvalues at the fixed point. Reductions that preserve the auto-
catalytic feedback channels of the De Kepper–Epstein skeleton (in particular
broCODE5VarNetwork, designed for Hopf bifurcation analysis) preserve
the capacity for oscillation, even if the quantitative bifurcation point shifts.
• Quantitative drift. Oscillation period and amplitude are L3-quantitative: they

Remark 12.31 (What 𝜋4 cannot see, for BR). By construction 𝜋4 retains only the scalar
rate constant, saturation list, and provenance tag per channel. It drops:
(i) the full elementary-step mechanism (which bonds form and break in each channel;
concerted versus stepwise pathways; radical versus closed-shell intermediates);
(ii) kinetic isotope effects — the rate change under H →D substitution at the methylene
hydrogens of malonic acid (predicted by transition-state theory but invisible to a
scalar rxnRate);
(iii) solvent and ionic-strength dependence beyond the reference conditions absorbed into
rxnRate;
(iv) pressure dependence and any temperature dependence not captured by rxnRate at
the reference temperature.
Any two BR mechanisms agreeing on the dynamical pair (𝑟𝑥𝑛𝑅𝑎𝑡𝑒, 𝑟𝑥𝑛𝑆𝑎𝑡𝑢𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛) per
channel are indistinguishable in the simulation, whether or not their provenance tags agree
(Proposition 12.28; rxnProvenance is metadata, not consulted by the rate or update
logic). This is the L3 →L4 forcing pair of the main tower applied to inorganic oscillating
chemistry — an honest categorical consequence of 𝜋4’s range, not an implementation
deficit. Recovery of the dropped data requires either a higher-detail simulator operating
at L4 (mechanism-resolved) or experimental inputs (KIE measurement, pressure-jump
kinetics) whose results would re-parameterise the L3 scalar at the new reference conditions.
This closes the theoretical development of the chapter. The operational functor Φop (§12.7)
is parameterised by (46), with 𝜋4 projecting all L4 information through a three-component
coarse representation; BR’s network variants are different L3 realisations comparable as
Markov kernels via (47). The simulation results of §12.9 test these constructions against
the briggsRauscherDE network running under the conditions of [35].

The empirical question is not whether the framework runs — by construction Φop and 𝐹
apply to any well-formed Network — but whether its predictions acquire visible empirical
content. We verify three predictions of the preceding sections:
(P1) The oscillator emerges. Both simulators — the SSA sampling 𝐹BR and the ODE
realising its Kurtz limit — exhibit relaxation-oscillator dynamics. This is the base
case for §12.8’s onset-preservation framework: network reductions can subsequently
be compared to this base.
(P2) The 𝛾-cell distinction is operational. The SSA samples and the ODE trajectory agree
where the rate-equation representation is faithful (high-copy spike phase) and diverge
where it is not (low-copy quiescent phase at finite 𝑉), matching the form of 𝛾SSA = 0
in total variation and 𝛾ODE in state-space/Wasserstein-1 metric predicted in §12.2
and §12.5.
(P3) The divergence is structurally interpretable. Where the two simulators differ, the
framework supplies the reason: the ODE realises the 𝑉→∞Kurtz limit, and
at 𝑉= 10−15 L this limit represents quiescent populations of low-copy species as
fractional ensemble means that do not correspond to any state of an individual
realisation.

12.9.3. Stochastic view: SSA samples of the exact CTMC
The SSA realisations show the same qualitative oscillator structure as the ODE, with three
concrete and framework-predicted differences:
• Period shift. The SSA mean inter-spike interval (≈1050 s) is approximately 15%
shorter than the ODE’s (≈1250 s). In a given realisation, rate-limiting integer
transitions in the slow recharge phase can fire earlier than the deterministic species-
mean trajectory predicts, advancing spike onset. The direction is consistent with
𝛾ODE’s state-space-level deviation between the Kurtz limit and the exact CTMC at
low copy (§12.2, §12.5); the magnitude is a phase-statistic that requires 𝑁≫6
realisations for a quantitative kernel-level estimate.
• Spike-peak agreement. Peak molecule counts in the SSA, converted to concentration,
agree with ODE peak concentrations to within a factor of two across all six species

12.9.5. Closing
The simulation results do not validate the framework in any absolute sense: a frame-
work with no empirical content can pass unfalsified by any data.
What the figures
establish instead is that the framework’s predictions for BR are structurally distinguish-
able from the generic statement “the simulator produces some output”.
The kernel
𝐹BR := 𝐹(Φop(𝑏𝑟𝑖𝑔𝑔𝑠𝑅𝑎𝑢𝑠𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑟𝐷𝐸)) ∈BorelStoch is a specific mathematical object
computed via the construction of §§12.2–12.8; its SSA samples and its ODE Kurtz limit
are two operational evaluations of this object (the SSA samples 𝐹BR directly; the ODE
realises its species-mean Kurtz limit), and their visible structural difference at the chosen
volume is the chapter’s 𝛾-cell decomposition in concrete form.
The framework earns its keep here in three concrete ways:
(1) It predicts. The SSA samples and ODE Kurtz limit must differ in low-copy regions
of state space, with the form of the difference determined by which semantic layer
(exact CTMC vs. 𝑉→∞Kurtz limit) is being evaluated. The figures confirm this.
The prediction could have failed in several ways — the two simulators could have
agreed in the quiescent phase, the ODE could have failed to oscillate while the SSA
succeeded (or vice versa), the peak amplitudes could have differed by orders of
magnitude — and none did.
(2) It supplies vocabulary.
Every numerical claim in this section is locatable in
the chapter’s framework decomposition: 𝑉is a user-chosen simulation parameter
(separate from Θsim); Θsim contains the parameterisation and network variant; the
simulator type selects between the SSA and ODE morphisms in Para𝑊(Hask); the
kernel 𝐹BR is the derived BorelStoch-object; 𝛾ODE is the Kurtz-limit deviation;
the discrete quiescent-phase chatter is L3-stochastic truth that the framework’s
L3-deterministic representation cannot capture at finite 𝑉. This decomposition is
tacit in standard simulation practice; the framework makes it explicit.
(3) It equips. Proposition 12.30 embeds every BR variant into BorelStoch via the same
𝐹◦Φop; comparison is then comparison of Markov kernels in a single category,
with metric choices (TV, Wasserstein-1, relative entropy) available. The variant
comparisons, KIE prediction, and volume sweep listed above are the natural next
steps; the machinery to perform them is in place.
The classical chemical phenomena of the Briggs–Rauscher oscillator — period, amplitude,
autocatalytic feedback, the distinction between the spike and quiescent phases — emerge
through this framework. What the framework adds is the discipline of distinguishing three
categories. Essential features — such as the oscillation onset itself — are tied to the L2
stoichiometric feedback topology and the L3 Jacobian sign-pattern; they survive across both
simulators and would survive across network variants retaining the autocatalytic skeleton.
Tunable features — the oscillation period (∼103 s at the chosen parameterisation) and spike
amplitudes — are physical functionals of the L3 rate constants and the 𝜋4-coarse L4 data

of §12.8; re-parameterising to classical batch BR conditions would shift them continuously
to the experimental 30–60 s regime. Scale-dependent representational artifacts — the
smooth ODE quiescent floors at ∼10−13 M for MnOH2+, and the ∼15% SSA-vs-ODE
period shift — are not chemistry but artifacts of evaluating an essentially-discrete process
through its continuous Kurtz limit. The floor values are valid ensemble means at all 𝑉
but acquire physical referents (as occupied discrete states) only at sufficiently large 𝑉; at
𝑉= 10−15 L they correspond to sub-unity counts that no individual realisation can occupy.
The 15% drift, distinct in V-dependence, is a 𝛾ODE residual that vanishes as 𝑉→∞by the
Kurtz theorem [106]. Both manifest at 𝑉= 10−15 L because the volume is too small for
the continuous limit to be faithful to individual discrete trajectories.
This tripartite separation is tacit in standard simulation practice; the framework makes it
explicit. Simulator outputs then become inputs to inference about chemistry — the essential-
versus-tunable boundary is what falsification tests should target; the scale-dependent
representational artifacts are what should be disregarded — rather than illustrations of
dynamics in which all three categories are silently conflated.

Three rules from undergraduate chemistry became provable theorems within the tower.
Hess’s Law is the functoriality of 𝐹𝐻: L0(𝑃) →(R, +): the equality 𝐹𝐻(𝑟2 ◦𝑟1) =
𝐹𝐻(𝑟2)+𝐹𝐻(𝑟1) is the monoidal-functor condition, not an empirical observation (Chapter 3).
Walden inversion is the statement that the permutation 𝜋𝜒∈Aut(L4(𝑃)) exchanging the
(𝑅)- and (𝑆)-enantiomers has no preimage in Aut(L4.5(𝑃)) under 𝜑4.5: the chirality-
flipping generator 𝐸∗∈𝐺∗(𝐺) = Aut(𝐺) ⋊Z𝑘
2 separates the enantiomers as objects of
L4.5 (Theorem 7.27). The Longuet–Higgins sign change is the non-vanishing of the first
Stiefel–Whitney class 𝑤1(𝐿𝑅0) ∈𝐻1(C𝑒(𝐺) \ ΣCI, Z/2) of the real ground-state eigenline
on loops linking the codimension-2 conical-intersection seam (§9.3); the complex Chern
class 𝑐1(𝐿0) ∈𝐻2 is the codimension-matched companion.
The forcing argument is structural. At each level, the unique minimal categorical extension
with non-trivial coker(𝜑𝑘) for the relevant reaction pair produces, as a theorem, what was
previously only a rule. The rules did not become theorems because the mathematics was
sharpened. They became theorems because the level was made explicit.
§13.2. A taxonomy of extension types
The nine constructions L0, L1, . . . , L7 are not nine independent acts of imagination. With
the full tower in view, they fall into seven types, distinguished by the kind of categorical
operation each performs; this classification could not be stated before all levels were
available.
The seven extension types
I (Free construction). L0 is the free symmetric monoidal category on the Petri net
of a reaction system (Meseguer–Montanari). Every subsequent level is an extension
of this base.
II (Functor decoration). L1, L2, L3 each add a monoidal functor on L0(𝑃) without
changing its objects or morphism type: 𝐹𝐻, 𝐹𝑆and the Gibbs functor 𝐹𝑇
𝐺, and the
kinetic functor 𝐹𝑃: L3 →Stoch respectively.

§13.3. Open constructions
Five constructions raised in the body remain open; each has a precise statement, identified
ingredients, and known obstructions.
C1: The continuous field for molecules. Construct {𝐴𝜀}𝜀∈[0,1] with 𝐴0 = 𝐶0(C𝑒(𝐺))

single 𝐶∗-algebraic framework for molecules.

Proximity to resolution
O1 and O2 are within reach with currently available tools: ingredients in place,
construction pending. C2 needs a single synthesis step. C3 requires a new technical
ingredient — the seam blow-up — but the surrounding framework is clear. C1 is the
deepest: it requires C2, C3, and a resolution of the Coulomb singularity problem, and
is the correct formulation of what it would mean to complete the L6 99K L7 step.
§13.4. Outlook
The tower has implications for three communities not previously in close contact.
For chemical reaction network theory. The Feinberg deficiency theory and the Craciun–
Yu and Anderson–Shiu multistationarity results sit entirely within L0 (combinatorial
hypotheses) and L3 (dynamical conclusions). The tower makes this level gap explicit for
the first time and suggests, via O1, a homological proof of the Deficiency Zero Theorem that
would place these landmark results inside a categorical framework rather than leaving them
as isolated facts. The open mechanistic network construction O2 extends Baez–Pollard
grey-boxing from L3 to L4, giving an algebraic foundation for compositional analysis of
reaction mechanisms.
For machine learning in chemistry. The Para dimension answers a question that becomes
urgent as ML models for chemistry scale: what does it mean for a model to be physically
correct at a given level? The answer is architectural: a model is physically correct at
L𝑘if and only if the level-𝑘exact functor factors through it. The equivariance groups
grow monotonically through the tower: Sym(S) at L0, Aut(𝐺) at L4, 𝐺∗(𝐺) at L4.5,
SE(3)⋊Aut𝜇(𝐺) at L5, and the 𝑈(𝑁) structure of the active Hilbert bundle at L6. A model
whose architecture respects only the L5 group cannot represent L6 phenomena: there is no
slot for the line-bundle holonomy that distinguishes adiabatic from non-adiabatic dynamics
— this is the architectural barrier currently separating photocatalysis and conical-intersection
chemistry from the mainstream ML-for-chemistry stack. Chapter 12 supplies one concrete
executable instance: the simulation functor Φop : Para(L0 ⊗L1 ⊗L2 ⊗L3) →Kl(𝐼𝑂)
composed with the denotational realisation 𝐹into the Markov category BorelStoch
(Fritz [103]), applied to the Briggs–Rauscher oscillator with the 𝜑-cell distinction between
exact CTMC and Kurtz-limit ODE made operational (§12.9).
For mathematical chemistry and mathematical physics. The constructions C1–C3 would
collectively provide the first rigorous categorical treatment of the Born–Oppenheimer
approximation as a limit rather than an ansatz.
The Landsman–Rieffel–Georgescu–
Hagedorn–PST literature has reached a point where all ingredients are available; the
obstacle is synthesis rather than any single missing result. O1, conversely, would connect
classical CRNT to homological algebra in a way that has been suspected since Feinberg’s
earliest papers but never made precise.
§13.5. Coda
A hydrogen atom transfers from carbon to oxygen in an enzyme active site. Whether that
transfer is governed by classical barrier-crossing or by quantum tunnelling depends on
429


## Page 430


Kyunghoon Han
Categorification of Chemical Reactions
which level of the tower the question is posed at. The enzyme does not know which level
the chemist is using. It operates at all of them simultaneously.
The tower does not add new chemistry. Hess’s Law was not more true after 𝐹𝐻was
defined. Walden inversion was not more real after the cokernel argument identified it as a
non-trivial automorphism class. The retinal photoisomerisation was not faster because the
Stiefel–Whitney class was computed around the conical-intersection seam. What the tower
adds is precision: each chemical fact is now located at the unique level where it can be
expressed, and the tools available at that level are exactly those needed to prove it.
Chemistry’s rules are not wrong. Their exceptions are not failures. They are coordinates.
The tower is the coordinate system.
The central result of this monograph is negative in form but positive in content. Negative:
no single category suffices to express all of chemistry. Positive: the minimal number of
categories needed, their order, and the unique forcing pair that makes each one necessary —
this is determined, not chosen.
The map is forced.
